The system uses explicit spatial temporal representations through de(cid:173) lay lines. SYREN uses implicit parametric temporal representa(cid:173) tions in formant transition classification through node activation onset, decay, and transition delays in sub-networks analogous to visual motion detector cells. SYREN recognizes 79% of six repe(cid:173) titions of 24 consonant-vowel syllables when tested on unseen data, and recognizes 100% of its training syllables.

SYREN uses implicit parametric temporal representa(cid:173) tions in formant transition classification through node activation onset, decay, and transition delays in sub-networks analogous to visual motion detector cells. paragraphs: SYREN recognizes syllables by using changes in a speech signal over time. It classifies how quickly formant centers move and in which direction, then adaptively associates these transition events with syllables. The approach treats the movement of speech features as information for recognition, making temporal structure central to the classification task.

The system represents time in two ways. Delay lines make timing explicit by arranging delayed information spatially within the network. Other timing information is implicit in when units activate, how their activity decays, and the delays between transitions. The formant-classification subnetworks using these dynamics are described as analogous to visual motion detectors.

SYREN recognizes all of its training syllables and achieves 79 percent recognition on unseen data in a test involving six repetitions of 24 consonant-vowel syllables. The difference between training and unseen performance shows the distinction between fitting learned examples and recognizing new ones. The contribution combines explicit delays with internal activation dynamics to use speech transitions for syllable recognition.
summary.tldr: SYREN combines delay lines and timed neural activity to recognize syllables from formant transitions, achieving 79 percent recognition on unseen data.

title: Temporal Representations in a Connectionist Speech System

abstract: This work extends computational learning theory to situations in which concepts vary over time, e.g., system identification of a time-varying plant. We have extended formal definitions of concepts and learning to provide a framework in which an algorithm can track a concept as it evolves over time. Given this framework and focusing on memory-based algorithms, we have derived some PAC-style sample complexity results that determine, for example, when tracking is feasible. We have also used a similar framework and focused on incremental tracking algorithms for which we have derived some bounds on the mistake or error rates for some specific concept classes.

Given this framework and focusing on memory-based algorithms, we have derived some PAC-style sample complexity results that determine, for example, when tracking is feasible. paragraphs: The paper extends computational learning theory to targets that change over time. A motivating example is identifying the behavior of a time-varying plant, or controlled system. The learning objective is ongoing tracking: an algorithm must continue following the concept as it evolves, so the formal definition of successful learning must account for that evolution.

The authors revise definitions of concepts and learning to support this setting. For memory-based algorithms, they derive sample-complexity results in the probably approximately correct, or PAC, style. These results concern the amount of evidence needed for learning guarantees and help identify circumstances in which tracking is feasible.

They also use a similar framework to study incremental tracking algorithms, deriving mistake or error-rate bounds for specific concept classes. The two analyses address complementary questions: what information makes tracking possible, and how many errors a tracking procedure may incur. The contribution is a theoretical framework for reasoning about adaptation when the target itself changes, with guarantees tied to the classes and algorithms analyzed.
summary.tldr: The paper formalizes learning changing concepts and derives sample requirements and error bounds for tracking them.

title: Learning Time-varying Concepts
Neural Network Methods for Optimization Problems

abstract: A biological neuron can be viewed as a device that maps a multidimen(cid:173) sional temporal event signal (dendritic postsynaptic activations) into a unidimensional temporal event signal (action potentials). We have designed a network, the Spatio-Temporal Event Mapping (STEM) architecture, which can learn to perform this mapping for arbitrary bio(cid:173) physical models of neurons. Such a network appropriately trained, called a STEM cell, can be used in place of a conventional compartmen(cid:173) tal model in simulations where only the transfer function is important, such as network simulations. The STEM cell offers advantages over compartmental models in terms of computational efficiency, analytical tractabili1ty, and as a framework for VLSI implementations of biologi(cid:173) cal neurons.

paragraphs: The paper represents a biological neuron through its transformation of incoming events into outgoing spikes. Inputs arrive as time-varying postsynaptic activations across the dendrites, while the output is a single sequence of action potentials. The authors design the Spatio-Temporal Event Mapping architecture, or STEM, to learn this relationship from biophysical neuron models.

A trained network, called a STEM cell, can replace a conventional compartmental model when the simulation only needs the neuron’s input-output behavior. This is the stated condition for substitution. The learned model preserves the relevant mapping for that purpose without requiring the simulation to use the original compartmental representation.

The authors identify advantages in computational efficiency, ease of mathematical analysis, and suitability as a framework for VLSI implementations. Network simulations are a motivating application because they can depend on how neurons respond to one another’s signals. The contribution is a trainable temporal abstraction of a neuron, with its usefulness tied explicitly to simulations where the transfer function is what matters.
summary.tldr: STEM learns a neuron’s temporal input-output mapping as an efficient substitute when simulations require only its transfer function.

title: Model of a Biological Neuron as a Temporal Neural Network

abstract: Images are ambiguous at each of many levels of a contextual hierarchy. Nevertheless, the high-level interpretation of most scenes is unambiguous, as evidenced by the superior performance of humans. This observation argues for global vision models, such as deformable templates. Unfortunately, such models are computationally intractable for unconstrained problems. We propose a compositional model in which primitives are recursively composed, subject to syntactic restrictions, to form tree-structured objects and object groupings. Ambiguity is propagated up the hierarchy in the form of multiple interpretations, which are later resolved by a Bayesian, equivalently minimum-description-Iength, cost functional.

Nevertheless, the high-level interpretation of most scenes is unambiguous, as evidenced by the superior performance of humans. This observation argues for global vision models, such as deformable templates. Unfortunately, such models are computationally intractable for unconstrained problems. We propose a compositional model in which primitives are recursively composed, subject to syntactic restrictions, to form tree-structured objects and object groupings. Ambiguity is propagated up the hierarchy in the form of multiple interpretations, which are later resolved by a Bayesian, equivalently minimum-description-Iength, cost functional.

paragraphs: An image can support several interpretations at the level of individual parts, even when its overall scene is readily understood. This paper treats that relationship between local ambiguity and global context as a central recognition problem. Global models can capture context, but the authors identify computational intractability as an obstacle for unconstrained recognition.

Their proposed alternative builds objects compositionally. Primitive elements are recursively combined under syntactic restrictions, producing tree-structured representations of objects and object groupings. The restrictions govern which combinations are permitted. This gives the model a structured way to connect small visual elements with larger interpretations at successive levels of a hierarchy.

The model carries multiple candidate interpretations upward instead of committing immediately to one local explanation. A Bayesian cost, equivalently expressed through minimum description length, later resolves those alternatives. In plain terms, the system judges competing explanations using a shared probabilistic or description-length criterion once broader context is available. The contribution is an architecture for preserving useful ambiguity while organizing the construction and evaluation of whole-object interpretations.
summary.tldr: A compositional vision model carries multiple interpretations through a hierarchy and resolves them with a Bayesian minimum-description-length criterion.

title: Compositionality, MDL Priors, and Object Recognition

abstract: The W-S (Wake-Sleep) algorithm is a simple learning rule for the models with hidden variables. It is shown that this algorithm can be applied to a factor analysis model which is a linear version of the Helmholtz ma(cid:173) chine. But even for a factor analysis model, the general convergence is not proved theoretically. In this article, we describe the geometrical un(cid:173) derstanding of the W-S algorithm in contrast with the EM (Expectation(cid:173) Maximization) algorithm and the em algorithm. As the result, we prove the convergence of the W-S algorithm for the factor analysis model. We also show the condition for the convergence in general models.

It is shown that this algorithm can be applied to a factor analysis model which is a linear version of the Helmholtz ma(cid:173) chine. But even for a factor analysis model, the general convergence is not proved theoretically. In this article, we describe the geometrical un(cid:173) derstanding of the W-S algorithm in contrast with the EM (Expectation(cid:173) Maximization) algorithm and the em algorithm. As the result, we prove the convergence of the W-S algorithm for the factor analysis model. We also show the condition for the convergence in general models.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether the wake-sleep learning algorithm converges when used to train models with hidden variables. The algorithm is simple and can be applied to factor analysis, described here as a linear version of a Helmholtz machine. Yet its convergence had not been theoretically established even for that setting.

The authors develop a geometric interpretation of wake-sleep and compare it with the EM algorithm and the separately named em algorithm. This perspective provides a way to examine the behavior of the learning procedure and relate it to other methods for fitting models with hidden variables.

Using that analysis, they prove convergence for the factor-analysis model. They also give a condition for convergence in more general models. The distinction matters: the factor-analysis result is a convergence proof for a specific model, while the broader result identifies a condition under which convergence follows. The paper therefore adds theoretical support to a learning rule whose simplicity alone does not establish its behavior.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis proves wake-sleep convergence for factor analysis and identifies a convergence condition for broader models.

title: Convergence of the Wake-Sleep Algorithm

abstract: We propose a novel clustering method that is an extension of ideas inher- ent to scale-space clustering and support-vector clustering. Like the lat- ter, it associates every data point with a vector in Hilbert space, and like the former it puts emphasis on their total sum, that is equal to the scale- space probability function. The novelty of our approach is the study of an operator in Hilbert space, represented by the Schr¨odinger equation of which the probability function is a solution. This Schr¨odinger equation contains a potential function that can be derived analytically from the probability function. We associate minima of the potential with cluster centers. The method has one variable parameter, the scale of its Gaussian kernel. We demonstrate its applicability on known data sets. By limiting the evaluation of the Schr¨odinger potential to the locations of data points, we can apply this method to problems in high dimensions.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a clustering method connecting scale-space and support-vector clustering ideas. Each data point is associated with a vector in Hilbert space, and the method emphasizes the sum of those vectors. That sum corresponds to the scale-space probability function, providing a shared representation from which the clustering construction begins.

The new step is to study an operator expressed through a Schrödinger equation for which that probability function is a solution. The authors derive the equation's potential function analytically from the probability function and identify potential minima with cluster centers. Thus, the grouping structure is read from a derived potential rather than solely from the original probability representation.

The method has one adjustable parameter, the scale of its Gaussian kernel, and is demonstrated on known datasets. To handle high-dimensional problems, the authors restrict potential evaluation to the observed data locations. This gives a way to apply the construction without evaluating the potential throughout the surrounding high-dimensional space.
summary.tldr: Quantum clustering identifies cluster centers as minima of a Schrödinger potential derived from a Gaussian-kernel probability representation.

title: The Method of Quantum Clustering

abstract: In classical large information retrieval systems, the system responds to a user initiated query with a list of results ranked by relevance. The users may further refine their query as needed. This process may result in a lengthy correspondence without conclusion. We propose an alternative active learning approach, where the sys(cid:173) tem responds to the initial user's query by successively probing the user for distinctions at multiple levels of abstraction. The system's initiated queries are optimized for speedy recovery and the user is permitted to respond with multiple selections or may reject the query. The information is in each case unambiguously incorporated by the system and the subsequent queries are adjusted to minimize the need for further exchange. The system's initiated queries are subject to resource constraints pertaining to the amount of infor(cid:173) mation that can be presented to the user per iteration.

We propose an alternative active learning approach, where the sys(cid:173) tem responds to the initial user's query by successively probing the user for distinctions at multiple levels of abstraction. The system's initiated queries are optimized for speedy recovery and the user is permitted to respond with multiple selections or may reject the query. paragraphs: The paper addresses a difficulty in information retrieval: a ranked list of results may leave the user repeatedly reformulating a query without reaching a satisfactory conclusion. It proposes an active learning approach in which the system takes responsibility for asking follow-up questions after the user's initial request. The interaction becomes a sequence of system-selected distinctions intended to clarify what the user wants.

These questions can operate at several levels of abstraction, allowing the search to be refined through different kinds of distinctions. Users may select multiple responses or reject a question. The method incorporates each of these responses unambiguously and adjusts its subsequent questions, so the conversation can use information beyond a single accepted choice.

Question selection is optimized to recover the desired information quickly and reduce further exchanges. It must also respect a resource constraint on how much information can be shown in each iteration. The approach therefore treats interaction design as part of retrieval itself: the system chooses what to ask while accounting for the limited amount it can present at once.
summary.tldr: An active retrieval system asks adaptive clarification questions designed to find desired information with fewer exchanges.

title: Active Information Retrieval

abstract: A new approach to inference in belief networks has been recently proposed, which is based on an algebraic representation of belief networks using multi{linear functions. According to this approach, the key computational question is that of representing multi{linear functions compactly, since inference reduces to a simple process of ev aluating and diﬁerentiating such functions. W e show here that mainstream inference algorithms based on jointrees are a special case of this approach in a v ery precise sense. W e use this result to prov e new properties of jointree algorithms, and then discuss some of its practical and theoretical implications.

paragraphs: The paper connects jointree inference in belief networks with an algebraic approach based on multilinear functions. In that algebraic view, inference is performed by evaluating and differentiating a function representing the network. The main computational challenge becomes finding a compact representation of that function, making representation size central to the usefulness of the approach.

The authors show that mainstream jointree algorithms are special cases of this algebraic framework in a precise sense. This establishes a formal relationship between familiar inference procedures and operations on multilinear functions. It gives jointree calculations an interpretation through evaluation and differentiation, placing those algorithms within a broader account of probabilistic computation.

The paper uses this relationship to prove new properties of jointree algorithms and discusses practical and theoretical implications. Its stated contribution is the correspondence and the results derived from it. By connecting the two views, it makes the algebraic formulation relevant to understanding established inference methods, rather than leaving it as a separate way to describe belief networks.
summary.tldr: The paper shows that jointree inference is a special case of evaluating and differentiating multilinear functions, enabling new theoretical results.

title: A Differential Semantics for Jointree Algorithms

abstract: We show that temporal logic and combinations of temporal logics and modal logics of knowledge can be effectively represented in ar(cid:173) tificial neural networks. We present a Translation Algorithm from temporal rules to neural networks, and show that the networks compute a fixed-point semantics of the rules. We also apply the translation to the muddy children puzzle, which has been used as a testbed for distributed multi-agent systems. We provide a complete solution to the puzzle with the use of simple neural networks, capa(cid:173) ble of reasoning about time and of knowledge acquisition through inductive learning.

We also apply the translation to the muddy children puzzle, which has been used as a testbed for distributed multi-agent systems. We provide a complete solution to the puzzle with the use of simple neural networks, capa(cid:173) ble of reasoning about time and of knowledge acquisition through inductive learning.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how neural networks can represent logical reasoning about time and knowledge. Temporal logic expresses relationships involving time, while modal logics of knowledge represent what agents know. The authors show that temporal logic and combinations of these two kinds of logic can be represented effectively within artificial neural networks.

Their main construction is an algorithm that translates temporal rules into networks. They show that the resulting networks compute a fixed-point semantics for those rules: the network computation corresponds to a stable interpretation of the logical system. This provides a formal connection between the rules being represented and the computation performed by the neural implementation.

The translation is applied to the muddy children puzzle, a test problem for distributed multi-agent systems. Simple neural networks provide a complete solution while supporting temporal reasoning and knowledge acquisition through inductive learning. The contribution combines a translation procedure, a semantics result, and an application showing how logical reasoning and learning can coexist in the proposed neural systems.
summary.tldr: A translation from temporal rules to neural networks preserves fixed-point semantics and supports a complete solution to the muddy children puzzle.

title: Reasoning about Time and Knowledge in Neural Symbolic Learning Systems

abstract: We present an improvement to the DP-SLAM algorithm for simultane- ous localization and mapping (SLAM) that maintains multiple hypothe- ses about densely populated maps (one full map per particle in a par- ticle ﬁlter) in time that is linear in all signiﬁcant algorithm parameters and takes constant (amortized) time per iteration. This means that the asymptotic complexity of the algorithm is no greater than that of a pure localization algorithm using a single map and the same number of parti- cles. We also present a hierarchical extension of DP-SLAM that uses a two level particle ﬁlter which models drift in the particle ﬁltering process itself. The hierarchical approach enables recovery from the inevitable drift that results from using a ﬁnite number of particles in a particle ﬁlter and permits the use of DP-SLAM in more challenging domains, while maintaining linear time asymptotic complexity.

This means that the asymptotic complexity of the algorithm is no greater than that of a pure localization algorithm using a single map and the same number of parti- cles. We also present a hierarchical extension of DP-SLAM that uses a two level particle ﬁlter which models drift in the particle ﬁltering process itself. The hierarchical approach enables recovery from the inevitable drift that results from using a ﬁnite number of particles in a particle ﬁlter and permits the use of DP-SLAM in more challenging domains, while maintaining linear time asymptotic complexity.

paragraphs: The paper improves DP-SLAM, an algorithm that estimates location while constructing a map. It maintains multiple hypotheses about densely populated maps, with a full map associated with each particle in a particle filter. The computational question is how to preserve this collection of map hypotheses without making its asymptotic cost exceed that of localization alone.

The improved algorithm has linear dependence on all significant algorithm parameters and constant amortized time per iteration. Amortized describes cost averaged across iterations. The stated asymptotic complexity is no greater than that of a localization algorithm using one map and the same number of particles, providing a specific computational comparison.

The authors also introduce a hierarchical extension with a two-level particle filter. It models drift arising within the particle filtering process itself, allowing recovery from drift caused by using finitely many particles. This permits application in more challenging domains while retaining linear asymptotic complexity. The two contributions address both the cost of maintaining map alternatives and the accumulation of filtering error.
summary.tldr: Improved DP-SLAM maintains dense map hypotheses efficiently, while a hierarchical particle filter enables recovery from finite-particle drift.

title: Hierarchical Linear/Constant Time SLAM Using Particle Filters for Dense Maps

abstract: We measure the ability of human observers to predict the next datum in a sequence that is generated by a simple statistical process undergoing change at random points in time. Accurate performance in this task requires the identification of changepoints. We assess individual differences between observers both empirically, and using two kinds of models: a Bayesian approach for change detection and a family of cognitively plausible fast and frugal models. Some individuals detect too many changes and hence perform sub-optimally due to excess variability. Other individuals do not detect enough changes, and perform sub-optimally because they fail to notice short-term temporal trends.

Accurate performance in this task requires the identification of changepoints. We assess individual differences between observers both empirically, and using two kinds of models: a Bayesian approach for change detection and a family of cognitively plausible fast and frugal models. Some individuals detect too many changes and hence perform sub-optimally due to excess variability. Other individuals do not detect enough changes, and perform sub-optimally because they fail to notice short-term temporal trends.

paragraphs: Predicting a changing sequence requires deciding when recent observations indicate a new regime rather than ordinary noise. This paper measures how people make that distinction in a simple statistical process with randomly occurring change points. Individual differences are assessed through both behavioral data and computational models.

The models include Bayesian change detection and cognitively plausible fast-and-frugal alternatives. They provide ways to characterize whether an observer responds too readily or too slowly to possible changes. Prediction quality therefore reflects both estimating the current process and deciding how much earlier evidence still applies.

Some observers infer too many changes and become excessively variable; others infer too few and miss short-term trends. The contribution explains contrasting errors through a shared adaptation problem. Good prediction requires a balance between stability and responsiveness, and the study shows that people can depart from that balance in opposite, behaviorally measurable ways.
summary.tldr: Human sequence-prediction errors reflect opposite change-detection biases: overreacting to noise or failing to notice genuine short-term shifts.

title: Prediction and Change Detection

abstract: Data sets involving multiple groups with shared characteristics frequently arise in practice. In this paper we extend hierarchical Dirichlet processes to model such data. Each group is assumed to be generated from a template mixture model with group level variability in both the mixing proportions and the component parameters. Variabilities in mixing proportions across groups are handled using hierarchical Dirichlet processes, also allowing for automatic determination of the number of components. In addition, each group is allowed to have its own compo- nent parameters coming from a prior described by a template mixture model. This group-level variability in the component parameters is handled using a random effects model. We present a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algo- rithm to estimate model parameters and demonstrate the method by applying it to the problem of modeling spatial brain activation patterns across multiple images collected via functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

Each group is assumed to be generated from a template mixture model with group level variability in both the mixing proportions and the component parameters. Variabilities in mixing proportions across groups are handled using hierarchical Dirichlet processes, also allowing for automatic determination of the number of components. In addition, each group is allowed to have its own compo- nent parameters coming from a prior described by a template mixture model. This group-level variability in the component parameters is handled using a random effects model. We present a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling algo- rithm to estimate model parameters and demonstrate the method by applying it to the problem of modeling spatial brain activation patterns across multiple images collected via functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI).

paragraphs: Grouped datasets often contain common patterns alongside differences between groups. This paper models that combination by extending hierarchical Dirichlet processes. It assumes that each group arises from a shared template mixture, while allowing both the proportions of its components and the parameters describing those components to vary across groups.

The hierarchical Dirichlet process handles differences in mixing proportions and allows the number of components to be determined automatically. A random effects model handles a second kind of variation: each group can have its own component parameters drawn from a prior specified through the template mixture. Thus, shared structure does not require every group to use identical component descriptions.

The authors present an MCMC sampling algorithm for estimating the model's parameters. They demonstrate the approach on spatial brain activation patterns across multiple fMRI images. The application illustrates the purpose of the extension: representing common mixture structure while accommodating group-specific differences in both the prevalence and the characteristics of its components.
summary.tldr: Adding random effects to hierarchical Dirichlet processes lets groups share mixture structure while varying both component proportions and component parameters.

title: Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes with Random Effects

abstract: We propose a probabilistic topic model for analyzing and extracting content-related annotations from noisy annotated discrete data such as web pages stored in social bookmarking services. In these services, since users can attach annotations freely, some annotations do not describe the semantics of the content, thus they are noisy, i.e. not content-related. The extraction of content-related annotations can be used as a preprocessing step in machine learning tasks such as text classification and image recognition, or can improve information retrieval performance. The proposed model is a generative model for content and annotations, in which the annotations are assumed to originate either from topics that generated the content or from a general distribution unrelated to the content. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method by using synthetic data and real social annotation data for text and images.

The extraction of content-related annotations can be used as a preprocessing step in machine learning tasks such as text classification and image recognition, or can improve information retrieval performance. paragraphs: Freely supplied annotations do not always describe the content they accompany. In social bookmarking and similar settings, this creates noise when annotations are used to learn about documents or images. This paper proposes a probabilistic topic model that separates content-related annotations from annotations unrelated to the content's meaning.

The model jointly generates content and annotations. It assumes that an annotation comes either from the topics responsible for the content or from a general distribution independent of that content. These two possible origins give the model an explicit way to represent the difference between semantically relevant annotations and background annotation noise.

The authors demonstrate the method using synthetic data and real social annotations for text and images. Extracted content-related annotations could serve as preprocessing for tasks such as text classification and image recognition, or help information retrieval. The contribution is a probabilistic treatment of relevance within the annotation model itself, with experiments supporting its effectiveness on the supplied types of annotation data.
summary.tldr: A topic model separates content-related annotations from background noise by modeling two possible sources for each annotation.

title: Modeling Social Annotation Data with Content Relevance using a Topic Model

abstract: We consider the minimization of a convex objective function defined on a Hilbert space, which is only available through unbiased estimates of its gradients. This problem includes standard machine learning algorithms such as kernel logistic regression and least-squares regression, and is commonly referred to as a stochastic approximation problem in the operations research community. We provide a non-asymptotic analysis of the convergence of two well-known algorithms, stochastic gradient descent (a.k.a.~Robbins-Monro algorithm) as well as a simple modification where iterates are averaged (a.k.a.~Polyak-Ruppert averaging). Our analysis suggests that a learning rate proportional to the inverse of the number of iterations, while leading to the optimal convergence rate in the strongly convex case, is not robust to the lack of strong convexity or the setting of the proportionality constant. This situation is remedied when using slower decays together with averaging, robustly leading to the optimal rate of convergence. We illustrate our theoretical results with simulations on synthetic and standard datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies minimizing a convex objective when only unbiased estimates of its gradients are available. The objective is defined on a Hilbert space, a setting that includes kernel logistic regression and least-squares regression. The authors analyze stochastic gradient descent and a modification that averages the successive iterates.

Their analysis is non-asymptotic, describing convergence after a finite number of iterations. It suggests that a learning rate decreasing inversely with the iteration count can achieve the optimal convergence rate under strong convexity. However, that choice is sensitive to both the absence of strong convexity and the constant that scales the learning rate.

The proposed remedy is to combine a more slowly decreasing learning rate with averaging. The analysis finds that this combination robustly reaches the optimal convergence rate in the setting studied. Simulations on synthetic and standard datasets illustrate the theoretical results. The practical message is that learning-rate decay and averaging should be considered together, because their combination affects both convergence and sensitivity to tuning.
summary.tldr: Finite-iteration analysis supports slower learning-rate decay with iterate averaging as a robust route to optimal stochastic-optimization convergence.

title: Non-Asymptotic Analysis of Stochastic Approximation Algorithms for Machine Learning

abstract: In modeling multivariate time series, it is important to allow time-varying smoothness in the mean and covariance process. In particular, there may be certain time intervals exhibiting rapid changes and others in which changes are slow. If such locally adaptive smoothness is not accounted for, one can obtain misleading inferences and predictions, with over-smoothing across erratic time intervals and under-smoothing across times exhibiting slow variation. This can lead to miscalibration of predictive intervals, which can be substantially too narrow or wide depending on the time. We propose a continuous multivariate stochastic process for time series having locally varying smoothness in both the mean and covariance matrix. This process is constructed utilizing latent dictionary functions in time, which are given nested Gaussian process priors and linearly related to the observed data through a sparse mapping. Using a differential equation representation, we bypass usual computational bottlenecks in obtaining MCMC and online algorithms for approximate Bayesian inference. The performance is assessed in simulations and illustrated in a financial application.

paragraphs: Several quantities observed over time may change gradually during one interval and abruptly during another. Applying the same degree of smoothing throughout can conceal rapid changes or exaggerate slow ones. It can also distort predictive uncertainty, making prediction intervals too narrow or too wide at different times.

This paper proposes a continuous multivariate stochastic process whose mean and covariance matrix can both vary in local smoothness. The construction uses hidden dictionary functions evolving over time, with nested Gaussian process priors governing those functions. A sparse linear mapping connects the hidden functions to the observations, providing a representation for changes in both typical values and relationships among the measured quantities.

title: Locally Adaptive Bayesian Multivariate Time Series

abstract: Branch-and-bound is a widely used method in combinatorial optimization, including mixed integer programming, structured prediction and MAP inference. While most work has been focused on developing problem-specific techniques, little is known about how to systematically design the node searching strategy on a branch-and-bound tree. We address the key challenge of learning an adaptive node searching order for any class of problem solvable by branch-and-bound. Our strategies are learned by imitation learning. We apply our algorithm to linear programming based branch-and-bound for solving mixed integer programs (MIP). We compare our method with one of the fastest open-source solvers, SCIP; and a very efficient commercial solver, Gurobi. We demonstrate that our approach achieves better solutions faster on four MIP libraries.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solves combinatorial optimization problems by exploring a tree of candidate subproblems. The order in which it visits nodes is an important part of that search. This paper addresses how to learn an adaptive node-searching strategy systematically, a question the authors distinguish from developing specialized techniques for individual optimization problems.

The proposed strategies are trained through imitation learning. The intended framework applies to problem classes solvable by branch-and-bound, while the concrete application uses branch-and-bound based on linear programming to solve mixed integer programs. Learning focuses on the order of exploration within the optimization procedure.

The authors compare their approach with SCIP, an open-source solver, and Gurobi, a commercial solver. Across four mixed integer programming libraries, they report obtaining better solutions faster. This is evidence for the value of learned search order in the tested settings. The broader contribution is to make a search strategy something that can be learned for a problem class, rather than relying entirely on manually designed choices.
summary.tldr: Imitation learning produces adaptive branch-and-bound search orders that find better solutions faster in tests on four mixed integer programming libraries.

title: Learning to Search in Branch and Bound Algorithms

abstract: We consider the problem of optimizing convex and concave functions with access to an erroneous zeroth-order oracle. In particular, for a given function $x \to f(x)$ we consider optimization when one is given access to absolute error oracles that return values in [f(x) - \epsilon,f(x)+\epsilon] or relative error oracles that return value in [(1+\epsilon)f(x), (1 +\epsilon)f (x)], for some \epsilon larger than 0. We show stark information theoretic impossibility results for minimizing convex functions and maximizing concave functions over polytopes in this model.

In particular, for a given function $x \to f(x)$ we consider optimization when one is given access to absolute error oracles that return values in [f(x) - \epsilon,f(x)+\epsilon] or relative error oracles that return value in [(1+\epsilon)f(x), (1 +\epsilon)f (x)], for some \epsilon larger than 0. paragraphs: The paper asks what can be achieved in convex optimization when function evaluations are erroneous. It considers zeroth-order access: an algorithm receives function values from an oracle rather than derivative information. The optimization tasks are minimizing convex functions and maximizing concave functions over polytopes, so both the shape of the objective and the feasible region are structured.

One error model allows each returned value to differ from the true value by at most a positive tolerance ε. The paper also considers a relative-error oracle formulation. These settings make the accuracy of the information supplied to the optimizer part of the problem itself, rather than treating function evaluation as an exact primitive.

The authors establish strong information-theoretic impossibility results in this model. Such results concern what the available observations can support, rather than merely the shortcomings of a particular optimization algorithm. Their significance is that convexity or concavity alone does not remove every obstacle created by erroneous value information in the studied optimization setting.
summary.tldr: The paper establishes information-theoretic impossibility results for convex and concave optimization over polytopes using erroneous function-value oracles.

title: Information-theoretic lower bounds for convex optimization with erroneous oracles

abstract: How can we efficiently propagate uncertainty in a latent state representation with recurrent neural networks? This paper introduces stochastic recurrent neural networks which glue a deterministic recurrent neural network and a state space model together to form a stochastic and sequential neural generative model. The clear separation of deterministic and stochastic layers allows a structured variational inference network to track the factorization of the model’s posterior distribution. By retaining both the nonlinear recursive structure of a recurrent neural network and averaging over the uncertainty in a latent path, like a state space model, we improve the state of the art results on the Blizzard and TIMIT speech modeling data sets by a large margin, while achieving comparable performances to competing methods on polyphonic music modeling.

paragraphs: The paper asks how recurrent neural networks can propagate uncertainty about a hidden state over time. It introduces stochastic recurrent neural networks by combining a deterministic recurrent network with a state-space model. The resulting generative model keeps nonlinear recurrent computation while also representing uncertainty along a sequence of latent states.

A key architectural choice is to separate deterministic and stochastic layers clearly. This allows a structured variational inference network to follow the factorization of the model's posterior distribution. In practical terms, the inference procedure is organized to reflect how uncertainty is structured in the generative model, while predictions can average over uncertain latent paths.

The authors report large improvements over prior state-of-the-art results on the Blizzard and TIMIT speech-modeling datasets. On polyphonic music modeling, performance is comparable to competing methods. The findings show strong benefits for the reported speech tasks while preserving a more qualified result for music, supporting the combination of recurrent nonlinear dynamics and explicit latent-state uncertainty as a useful sequential modeling approach.
summary.tldr: Combining recurrent networks with stochastic state-space layers improves reported speech-modeling results while remaining competitive on polyphonic music.

title: Sequential Neural Models with Stochastic Layers

abstract: A body of recent work in modeling neural activity focuses on recovering low- dimensional latent features that capture the statistical structure of large-scale neural populations. Most such approaches have focused on linear generative models, where inference is computationally tractable. Here, we propose fLDS, a general class of nonlinear generative models that permits the firing rate of each neuron to vary as an arbitrary smooth function of a latent, linear dynamical state. This extra flexibility allows the model to capture a richer set of neural variability than a purely linear model, but retains an easily visualizable low-dimensional latent space. To fit this class of non-conjugate models we propose a variational inference scheme, along with a novel approximate posterior capable of capturing rich temporal correlations across time. We show that our techniques permit inference in a wide class of generative models.We also show in application to two neural datasets that, compared to state-of-the-art neural population models, fLDS captures a much larger proportion of neural variability with a small number of latent dimensions, providing superior predictive performance and interpretability.

Linear generative models make inference manageable, but constrain how those hidden variables explain recorded activity. The paper introduces fLDS, which retains a low-dimensional state with linear dynamics while allowing richer relationships to individual neurons.

In fLDS, each neuron's firing rate can be any smooth function of the latent dynamical state. This nonlinear observation mapping expands the variation the model can represent while preserving a latent space that is easy to visualize. To fit the resulting non-conjugate models, the authors develop variational inference with an approximate posterior designed to capture substantial temporal correlations.

On two neural datasets, fLDS explains a much larger share of neural variability using few latent dimensions than the state-of-the-art population models compared. The authors also report better prediction and interpretability. These findings support separating simple hidden dynamics from flexible observation mappings, and the inference techniques are shown to apply across a wide class of generative models.
summary.tldr: fLDS combines linear latent dynamics with nonlinear firing-rate mappings to capture neural variability in a compact, interpretable representation.

title: Linear dynamical neural population models through nonlinear embeddings

abstract: We present a novel neural network algorithm, the Tensor Switching (TS) network, which generalizes the Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) nonlinearity to tensor-valued hidden units. The TS network copies its entire input vector to different locations in an expanded representation, with the location determined by its hidden unit activity. In this way, even a simple linear readout from the TS representation can implement a highly expressive deep-network-like function. The TS network hence avoids the vanishing gradient problem by construction, at the cost of larger representation size. We develop several methods to train the TS network, including equivalent kernels for infinitely wide and deep TS networks, a one-pass linear learning algorithm, and two backpropagation-inspired representation learning algorithms. Our experimental results demonstrate that the TS network is indeed more expressive and consistently learns faster than standard ReLU networks.

paragraphs: Tensor Switching networks extend the ReLU nonlinearity to tensor-valued hidden units. Their central operation copies the entire input vector into different locations of an expanded representation. Hidden-unit activity determines the destination, so the representation records input information in a form that depends on which switches are active.

This construction allows even a linear readout to implement a highly expressive function resembling those produced by deep networks. The authors state that the architecture avoids the vanishing gradient problem by construction, with a larger representation as the explicit cost. Expressive power is therefore tied to how inputs are arranged in that expanded representation.

Experiments show greater expressivity and consistently faster learning than standard ReLU networks in the tested settings. Together, the architecture and training methods explore a different route to expressive neural computation, while making the representation-size trade-off explicit.
summary.tldr: Tensor Switching networks route whole inputs into expanded representations, avoiding vanishing gradients by construction at the cost of greater representation size.

title: Tensor Switching Networks

abstract: In this paper, we develop a novel {\bf ho}moto{\bf p}y {\bf s}moothing (HOPS) algorithm for solving a family of non-smooth problems that is composed of a non-smooth term with an explicit max-structure and a smooth term or a simple non-smooth term whose proximal mapping is easy to compute. The best known iteration complexity for solving such non-smooth optimization problems is $O(1/\epsilon)$ without any assumption on the strong convexity. In this work, we will show that the proposed HOPS achieved a lower iteration complexity of $\tilde O(1/\epsilon^{1-\theta})$ with $\theta\in(0,1]$ capturing the local sharpness of the objective function around the optimal solutions. To the best of our knowledge, this is the lowest iteration complexity achieved so far for the considered non-smooth optimization problems without strong convexity assumption. The HOPS algorithm employs Nesterov's smoothing technique and Nesterov's accelerated gradient method and runs in stages, which gradually decreases the smoothing parameter in a stage-wise manner until it yields a sufficiently good approximation of the original function. We show that HOPS enjoys a linear convergence for many well-known non-smooth problems (e.g., empirical risk minimization with a piece-wise linear loss function and $\ell_1$ norm regularizer, finding a point in a polyhedron, cone programming, etc). Experimental results verify the effectiveness of HOPS in comparison with Nesterov's smoothing algorithm and the primal-dual style of first-order methods.

paragraphs: HOPS addresses structured nonsmooth optimization problems containing a term expressed as an explicit maximum. The remaining term must either be smooth or have an easily computed proximal mapping. For this family, the paper seeks better iteration complexity without assuming strong convexity, a condition often used to obtain faster optimization guarantees.

The algorithm combines Nesterov smoothing with accelerated gradient optimization and works in stages. It gradually reduces the smoothing parameter so that the optimized approximation increasingly resembles the original objective. Its bound is Õ(1/ε^(1−θ)), with θ between zero and one measuring local sharpness around optimal solutions. The improvement over O(1/ε) is therefore linked to that local geometry.

The authors establish linear convergence for several familiar nonsmooth problems, including empirical risk minimization with piecewise-linear loss and l1 regularization, finding a point in a polyhedron, and cone programming. Experiments support its effectiveness against Nesterov smoothing and primal-dual first-order methods. The result shows how progressively refined smoothing can exploit local sharpness even without a strong-convexity assumption.
summary.tldr: Staged smoothing exploits local objective sharpness to improve nonsmooth optimization complexity without assuming strong convexity.

title: Homotopy Smoothing for Non-Smooth Problems with Lower Complexity than $O(1/\epsilon)$

abstract: This work provides performance guarantees for the greedy solution of experimental design problems. In particular, it focuses on A- and E-optimal designs, for which typical guarantees do not apply since the mean-square error and the maximum eigenvalue of the estimation error covariance matrix are not supermodular. To do so, it leverages the concept of approximate supermodularity to derive non-asymptotic worst-case suboptimality bounds for these greedy solutions. These bounds reveal that as the SNR of the experiments decreases, these cost functions behave increasingly as supermodular functions. As such, greedy A- and E-optimal designs approach (1-1/e)-optimality. These results reconcile the empirical success of greedy experimental design with the non-supermodularity of the A- and E-optimality criteria.
originalAbstract: This work provides performance guarantees for the greedy solution of experimental design problems. In particular, it focuses on A- and E-optimal designs, for which typical guarantees do not apply since the mean-square error and the maximum eigenvalue of the estimation error covariance matrix are not supermodular. To do so, it leverages the concept of approximate supermodularity to derive non-asymptotic worst-case suboptimality bounds for these greedy solutions. These bounds reveal that as the SNR of the experiments decreases, these cost functions behave increasingly as supermodular functions. As such, greedy A- and E-optimal designs approach (1-1/e)-optimality. These results reconcile the empirical success of greedy experimental design with the non-supermodularity of the A- and E-optimality criteria.

paragraphs: Experimental design involves choosing measurements that will make an estimate informative. Greedy methods build a design through successive choices, but standard performance guarantees rely on mathematical structure that some important objectives lack. This paper studies A-optimal and E-optimal design, which concern mean-square estimation error and the largest eigenvalue of the estimation error covariance matrix.

Neither of these objectives is supermodular, so the usual guarantee cannot be applied directly. The authors instead measure approximate supermodularity and use it to derive finite, worst-case bounds on how far greedy solutions can fall short. This makes the analysis useful without requiring the objectives to possess the exact structural property.

The bounds show that the objectives behave increasingly like supermodular functions as experimental signal-to-noise ratios decrease. In that regime, the greedy designs approach a 1−1/e optimality guarantee. The result helps explain why greedy experimental design can work well empirically despite failing the standard supermodularity test. This concerns the quality of selection relative to the optimum, not a claim that noisier measurements provide more information.
summary.tldr: Approximate supermodularity gives worst-case guarantees for greedy A- and E-optimal experimental designs, with stronger guarantees as signal-to-noise ratios decrease.

title: Approximate Supermodularity Bounds for Experimental Design

abstract: Frank-Wolfe (FW) algorithms with linear convergence rates have recently achieved great efficiency in many applications. Garber and Meshi (2016) designed a new decomposition-invariant pairwise FW variant with favorable dependency on the domain geometry. Unfortunately, it applies only to a restricted class of polytopes and cannot achieve theoretical and practical efficiency at the same time. In this paper, we show that by employing an away-step update, similar rates can be generalized to arbitrary polytopes with strong empirical performance. A new "condition number" of the domain is introduced which allows leveraging the sparsity of the solution. We applied the method to a reformulation of SVM, and the linear convergence rate depends, for the first time, on the number of support vectors.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe methods address optimization problems with geometric constraints, and variants with linear convergence have proved efficient in applications. This paper builds on a decomposition-invariant pairwise variant with favorable dependence on the constraint geometry. That earlier approach, however, applies only to a restricted class of polytopes and has difficulty combining theoretical efficiency with practical efficiency.

Its role is to let the analysis take advantage of sparsity in the solution, connecting convergence behavior to more specific structure than a description of the full feasible region alone.

The method shows strong empirical performance and is applied to a reformulation of the support vector machine problem. In that application, the linear convergence rate depends on the number of support vectors, which the authors identify as a first. This makes the structure of the resulting classifier directly relevant to the optimization guarantee.
summary.tldr: An away-step Frank-Wolfe method extends decomposition-invariant convergence results to general polytopes while exploiting solution sparsity.

title: Decomposition-Invariant Conditional Gradient for General Polytopes with Line Search

abstract: This paper presents the key algorithmic techniques behind CatBoost, a new gradient boosting toolkit. Their combination leads to CatBoost outperforming other publicly available boosting implementations in terms of quality on a variety of datasets. Two critical algorithmic advances introduced in CatBoost are the implementation of ordered boosting, a permutation-driven alternative to the classic algorithm, and an innovative algorithm for processing categorical features. Both techniques were created to fight a prediction shift caused by a special kind of target leakage present in all currently existing implementations of gradient boosting algorithms. In this paper, we provide a detailed analysis of this problem and demonstrate that proposed algorithms solve it effectively, leading to excellent empirical results.

In this setting, information from training targets enters the learning procedure in a way that produces a mismatch in predictions. The authors analyze this problem as a weakness of the boosting implementations they discuss.

CatBoost addresses the issue through two connected advances. Ordered boosting uses permutations to organize learning as an alternative to the classic boosting procedure. A separate algorithm handles categorical features. Both are designed around the same objective: counteracting the leakage responsible for prediction shift.

The authors report that these techniques effectively address the analyzed problem and that their combination improves predictive quality over other publicly available boosting implementations across a variety of datasets. The contribution therefore connects an explanation of a learning bias with practical algorithm changes. The performance finding is empirical across the evaluated datasets, rather than a claim that CatBoost wins on every prediction problem.
summary.tldr: CatBoost combines ordered boosting and categorical-feature processing to counter target leakage and improve predictive quality.

title: CatBoost: unbiased boosting with categorical features

abstract: In this paper we study the fundamental problems of maximizing a continuous non monotone submodular function over a hypercube, with and without coordinate-wise concavity. This family of optimization problems has several applications in machine learning, economics, and communication systems. Our main result is the first 1/2 approximation algorithm for continuous submodular function maximization; this approximation factor of is the best possible for algorithms that use only polynomially many queries. For the special case of DR-submodular maximization, we provide a faster 1/2-approximation algorithm that runs in (almost) linear time. Both of these results improve upon prior work [Bian et al., 2017, Soma and Yoshida, 2017, Buchbinder et al., 2012]. Our first algorithm is a single-pass algorithm that uses novel ideas such as reducing the guaranteed approximation problem to analyzing a zero-sum game for each coordinate, and incorporates the geometry of this zero-sum game to fix the value at this coordinate. Our second algorithm is a faster single-pass algorithm that exploits coordinate-wise concavity to identify a monotone equilibrium condition sufficient for getting the required approximation guarantee, and hunts for the equilibrium point using binary search. We further run experiments to verify the performance of our proposed algorithms in related machine learning applications.

title: Optimal Algorithms for Continuous Non-monotone Submodular and DR-Submodular Maximization

abstract: We address reinforcement learning problems with finite state and action spaces where the underlying MDP has some known structure that could be potentially exploited to minimize the exploration rates of suboptimal (state, action) pairs. For any arbitrary structure, we derive problem-specific regret lower bounds satisfied by any learning algorithm. These lower bounds are made explicit for unstructured MDPs and for those whose transition probabilities and average reward functions are Lipschitz continuous w.r.t. the state and action. For Lipschitz MDPs, the bounds are shown not to scale with the sizes S and A of the state and action spaces, i.e., they are smaller than c log T where T is the time horizon and the constant c only depends on the Lipschitz structure, the span of the bias function, and the minimal action sub-optimality gap. This contrasts with unstructured MDPs where the regret lower bound typically scales as SA log T. We devise DEL (Directed Exploration Learning), an algorithm that matches our regret lower bounds. We further simplify the algorithm for Lipschitz MDPs, and show that the simplified version is still able to efficiently exploit the structure.

This paper studies finite state and action spaces where the underlying decision process has known structure. The central question is how that structure can reduce the exploration needed to distinguish useful choices from suboptimal ones.

The authors derive problem-specific regret lower bounds for arbitrary structure and make them explicit for unstructured and Lipschitz decision processes. In the Lipschitz case, transition probabilities and average rewards vary in a controlled way across states and actions. The resulting lower bounds are below c log T, with c determined by structural properties, the bias-function span, and the smallest action gap, rather than directly by state and action counts.

For unstructured problems, the lower bound typically scales as SA log T. The authors introduce Directed Exploration Learning, which matches their bounds, and give a simplified Lipschitz version that still exploits structure efficiently. The result links the information required for exploration to an algorithm that attains the corresponding regret bounds.
summary.tldr: Problem-specific regret bounds and Directed Exploration Learning show how known structure can reduce reinforcement-learning exploration costs.

title: Exploration in Structured Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We consider black box optimization of an unknown function in the nonparametric Gaussian process setting when the noise in the observed function values can be heavy tailed. This is in contrast to existing literature that typically assumes sub-Gaussian noise distributions for queries. Under the assumption that the unknown function belongs to the Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space (RKHS) induced by a kernel, we first show that an adaptation of the well-known GP-UCB algorithm with reward truncation enjoys sublinear $\tilde{O}(T^{\frac{2 + \alpha}{2(1+\alpha)}})$ regret even with only the $(1+\alpha)$-th moments, $\alpha \in (0,1]$, of the reward distribution being bounded ($\tilde{O}$ hides logarithmic factors). However, for the common squared exponential (SE) and Mat\'{e}rn kernels, this is seen to be significantly larger than a fundamental $\Omega(T^{\frac{1}{1+\alpha}})$ lower bound on regret. We resolve this gap by developing novel Bayesian optimization algorithms, based on kernel approximation techniques, with regret bounds matching the lower bound in order for the SE kernel. We numerically benchmark the algorithms on environments based on both synthetic models and real-world data sets.

Such heavy-tailed observations fall outside the sub-Gaussian noise assumptions commonly used in Bayesian optimization. The analysis assumes that the function belongs to the reproducing kernel Hilbert space associated with a chosen kernel, and that a specified moment of the reward distribution is bounded.

The authors first adapt GP-UCB by truncating rewards, limiting the influence of extreme observations. They prove sublinear regret under these weaker noise assumptions. Sublinear regret means that the accumulated cost of imperfect choices grows more slowly than the number of evaluations, so the average cost per evaluation decreases.

However, this initial guarantee remains substantially above a fundamental lower bound for common kernels. The authors then develop algorithms using kernel approximations, obtaining regret bounds that match the lower bound in order for the squared exponential kernel. They also benchmark their methods using synthetic environments and environments based on real datasets.
summary.tldr: Kernel approximation methods provide Bayesian optimization guarantees under heavy-tailed noise, matching the regret lower bound in order for the squared exponential kernel.

title: Bayesian Optimization under Heavy-tailed Payoffs

abstract: A longstanding goal in deep learning research has been to precisely characterize training and generalization. However, the often complex loss landscapes of neural networks have made a theory of learning dynamics elusive. In this work, we show that for wide neural networks the learning dynamics simplify considerably and that, in the infinite width limit, they are governed by a linear model obtained from the first-order Taylor expansion of the network around its initial parameters. Furthermore, mirroring the correspondence between wide Bayesian neural networks and Gaussian processes, gradient-based training of wide neural networks with a squared loss produces test set predictions drawn from a Gaussian process with a particular compositional kernel. While these theoretical results are only exact in the infinite width limit, we nevertheless find excellent empirical agreement between the predictions of the original network and those of the linearized version even for finite practically-sized networks. This agreement is robust across different architectures, optimization methods, and loss functions.

This paper shows that the dynamics simplify in the infinite-width limit. Training is governed by the linear model obtained from a first-order Taylor expansion around the initial parameters, making the initial network a reference point for its subsequent evolution.

The linearity is with respect to changes in parameters around initialization. The authors also establish that gradient-based training with squared loss produces test predictions drawn from a Gaussian process with a particular compositional kernel. This connects the training behavior of wide networks to a probabilistic description of their predictions, complementing the correspondence with wide Bayesian neural networks.

That agreement persists across the tested architectures, optimization methods, and loss functions. The results therefore offer both an exact limiting description and empirical evidence that the description can remain useful for networks of practical size.
summary.tldr: Infinite-width networks follow their linearization around initialization during training, with strong empirical agreement also observed in practical finite networks.

title: Wide Neural Networks of Any Depth Evolve as Linear Models Under Gradient Descent

abstract: Text-based interactive recommendation provides richer user preferences and has demonstrated advantages over traditional interactive recommender systems. However, recommendations can easily violate preferences of users from their past natural-language feedback, since the recommender needs to explore new items for further improvement. To alleviate this issue, we propose a novel constraint-augmented reinforcement learning (RL) framework to efficiently incorporate user preferences over time. Specifically, we leverage a discriminator to detect recommendations violating user historical preference, which is incorporated into the standard RL objective of maximizing expected cumulative future rewards. Our proposed framework is general and is further extended to the task of constrained text generation. Empirical results show that the proposed method yields consistent improvement relative to standard RL methods.

Empirical results show that the proposed method yields consistent improvement relative to standard RL methods.

paragraphs: Interactive recommenders can learn detailed preferences from users' natural-language feedback. Yet exploring new items can lead a system to recommend something that contradicts a preference the user already expressed. This paper addresses the tension between gathering information through exploration and making recommendations consistent with the accumulated conversation.

The proposed framework augments reinforcement learning with a discriminator that detects violations of historical user preferences. That signal is incorporated into the usual objective of maximizing expected cumulative future reward. The approach gives past feedback a role in evaluating candidate recommendations as learning continues, rather than relying on reward maximization alone to account for those preferences.

The authors also extend the framework to constrained text generation, demonstrating that its formulation applies beyond recommendation. Empirical results show consistent improvements over standard reinforcement learning methods. These findings support incorporating a learned preference-violation signal into sequential decision making, while the stated aim is to reduce violations rather than guarantee that every generated recommendation satisfies every past preference.
summary.tldr: A learned preference-violation detector augments reinforcement learning to improve interactive recommendations and constrained text generation.

title: Text-Based Interactive Recommendation via Constraint-Augmented Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We study the effect of the stochastic gradient noise on the training of generative adversarial networks (GANs) and show that it can prevent the convergence of standard game optimization methods, while the batch version converges. We address this issue with a novel stochastic variance-reduced extragradient (SVRE) optimization algorithm, which for a large class of games improves upon the previous convergence rates proposed in the literature. We observe empirically that SVRE performs similarly to a batch method on MNIST while being computationally cheaper, and that SVRE yields more stable GAN training on standard datasets.

We observe empirically that SVRE performs similarly to a batch method on MNIST while being computationally cheaper, and that SVRE yields more stable GAN training on standard datasets.

paragraphs: Training a generative adversarial network involves optimizing a game, and noisy gradient estimates can change whether the optimization converges. This paper studies that noise directly. It shows that stochastic gradients can prevent convergence for standard game-optimization methods even in cases where their batch counterparts converge, making gradient noise a substantive obstacle to training.

The proposed stochastic variance-reduced extragradient algorithm, abbreviated SVRE, addresses that obstacle by reducing variance within an extragradient method. The authors establish improved convergence rates over previous results for a large class of games. This theoretical contribution connects the treatment of stochastic noise to stronger optimization guarantees for that class.

In experiments on MNIST, SVRE behaves similarly to a batch method while requiring less computation. The authors also observe more stable GAN training on standard datasets. These findings suggest that reducing noise can retain useful behavior associated with batch optimization while lowering its computational cost. The empirical stability results complement the game-level analysis, rather than asserting convergence for every possible GAN training problem.
summary.tldr: SVRE reduces stochastic gradient noise in game optimization, improving theoretical convergence rates and empirical GAN training stability.

title: Reducing Noise in GAN Training with Variance Reduced Extragradient

abstract: Recent advances in optical voltage sensors have brought us closer to a critical goal in cellular neuroscience: imaging the full spatiotemporal voltage on a dendritic tree. However, current sensors and imaging approaches still face significant limitations in SNR and sampling frequency; therefore statistical denoising and interpolation methods remain critical for understanding single-trial spatiotemporal dendritic voltage dynamics. Previous denoising approaches were either based on an inadequate linear voltage model or scaled poorly to large trees. Here we introduce a scalable fully Bayesian approach. We develop a generative nonlinear model that requires few parameters per compartment of the cell but is nonetheless flexible enough to sample realistic spatiotemporal data. The model captures different dynamics in each compartment and leverages biophysical knowledge to constrain intra- and inter-compartmental dynamics. We obtain a full posterior distribution over spatiotemporal voltage via an augmented Gibbs sampling algorithm. The nonlinear smoother model outperforms previously developed linear methods, and scales to much larger systems than previous methods based on sequential Monte Carlo approaches.

paragraphs: Optical sensors bring researchers closer to observing voltage throughout a neuron’s dendritic tree, but noisy measurements and limited sampling rates complicate interpretation. Statistical methods must therefore denoise and interpolate the signals to recover voltage dynamics from a single trial. Earlier approaches used limited linear models or struggled to scale to large trees.

The authors introduce a fully Bayesian nonlinear generative model with relatively few parameters for each cell compartment. It accommodates different dynamics across compartments and incorporates biophysical knowledge to constrain behavior both within and between them. This combines a flexible account of voltage evolution with structure supplied by the biology.

An augmented Gibbs sampling algorithm estimates a full posterior distribution over voltage across space and time. The output therefore includes uncertainty about the reconstructed dynamics. The nonlinear smoother outperforms previous linear methods and handles much larger systems than earlier sequential Monte Carlo approaches. The findings address both modeling capacity and computational scale, making richer statistical reconstruction feasible for larger dendritic systems.
summary.tldr: A nonlinear Bayesian model reconstructs dendritic voltage with uncertainty while scaling to larger systems than previous sampling approaches.

title: Scalable Bayesian inference of dendritic voltage via spatiotemporal recurrent state space models

abstract: Learning non-deterministic dynamics and intrinsic factors from images obtained through physical experiments is at the intersection of machine learning and material science. Disentangling the origins of uncertainties involved in microstructure growth, for example, is of great interest because future states vary due to thermal fluctuation and other environmental factors. To this end we propose a flow-based image-to-image model, called Flow U-Net with Squeeze modules (FUNS), that allows us to disentangle the features while retaining the ability to generate highquality diverse images from condition images. Our model successfully captures probabilistic phenomena by incorporating a U-Net-like architecture into the flowbased model. In addition, our model automatically separates the diversity of target images into condition-dependent/independent parts. We demonstrate that the quality and diversity of the images generated for microstructure growth and CelebA datasets outperform existing variational generative models.

paragraphs: Images from physical experiments can have multiple plausible future states. In microstructure growth, for example, thermal fluctuations and environmental factors contribute to that variability. The paper studies how to generate diverse images from a conditioning image while also separating features associated with different sources of variation.

The proposed model, Flow U-Net with Squeeze modules, combines a flow-based image model with a U-Net-like architecture. The authors report that this combination captures probabilistic phenomena while retaining high image quality and diversity. It also automatically separates variation in target images into parts that depend on the conditioning image and parts that are independent of it.

Experiments cover microstructure growth and the CelebA dataset. The authors report that generated images outperform those of existing variational generative models in both quality and diversity. The contribution therefore joins conditional image generation with a distinction between two kinds of variability, addressing both the range of possible outputs and how that range relates to the supplied input image.
summary.tldr: FUNS generates diverse conditional images while separating target variation into components that depend on the input image and components that do not.

title: Flow-based Image-to-Image Translation with Feature Disentanglement

abstract: Progress in the field of machine learning has been fueled by the introduction of benchmark datasets pushing the limits of existing algorithms. Enabling the design of datasets to test specific properties and failure modes of learning algorithms is thus a problem of high interest, as it has a direct impact on innovation in the field. In this sense, we introduce Synbols — Synthetic Symbols — a tool for rapidly generating new datasets with a rich composition of latent features rendered in low resolution images. Synbols leverages the large amount of symbols available in the Unicode standard and the wide range of artistic font provided by the open font community. Our tool's high-level interface provides a language for rapidly generating new distributions on the latent features, including various types of textures and occlusions. To showcase the versatility of Synbols, we use it to dissect the limitations and flaws in standard learning algorithms in various learning setups including supervised learning, active learning, out of distribution generalization, unsupervised representation learning, and object counting.
