paragraphs: Synbols is a tool for creating synthetic image datasets that probe particular properties and failure modes of learning algorithms. Its motivation is that benchmark design influences what researchers can discover about a method. Being able to construct a dataset around a specific question makes that dataset an instrument for examining algorithm behavior.

The tool renders low-resolution images using Unicode symbols and artistic fonts from the open font community. Its high-level interface allows users to specify distributions over the underlying features that produce an image, including textures and occlusions. This makes it possible to vary the composition of generated data while working through a common dataset-generation interface.

The authors demonstrate Synbols across supervised learning, active learning, generalization outside the training distribution, unsupervised representation learning, and object counting. In these settings, they use generated datasets to examine limitations and flaws in standard algorithms. The contribution is both a practical generator and a demonstration that controlled synthetic data can support targeted investigation across several learning problems.
summary.tldr: Synbols generates controllable synthetic symbol images for investigating learning algorithms' properties and failure modes.

title: Synbols: Probing Learning Algorithms with Synthetic Datasets

abstract: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has shown great potentials in finding better neural network designs. Sample-based NAS is the most reliable approach which aims at exploring the search space and evaluating the most promising architectures. However, it is computationally very costly. As a remedy, the one-shot approach has emerged as a popular technique for accelerating NAS using weight-sharing. However, due to the weight-sharing of vastly different networks, the one-shot approach is less reliable than the sample-based approach. In this work, we propose BONAS (Bayesian Optimized Neural Architecture Search), a sample-based NAS framework which is accelerated using weight-sharing to evaluate multiple related architectures simultaneously. Specifically, we apply Graph Convolutional Network predictor as a surrogate model for Bayesian Optimization to select multiple related candidate models in each iteration. We then apply weight-sharing to train multiple candidate models simultaneously. This approach not only accelerates the traditional sample-based approach significantly, but also keeps its reliability. This is because weight-sharing among related architectures are more reliable than those in the one-shot approach. Extensive experiments are conducted to verify the effectiveness of our method over many competing algorithms.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search seeks effective network designs, but evaluating candidate networks can be expensive. Sample-based search focuses computation on promising candidates and offers reliable evaluations. One-shot search reduces costs by sharing weights across many architectures, although sharing among very different networks can make their evaluations less reliable. BONAS aims to combine the strengths of these approaches.

The method uses Bayesian optimization to guide the search, with a graph convolutional network predicting candidate performance. At each iteration, it selects several related architectures. Those candidates then share weights during simultaneous training, reducing the computation required to evaluate the selected group. The relationship among candidates is central to the design, rather than an incidental property of the search.

The authors report that this restricted form of sharing substantially accelerates sample-based search while preserving its reliability. Their explanation is that related architectures can share weights more reliably than the diverse architectures used in one-shot search. Experiments against numerous competing methods support the framework's effectiveness, connecting computational savings to a more selective use of weight sharing.
summary.tldr: BONAS accelerates architecture search by using Bayesian optimization to select related networks that can share weights more reliably.

title: Bridging the Gap between Sample-based and One-shot Neural Architecture Search with BONAS

abstract: We posit that a reinforcement learning (RL) agent will perform better when it uses representations that are better at predicting the future, particularly in terms of few-shot learning and domain adaptation. To test that hypothesis, we introduce an objective based on Deep InfoMax (DIM) which trains the agent to predict the future by maximizing the mutual information between its internal representation of successive timesteps. We provide an intuitive analysis of the convergence properties of our approach from the perspective of Markov chain mixing times, and argue that convergence of the lower bound on mutual information is related to the inverse absolute spectral gap of the transition model. We test our approach in several synthetic settings, where it successfully learns representations that are predictive of the future. Finally, we augment C51, a strong distributional RL agent, with our temporal DIM objective and demonstrate on a continual learning task (inspired by Ms.~PacMan) and on the recently introduced Procgen environment that our approach improves performance, which supports our core hypothesis.

paragraphs: This paper tests the idea that reinforcement learning agents benefit from internal representations that retain information useful for predicting the future. The motivation particularly concerns learning from few examples and adapting across domains. Instead of relying solely on the agent’s usual learning objective, the authors add a temporal objective based on Deep InfoMax.

The new objective maximizes mutual information between the agent’s representations at successive time steps. In plain terms, it encourages neighboring representations to contain information about one another. The authors also give an intuitive convergence analysis using Markov chain mixing times, arguing that convergence of the mutual-information lower bound relates to the inverse absolute spectral gap of the transition model.

Synthetic experiments show that the method learns representations predictive of future states. The authors then add the objective to C51, a distributional reinforcement learning agent, and report performance improvements on a continual-learning task inspired by Ms. PacMan and on Procgen. These findings support their hypothesis in the evaluated settings without establishing that predictive representations improve every reinforcement learning task.
summary.tldr: A temporal mutual-information objective learns future-predictive representations and improves a reinforcement learning agent on the evaluated tasks.

title: Deep Reinforcement and InfoMax Learning

abstract: Unlike in the traditional statistical modeling for which a user typically hand-specify a prior, Neural Processes (NPs) implicitly define a broad class of stochastic processes with neural networks. Given a data stream, NP learns a stochastic process that best describes the data. While this ``data-driven'' way of learning stochastic processes has proven to handle various types of data, NPs still relies on an assumption that uncertainty in stochastic processes is modeled by a single latent variable, which potentially limits the flexibility. To this end, we propose the Bootstrapping Neural Process (BNP), a novel extension of the NP family using the bootstrap. The bootstrap is a classical data-driven technique for estimating uncertainty, which allows BNP to learn the stochasticity in NPs without assuming a particular form. We demonstrate the efficacy of BNP on various types of data and its robustness in the presence of model-data mismatch.

paragraphs: Neural Processes use neural networks to learn stochastic processes from data, allowing uncertainty and variation to be modeled through a learned representation. This differs from a traditional workflow in which a user explicitly chooses a prior. However, the paper identifies a potentially restrictive assumption: uncertainty in the process is represented through a single latent variable.

The proposed Bootstrapping Neural Process uses the bootstrap, a classical data-driven technique for estimating uncertainty. This gives the model another way to learn stochastic variation without assuming a particular form for it. The motivation is to make uncertainty modeling more flexible while retaining the broader Neural Process approach of learning from data.

The authors demonstrate the method on several types of data and report robustness when the model and data are mismatched. That finding matters because the proposed change addresses how uncertainty is represented, rather than only how predictions are produced. The evidence supports bootstrapping as a useful extension of Neural Processes when their original uncertainty assumption may be limiting.
summary.tldr: Bootstrapping Neural Processes use bootstrap-based uncertainty estimation to increase flexibility and demonstrate robustness to model-data mismatch.

title: Bootstrapping neural processes

abstract: Spectral clustering and $k$-means, both as two major traditional clustering methods, are still attracting a lot of attention, although a variety of novel clustering algorithms have been proposed in recent years. Firstly, a unified framework of $k$-means and ratio-cut is revisited, and a novel and efficient clustering algorithm is then proposed based on this framework. The time and space complexity of our method are both linear with respect to the number of samples, and are independent of the number of clusters to construct, more importantly. These properties mean that it is easily scalable and applicable to large practical problems. Extensive experiments on 12 real-world benchmark and 8 facial datasets validate the advantages of the proposed algorithm compared to the state-of-the-art clustering algorithms. In particular, over 15x and 7x speed-up can be obtained with respect to $k$-means on the synthetic dataset of 1 million samples and the benchmark dataset (CelebA) of 200k samples, respectively [GitHub].

This paper revisits a framework that connects k-means with ratio-cut, bringing two established clustering viewpoints into a shared formulation. The authors use that connection to develop a new efficient clustering algorithm.

The stated time and memory complexities both grow linearly with the number of samples. More unusually, these complexities are independent of the number of clusters being constructed. These properties matter because increasing the dataset size or requesting more groups can otherwise make clustering difficult to scale to large practical problems.

These are results for the named comparisons, supporting the algorithm's practical scaling benefits alongside its complexity claims.
summary.tldr: A unified view of k-means and ratio-cut yields clustering with linear time and memory complexity independent of the number of clusters.

title: Efficient Clustering Based On A Unified View Of $K$-means And Ratio-cut

abstract: A significant effort has been made to train neural networks that replicate algorithmic reasoning, but they often fail to learn the abstract concepts underlying these algorithms. This is evidenced by their inability to generalize to data distributions that are outside of their restricted training sets, namely larger inputs and unseen data. We study these generalization issues at the level of numerical subroutines that comprise common algorithms like sorting, shortest paths, and minimum spanning trees. First, we observe that transformer-based sequence-to-sequence models can learn subroutines like sorting a list of numbers, but their performance rapidly degrades as the length of lists grows beyond those found in the training set. We demonstrate that this is due to attention weights that lose fidelity with longer sequences, particularly when the input numbers are numerically similar. To address the issue, we propose a learned conditional masking mechanism, which enables the model to strongly generalize far outside of its training range with near-perfect accuracy on a variety of algorithms. Second, to generalize to unseen data, we show that encoding numbers with a binary representation leads to embeddings with rich structure once trained on downstream tasks like addition or multiplication. This allows the embedding to handle missing data by faithfully interpolating numbers not seen during training.

paragraphs: A neural network can learn to perform an algorithm on training-sized inputs yet fail when the inputs grow or contain unfamiliar values. This paper examines those failures through numerical subroutines used in sorting, shortest-path computation, and minimum spanning trees. It separates generalization to longer inputs from generalization to unseen numbers.

For transformer sequence models, the authors observe that sorting performance deteriorates beyond the list lengths seen during training. They attribute this to attention weights losing fidelity, particularly when numbers are close in value. A learned conditional masking mechanism addresses that problem and produces near-perfect accuracy far beyond the training range on a variety of algorithms.

For unseen numerical values, the paper uses binary number encodings. Training on tasks such as addition or multiplication gives the resulting embeddings useful structure, allowing faithful interpolation of numbers absent from training. The two contributions address different obstacles to algorithmic generalization: maintaining reliable selection over longer sequences and representing numerical relationships that extend beyond the observed examples.
summary.tldr: Conditional attention masking and binary number encodings improve neural algorithm execution on longer inputs and numerical values absent from training.

title: Neural Execution Engines: Learning to Execute Subroutines

abstract: We extend the Approximate-Proximal Point (aProx) family of model-based methods for solving stochastic convex optimization problems, including stochastic subgradient, proximal point, and bundle methods, to the minibatch setting. To do this, we propose two minibatched algorithms for which we prove a non-asymptotic upper bound on the rate of convergence, revealing a linear speedup in minibatch size. In contrast to standard stochastic gradient methods, these methods may have linear speedup in the minibatch setting even for non-smooth functions. Our algorithms maintain the desirable traits characteristic of the aProx family, such as robustness to initial step size choice. Additionally, we show improved convergence rates for "interpolation" problems, which (for example) gives a new parallelization strategy for alternating projections. We corroborate our theoretical results with extensive empirical testing, which demonstrates the gains provided by accurate modeling and minibatching.

paragraphs: This paper extends approximate proximal-point methods to optimization updates that use minibatches of observations. The setting is stochastic convex optimization, and the broader method family includes stochastic subgradient, proximal-point, and bundle methods. The central question is how combining multiple observations per update changes convergence and practical behavior.

The authors propose two minibatch algorithms and prove finite-time convergence bounds that reveal a linear speedup with minibatch size. Unlike standard stochastic gradient methods, these methods may obtain that speedup even for nonsmooth objectives. They also retain a characteristic benefit of the approximate proximal-point family: robustness to the initial choice of step size.

For interpolation problems, the paper derives improved convergence rates and identifies a new way to parallelize alternating projections. Extensive experiments support the gains from accurate modeling and minibatching. The contribution therefore concerns both the amount of progress each update can make and how optimization can benefit from processing data together, with the nonsmooth speedup stated as a possibility rather than an unconditional property of every objective.
summary.tldr: Two minibatch approximate proximal-point algorithms provide convergence guarantees and can achieve linear minibatch speedups even for nonsmooth objectives.

title: Minibatch Stochastic Approximate Proximal Point Methods

abstract: Causal structure learning is a key problem in many domains. Causal structures can be learnt by performing experiments on the system of interest. We address the largely unexplored problem of designing a batch of experiments that each simultaneously intervene on multiple variables. While potentially more informative than the commonly considered single-variable interventions, selecting such interventions is algorithmically much more challenging, due to the doubly-exponential combinatorial search space over sets of composite interventions. In this paper, we develop efficient algorithms for optimizing different objective functions quantifying the informativeness of a budget-constrained batch of experiments. By establishing novel submodularity properties of these objectives, we provide approximation guarantees for our algorithms. Our algorithms empirically perform superior to both random interventions and algorithms that only select single-variable interventions.

paragraphs: Learning a system's causal structure can require experiments that deliberately change its variables. This paper studies how to select a batch of experiments when each experiment may intervene on several variables simultaneously. Such interventions can be more informative than changing one variable at a time, but choosing them creates a much larger search problem.

The authors formulate several objectives for measuring the informativeness of an experiment batch under a budget. They establish submodularity properties of these objectives and use those properties to develop efficient selection algorithms with approximation guarantees. This supplies a principled way to search a space of composite interventions that would otherwise be prohibitively large.

In experiments, the proposed algorithms outperform both random intervention choices and algorithms restricted to single-variable interventions. The findings support considering coordinated changes to multiple variables when planning causal discovery experiments. The theoretical contribution concerns how closely the efficient algorithms approximate their design objectives, while the empirical contribution demonstrates benefits of their selected batches in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Submodularity-based algorithms select informative batches of multi-variable causal interventions with approximation guarantees and strong empirical results.

title: Near-Optimal Multi-Perturbation Experimental Design for Causal Structure Learning

abstract: Graph embedding, which represents real-world entities in a mathematical space, has enabled numerous applications such as analyzing natural languages, social networks, biochemical networks, and knowledge bases.It has been experimentally shown that graph embedding in hyperbolic space can represent hierarchical tree-like data more effectively than embedding in linear space, owing to hyperbolic space's exponential growth property. However, since the theoretical comparison has been limited to ideal noiseless settings, the potential for the hyperbolic space's property to worsen the generalization error for practical data has not been analyzed.In this paper, we provide a generalization error bound applicable for graph embedding both in linear and hyperbolic spaces under various negative sampling settings that appear in graph embedding. Our bound states that error is polynomial and exponential with respect to the embedding space's radius in linear and hyperbolic spaces, respectively, which implies that hyperbolic space's exponential growth property worsens the error.Using our bound, we clarify the data size condition on which graph embedding in hyperbolic space can represent a tree better than in Euclidean space by discussing the bias-variance trade-off.Our bound also shows that imbalanced data distribution, which often appears in graph embedding, can worsen the error.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings represent entities as points in a mathematical space. Hyperbolic space can represent tree-like hierarchies effectively because its available space grows exponentially. The paper asks how that same geometric property affects generalization when learning from practical data, extending a theoretical comparison previously restricted to idealized noiseless settings.

The authors derive a generalization-error bound covering linear and hyperbolic embeddings under various negative-sampling setups. In this bound, dependence on the embedding space's radius is polynomial for linear space and exponential for hyperbolic space. The geometry that helps represent hierarchies can therefore also increase the statistical burden reflected by the bound.

The analysis uses a bias-variance trade-off to identify a data-size condition under which hyperbolic embeddings can represent a tree better than Euclidean embeddings. It also shows that an imbalanced data distribution can worsen the error bound. The resulting comparison makes the choice of geometry depend on both representational fit and the amount and distribution of available data.
summary.tldr: Generalization bounds reveal a trade-off between hyperbolic embeddings' ability to represent trees and their stronger radius-dependent statistical cost.

title: Generalization Bounds for Graph Embedding Using Negative Sampling: Linear vs Hyperbolic

abstract: The simultaneous rise of machine learning as a service and concerns over user privacy have increasingly motivated the need for private inference (PI). While recent work demonstrates PI is possible using cryptographic primitives, the computational overheads render it impractical. State-of-art deep networks are inadequate in this context because the source of slowdown in PI stems from the ReLU operations whereas optimizations for plaintext inference focus on reducing FLOPs. In this paper we re-think ReLU computations and propose optimizations for PI tailored to properties of neural networks. Specifically, we reformulate ReLU as an approximate sign test and introduce a novel truncation method for the sign test that significantly reduces the cost per ReLU. These optimizations result in a specific type of stochastic ReLU. The key observation is that the stochastic fault behavior is well suited for the fault-tolerant properties of neural network inference. Thus, we provide significant savings without impacting accuracy. We collectively call the optimizations Circa and demonstrate improvements of up to 4.7$\times$ storage and 3$\times$ runtime over baseline implementations; we further show that Circa can be used on top of recent PI optimizations to obtain 1.8$\times$ additional speedup.

paragraphs: Private inference uses cryptographic operations to run a neural network while protecting user privacy, but those operations can impose substantial computational costs. This paper focuses on a mismatch between ordinary inference optimization and private inference: reducing arithmetic work does not directly address the expensive ReLU operations that dominate the latter setting.

Circa reworks a ReLU computation as an approximate test of whether a value is positive. A new truncation method makes that sign test cheaper, producing a particular form of stochastic ReLU. The approach rests on the observation that the resulting pattern of occasional errors fits the fault tolerance of neural network inference, allowing cheaper computations without affecting accuracy in the reported results.

The authors demonstrate storage improvements of up to 4.7 times and runtime improvements of up to 3 times over baseline implementations. Applying Circa alongside recent private-inference optimizations yields an additional 1.8-times speedup. These results make the operation being optimized central to the contribution: private inference benefits from targeting its cryptographic bottlenecks directly.
summary.tldr: Circa makes private inference cheaper by replacing expensive ReLU computations with stochastic approximations that preserve accuracy in the reported evaluations.

title: Circa: Stochastic ReLUs for Private Deep Learning

abstract: The majority of existing multimodal sequential learning methods focus on how to obtain effective representations and ignore the importance of multimodal fusion. Bilinear attention network (BAN) is a commonly used fusion method, which leverages tensor operations to associate the features of different modalities. However, BAN has a poor compatibility for more modalities, since the computational complexity of the attention map increases exponentially with the number of modalities. Based on this concern, we propose a new method called generalizable multi-linear attention network (MAN), which can associate as many modalities as possible in linear complexity with hierarchical approximation decomposition (HAD). Besides, considering the fact that softmax attention kernels cannot be decomposed as linear operation directly, we adopt the addition random features (ARF) mechanism to approximate the non-linear softmax functions with enough theoretical analysis. We conduct extensive experiments on four datasets of three tasks (multimodal sentiment analysis, multimodal speaker traits recognition, and video retrieval), the experimental results show that MAN could achieve competitive results compared with the state-of-the-art methods, showcasing the effectiveness of the approximation decomposition and addition random features mechanism.

paragraphs: Multimodal learning must combine information from different modalities as well as represent each one effectively. The paper focuses on this fusion step. Bilinear attention uses tensor operations to associate features, but extending its attention map to more modalities incurs exponentially increasing computational complexity, making broader combinations difficult.

The proposed Multi-linear Attention Network, or MAN, uses hierarchical approximation decomposition to associate modalities with linear rather than exponential complexity in their number. A further obstacle is that the nonlinear softmax attention function cannot be decomposed directly into linear operations. The authors address this with addition random features, which approximate softmax and are accompanied by theoretical analysis.

Experiments span four datasets and three tasks: sentiment analysis, speaker-trait recognition, and video retrieval. MAN achieves competitive results relative to state-of-the-art methods. These findings support the practical usefulness of the two approximation mechanisms together: they make multimodal fusion more computationally manageable while retaining effective performance on the evaluated tasks, without requiring an exact decomposition of the original softmax operation.
summary.tldr: MAN uses hierarchical decomposition and random-feature approximation to make attention-based multimodal fusion scale linearly with the number of modalities.

title: Generalizable Multi-linear Attention Network

abstract: Pretrained language models (LMs) perform well on many tasks even when learning from a few examples, but prior work uses many held-out examples to tune various aspects of learning, such as hyperparameters, training objectives, and natural language templates ("prompts"). Here, we evaluate the few-shot ability of LMs when such held-out examples are unavailable, a setting we call true few-shot learning. We test two model selection criteria, cross-validation and minimum description length, for choosing LM prompts and hyperparameters in the true few-shot setting. On average, both marginally outperform random selection and greatly underperform selection based on held-out examples. Moreover, selection criteria often prefer models that perform significantly worse than randomly-selected ones. We find similar results even when taking into account our uncertainty in a model's true performance during selection, as well as when varying the amount of computation and number of examples used for selection. Overall, our findings suggest that prior work significantly overestimated the true few-shot ability of LMs given the difficulty of few-shot model selection.

paragraphs: A language model may learn a task from a few examples while still relying on many additional examples to choose prompts or hyperparameters. This paper examines few-shot learning when those held-out examples are unavailable. It calls this true few-shot learning and makes model selection part of the difficulty being measured.

The authors test cross-validation and minimum description length as ways to choose prompts and hyperparameters from scarce data. On average, both perform only slightly better than random selection and substantially worse than selection using held-out examples. They also frequently select models that perform considerably worse than randomly chosen alternatives, showing that the average advantage can conceal unreliable choices.

Similar results persist when selection accounts for uncertainty about model performance and when the authors vary computation and the number of examples used. The findings suggest that earlier work substantially overestimated true few-shot ability by benefiting from additional selection data. The central implication is that learning from a few examples and reliably choosing how to learn from them are both necessary parts of evaluating this setting.
summary.tldr: Without held-out selection examples, tested prompt and hyperparameter selection methods barely beat random choice on average, challenging earlier few-shot evaluations.

title: True Few-Shot Learning with Language Models

abstract: Recent works on Bayesian neural networks (BNNs) have highlighted the need to better understand the implications of using Gaussian priors in combination with the compositional structure of the network architecture. Similar in spirit to the kind of analysis that has been developed to devise better initialization schemes for neural networks (cf. He- or Xavier initialization), we derive a precise characterization of the prior predictive distribution of finite-width ReLU networks with Gaussian weights.While theoretical results have been obtained for their heavy-tailedness,the full characterization of the prior predictive distribution (i.e. its density, CDF and moments), remained unknown prior to this work. Our analysis, based on the Meijer-G function, allows us to quantify the influence of architectural choices such as the width or depth of the network on the resulting shape of the prior predictive distribution. We also formally connect our results to previous work in the infinite width setting, demonstrating that the moments of the distribution converge to those of a normal log-normal mixture in the infinite depth limit. Finally, our results provide valuable guidance on prior design: for instance, controlling the predictive variance with depth- and width-informed priors on the weights of the network.

paragraphs: A Gaussian prior on neural-network weights does not by itself describe the distribution of the network's predictions before observing data. The composition of layers also matters. This paper derives a precise prior predictive distribution for finite-width ReLU networks with Gaussian weights, addressing how architectural choices transform assumptions about weights into assumptions about outputs.

Earlier theoretical work had established heavy-tailed behavior, but the full distribution remained uncharacterized. Using the Meijer-G function, the authors obtain its density, cumulative distribution function, and moments. This enables them to quantify how width and depth influence the distribution's shape, going beyond the observation that its tails can be heavy.

The analysis also connects to previous infinite-width work and shows convergence of moments to those of a normal log-normal mixture in an infinite-depth limit. These findings provide guidance for choosing priors with architecture in mind. One stated application is controlling predictive variance through weight priors informed by both depth and width, making prior design responsive to the network that uses it.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes output distributions induced by Gaussian weights in finite-width ReLU networks, clarifying how architecture should inform prior design.

title: Precise characterization of the prior predictive distribution of deep ReLU networks

abstract: Machine learning advances in the last decade have relied significantly on large-scale datasets that continue to grow in size. Increasingly, those datasets also contain different data modalities. However, large multi-modal datasets are hard to annotate, and annotations may contain biases that we are often unaware of. Deep-net-based classifiers, in turn, are prone to exploit those biases and to find shortcuts. To study and quantify this concern, we introduce the perceptual score, a metric that assesses the degree to which a model relies on the different subsets of the input features, i.e., modalities. Using the perceptual score, we find a surprisingly consistent trend across four popular datasets: recent, more accurate state-of-the-art multi-modal models for visual question-answering or visual dialog tend to perceive the visual data less than their predecessors. This is concerning as answers are hence increasingly inferred from textual cues only. Using the perceptual score also helps to analyze model biases by decomposing the score into data subset contributions. We hope to spur a discussion on the perceptiveness of multi-modal models and also hope to encourage the community working on multi-modal classifiers to start quantifying perceptiveness via the proposed perceptual score.

paragraphs: A model given both images and text may obtain accurate answers without relying strongly on the images. Biases in large multimodal datasets can make textual shortcuts effective, even when the task is intended to require visual understanding. This paper introduces the perceptual score to quantify how much a model relies on different input modalities.

The score assesses dependence on subsets of input features, allowing the authors to examine whether visual information contributes to a model’s behavior. It can also be decomposed into contributions from subsets of the data. That decomposition helps investigate where particular patterns of reliance and bias occur within a dataset.

Across four popular datasets for visual question answering or visual dialog, the authors find a consistent trend: newer, more accurate state-of-the-art models tend to rely less on visual data than their predecessors. The finding shows why overall accuracy alone can obscure changes in how a multimodal model uses its inputs. The proposed metric provides an additional way to examine that behavior.
summary.tldr: The perceptual score measures modality reliance and reveals that higher multimodal accuracy can accompany reduced use of visual information.

title: Perceptual Score: What Data Modalities Does Your Model Perceive?

abstract: Consider learning a decision support assistant to serve as an intermediary between (oracle) expert behavior and (imperfect) human behavior: At each time, the algorithm observes an action chosen by a fallible agent, and decides whether to *accept* that agent's decision, *intervene* with an alternative, or *request* the expert's opinion. For instance, in clinical diagnosis, fully-autonomous machine behavior is often beyond ethical affordances, thus real-world decision support is often limited to monitoring and forecasting. Instead, such an intermediary would strike a prudent balance between the former (purely prescriptive) and latter (purely descriptive) approaches, while providing an efficient interface between human mistakes and expert feedback. In this work, we first formalize the sequential problem of *online decision mediation*---that is, of simultaneously learning and evaluating mediator policies from scratch with *abstentive feedback*: In each round, deferring to the oracle obviates the risk of error, but incurs an upfront penalty, and reveals the otherwise hidden expert action as a new training data point. Second, we motivate and propose a solution that seeks to trade off (immediate) loss terms against (future) improvements in generalization error; in doing so, we identify why conventional bandit algorithms may fail. Finally, through experiments and sensitivities on a variety of datasets, we illustrate consistent gains over applicable benchmarks on performance measures with respect to the mediator policy, the learned model, and the decision-making system as a whole.

paragraphs: Online decision mediation places a learning assistant between a fallible decision maker and an expert. At each step, the assistant can accept the proposed action, replace it, or ask the expert. The problem is to learn when each response is worthwhile while simultaneously making decisions, rather than assuming that a useful mediation policy already exists.

The feedback structure creates a distinctive tradeoff. Asking the expert avoids error in the formalized setting and reveals an otherwise hidden expert action that becomes training data, but it also incurs an immediate penalty. An expert request can therefore affect both the present decision and the quality of future decisions.

The proposed solution weighs immediate losses against future improvements in generalization error. The authors also explain why conventional bandit algorithms may fail to address this combination. Experiments and sensitivity analyses across multiple datasets show consistent gains over applicable benchmarks, measured at the levels of the mediator policy, learned model, and overall decision system. The contribution is a framework for learning selective intervention while accounting for the future value of expert feedback.
summary.tldr: Online decision mediation learns when to accept, override, or seek expert advice by balancing immediate costs against future learning benefits.

title: Online Decision Mediation

abstract: Pure exploration in multi-armed bandits has emerged as an important framework for modeling decision making and search under uncertainty. In modern applications however, one is often faced with a tremendously large number of options and even obtaining one observation per option may be too costly rendering traditional pure exploration algorithms ineffective. Fortunately, one often has access to similarity relationships amongst the options that can be leveraged. In this paper, we consider the pure exploration problem in stochastic multi-armed bandits where the similarities between the arms is captured by a graph and the rewards may be represented as a smooth signal on this graph. In particular, we consider the problem of finding the arm with the maximum reward (i.e., the maximizing problem) or one that has sufficiently high reward (i.e., the satisficing problem) under this model. We propose novel algorithms GRUB (GRaph based UcB) and zeta-GRUB for these problems and provide theoretical characterization of their performance which specifically elicits the benefit of the graph side information. We also prove a lower bound on the data requirement that shows a large class of problems where these algorithms are near-optimal. We complement our theory with experimental results that show the benefit of capitalizing on such side information.

paragraphs: When a decision problem offers an enormous number of options, observing every option even once may be too expensive. This paper studies pure exploration in stochastic multi-armed bandits when a graph describes similarities among the options. Its model assumes that rewards can be represented as a smooth signal on that graph.

The authors consider two goals: finding the option with the greatest reward and finding one whose reward is sufficiently high. They introduce GRUB and zeta-GRUB for these maximizing and satisficing problems. Their theoretical analysis explicitly characterizes the benefit of graph information, showing how relationships among options can help guide exploration.

A lower bound on required data identifies a large class of problems where the algorithms are near-optimal. Experiments also demonstrate benefits from using the graph. The important qualification is that the graph is paired with the reward-smoothness model: its value comes from providing relevant structure about the rewards, allowing exploration to use more than isolated observations of individual options.
summary.tldr: GRUB and zeta-GRUB use graph relationships and reward smoothness to efficiently find the best or a sufficiently rewarding option.

title: Maximizing and Satisficing in Multi-armed Bandits with Graph Information

abstract: Modern autonomous systems rely on perception modules to process complex sensor measurements into state estimates. These estimates are then passed to a controller, which uses them to make safety-critical decisions. It is therefore important that we design perception systems to minimize errors that reduce the overall safety of the system. We develop a risk-driven approach to designing perception systems that accounts for the effect of perceptual errors on the performance of the fully-integrated, closed-loop system. We formulate a risk function to quantify the effect of a given perceptual error on overall safety, and show how we can use it to design safer perception systems by including a risk-dependent term in the loss function and generating training data in risk-sensitive regions. We evaluate our techniques on a realistic vision-based aircraft detect and avoid application and show that risk-driven design reduces collision risk by 37% over a baseline system.

It is therefore important that we design perception systems to minimize errors that reduce the overall safety of the system. We develop a risk-driven approach to designing perception systems that accounts for the effect of perceptual errors on the performance of the fully-integrated, closed-loop system. We formulate a risk function to quantify the effect of a given perceptual error on overall safety, and show how we can use it to design safer perception systems by including a risk-dependent term in the loss function and generating training data in risk-sensitive regions. We evaluate our techniques on a realistic vision-based aircraft detect and avoid application and show that risk-driven design reduces collision risk by 37% over a baseline system.

paragraphs: An autonomous system's perception module converts sensor measurements into estimates that a controller uses to act. A perception error matters for safety through the decisions it causes downstream. This paper designs perception around those consequences, evaluating errors in the context of the complete system operating in a closed loop.

The authors formulate a risk function that quantifies how a particular perceptual error affects overall safety. They use that function in two ways: adding a risk-dependent term to the training loss and generating training data in regions where risk is important. Both mechanisms direct learning toward errors and situations with greater safety consequences.

The approach is evaluated in a realistic aircraft detect-and-avoid application using vision. The reported design reduces collision risk by 37% relative to a baseline system. This demonstrates an application-specific benefit from connecting perception training to controller outcomes. The central contribution is a method for bringing system-level safety consequences into both the learning objective and the choice of training data.
summary.tldr: Training perception around downstream safety risk reduces collision risk by 37% in the evaluated vision-based aircraft application.

title: Risk-Driven Design of Perception Systems

abstract: Currently, pre-trained models can be considered the default choice for a wide range of NLP tasks. Despite their SoTA results, there is practical evidence that these models may require a different number of computing layers for different input sequences, since evaluating all layers leads to overconfidence in wrong predictions (namely overthinking). This problem can potentially be solved by implementing adaptive computation time approaches, which were first designed to improve inference speed. Recently proposed PonderNet may be a promising solution for performing an early exit by treating the exit layer's index as a latent variable. However, the originally proposed exit criterion, relying on sampling from trained posterior distribution on the probability of exiting from the $i$-th layer, introduces major variance in exit layer indices, significantly reducing the resulting model's performance. In this paper, we propose improving PonderNet with a novel deterministic Q-exit criterion and a revisited model architecture. We adapted the proposed mechanism to ALBERT and RoBERTa and compared it with recent methods for performing an early exit. We observed that the proposed changes can be considered significant improvements on the original PonderNet architecture and outperform PABEE on a wide range of GLUE tasks. In addition, we also performed an in-depth ablation study of the proposed architecture to further understand Lambda layers and their performance.

Running every layer can sometimes increase confidence in an incorrect answer, a behavior described as overthinking. This paper investigates adaptive early exit, which lets processing stop at different depths, as a potential response to that problem.

PonderNet models the exit layer as a latent variable, but its original exit rule samples from a learned distribution. The findings support the proposed exit rule and architectural changes as useful ways to implement adaptive depth in the evaluated language models.
summary.tldr: PALBERT improves adaptive early exit with a deterministic stopping rule and revised architecture for ALBERT and RoBERTa.

title: PALBERT: Teaching ALBERT to Ponder

abstract: In recent years there has been significant progress in the field of 3D learning on classification, detection and segmentation problems. The vast majority of the existing studies focus on canonical closed-set conditions, neglecting the intrinsic open nature of the real-world. This limits the abilities of robots and autonomous systems involved in safety-critical applications that require managing novel and unknown signals. In this context exploiting 3D data can be a valuable asset since it provides rich information about the geometry of perceived objects and scenes. With this paper we provide the first broad study on 3D Open Set learning. We introduce 3DOS: a novel testbed for semantic novelty detection that considers several settings with increasing difficulties in terms of semantic (category) shift, and covers both in-domain (synthetic-to-synthetic, real-to-real) and cross-domain (synthetic-to-real) scenarios. Moreover, we investigate the related 2D Open Set literature to understand if and how its recent improvements are effective on 3D data. Our extensive benchmark positions several algorithms in the same coherent picture, revealing their strengths and limitations. The results of our analysis may serve as a reliable foothold for future tailored 3D Open Set methods.

paragraphs: A 3D recognition system can encounter objects outside the categories it learned during training. Standard closed-set evaluations largely leave this situation out, even though recognizing unfamiliar inputs matters for robots and autonomous systems. This paper studies semantic novelty detection on point clouds: identifying unfamiliar object categories from their three-dimensional geometry.

The authors introduce 3DOS, a benchmark with settings that become increasingly difficult in their category shifts. It includes synthetic-to-synthetic and real-to-real evaluation, as well as synthetic-to-real evaluation. This organization makes it possible to examine novelty detection both within a data domain and when the source of the data also changes.

The study also evaluates whether advances from 2D open-set recognition carry over to 3D inputs. Comparing several algorithms within a common benchmark reveals their respective strengths and limitations. The contribution is a shared basis for understanding and evaluating the problem, with findings that may guide methods designed specifically for 3D novelty detection.
summary.tldr: 3DOS benchmarks detection of unfamiliar categories in point clouds across category shifts and synthetic-to-real changes.

title: 3DOS: Towards 3D Open Set Learning - Benchmarking and Understanding Semantic Novelty Detection on Point Clouds

abstract: Video-language models suffer from forgetting old/learned knowledge when trained with streaming data. In this work, we thus propose a continual video-language modeling (CVLM) setting, where models are supposed to be sequentially trained on five widely-used video-text datasets with different data distributions. Although most of existing continual learning methods have achieved great success by exploiting extra information (e.g., memory data of past tasks) or dynamically extended networks, they cause enormous resource consumption when transferred to our CVLM setting. To overcome the challenges (i.e., catastrophic forgetting and heavy resource consumption) in CVLM, we propose a novel cross-modal MoCo-based model with bidirectional momentum update (BMU), termed BMU-MoCo. Concretely, our BMU-MoCo has two core designs: (1) Different from the conventional MoCo, we apply the momentum update to not only momentum encoders but also encoders (i.e., bidirectional) at each training step, which enables the model to review the learned knowledge retained in the momentum encoders. (2) To further enhance our BMU-MoCo by utilizing earlier knowledge, we additionally maintain a pair of global momentum encoders (only initialized at the very beginning) with the same BMU strategy. Extensive results show that our BMU-MoCo remarkably outperforms recent competitors w.r.t. video-text retrieval performance and forgetting rate, even without using any extra data or dynamic networks.

paragraphs: Video-language models can forget previously learned relationships when training continues on new data. The paper studies this problem through a continual learning setting in which a model encounters five video-text datasets sequentially, each with a different distribution. Methods that retain past training examples or expand the network can become resource intensive in this setting.

BMU-MoCo modifies a cross-modal momentum-encoder model so that information moves in both directions during training. Momentum updates affect both the momentum encoders and the main encoders at every step. This lets the main model revisit knowledge retained in the momentum encoders while learning from the current dataset.

The method also maintains a pair of global momentum encoders initialized only at the start, using the same bidirectional update strategy to draw on earlier knowledge. Experiments report better video-text retrieval and less forgetting than recent competitors, without extra data or dynamically growing networks. The contribution is a mechanism for retaining useful knowledge within the model’s update process while continuing to adapt to changing video-text data.
summary.tldr: BMU-MoCo uses bidirectional momentum updates to improve continual video-text learning without extra data or growing networks.

title: BMU-MoCo: Bidirectional Momentum Update for Continual Video-Language Modeling

abstract: Adapting to the changes in transition dynamics is essential in robotic applications. By learning a conditional policy with a compact context, context-aware meta-reinforcement learning provides a flexible way to adjust behavior according to dynamics changes. However, in real-world applications, the agent may encounter complex dynamics changes. Multiple confounders can influence the transition dynamics, making it challenging to infer accurate context for decision-making. This paper addresses such a challenge by decomposed mutual information optimization (DOMINO) for context learning, which explicitly learns a disentangled context to maximize the mutual information between the context and historical trajectories while minimizing the state transition prediction error. Our theoretical analysis shows that DOMINO can overcome the underestimation of the mutual information caused by multi-confounded challenges via learning disentangled context and reduce the demand for the number of samples collected in various environments. Extensive experiments show that the context learned by DOMINO benefits both model-based and model-free reinforcement learning algorithms for dynamics generalization in terms of sample efficiency and performance in unseen environments.

paragraphs: A robot may need to change its behavior when the environment's transition dynamics change. Context-aware meta-reinforcement learning addresses this by conditioning behavior on a compact description of the current dynamics. The difficulty studied here is that several underlying influences can change those dynamics together, making a useful context harder to infer from experience.

DOMINO learns a disentangled context, separating information about these influences within the representation. Its objective combines two goals: retaining information shared between the context and past trajectories, and reducing errors in predicting state transitions. The representation is therefore trained both to summarize relevant experience and to help explain how the environment changes from one state to the next.

The theoretical analysis shows that this decomposition can address underestimation of mutual information in the presence of multiple confounders and reduce sample requirements across environments. Experiments find benefits for both model-based and model-free reinforcement learning, including better sample efficiency and performance in unseen environments. The results support context decomposition as a useful route to adapting across changing dynamics.
summary.tldr: DOMINO learns disentangled context representations to help reinforcement-learning agents adapt more efficiently to changes in environment dynamics.

title: DOMINO: Decomposed Mutual Information Optimization for Generalized Context in Meta-Reinforcement Learning

abstract: The application of machine learning in safety-critical systems requires a reliable assessment of uncertainty.However, deep neural networks are known to produce highly overconfident predictions on out-of-distribution (OOD) data.Even if trained to be non-confident on OOD data, one can still adversarially manipulate OOD data so that the classifier again assigns high confidence to the manipulated samples.We show that two previously published defenses can be broken by better adapted attacks, highlighting the importance of robustness guarantees around OOD data.Since the existing method for this task is hard to train and significantly limits accuracy, we construct a classifier that can simultaneously achieve provably adversarially robust OOD detection and high clean accuracy.Moreover, by slightly modifying the classifier's architecture our method provably avoids the asymptotic overconfidence problem of standard neural networks.We provide code for all our experiments.

paragraphs: A classifier can make highly confident predictions on inputs outside its training distribution. Training it to lower confidence on unfamiliar data does not necessarily solve the problem: an attacker can modify those inputs to restore high confidence. This paper investigates detection that remains reliable under adversarial manipulation of out-of-distribution data.

The authors show that better-adapted attacks break two previously published defenses. This motivates guarantees around unfamiliar inputs, beyond empirical resistance to particular attacks. They then construct a classifier that can combine provably robust out-of-distribution detection with high accuracy on clean data, addressing the training difficulty and accuracy restrictions associated with an existing guaranteed approach.

A small architectural modification additionally provides a proof that the classifier avoids the asymptotic overconfidence problem of standard neural networks. These are related but distinct contributions: resisting adversarial manipulation around out-of-distribution data and avoiding a problematic limiting confidence behavior. Together, they show that the stated robustness properties can coexist with strong clean-data classification, rather than requiring the accuracy compromise described for the earlier method.
summary.tldr: The paper constructs a classifier combining provably adversarially robust out-of-distribution detection with high clean accuracy and an architectural remedy for asymptotic overconfidence.

title: Provably Adversarially Robust Detection of Out-of-Distribution Data (Almost) for Free

abstract: Neural architecture search (NAS) has gained immense popularity owing to its ability to automate neural architecture design. A number of training-free metrics are recently proposed to realize NAS without training, hence making NAS more scalable. Despite their competitive empirical performances, a unified theoretical understanding of these training-free metrics is lacking. As a consequence, (a) the relationships among these metrics are unclear, (b) there is no theoretical interpretation for their empirical performances, and (c) there may exist untapped potential in existing training-free NAS, which probably can be unveiled through a unified theoretical understanding. To this end, this paper presents a unified theoretical analysis of gradient-based training-free NAS, which allows us to (a) theoretically study their relationships, (b) theoretically guarantee their generalization performances, and (c) exploit our unified theoretical understanding to develop a novel framework named hybrid NAS (HNAS) which consistently boosts training-free NAS in a principled way. Remarkably, HNAS can enjoy the advantages of both training-free (i.e., the superior search efficiency) and training-based (i.e., the remarkable search effectiveness) NAS, which we have demonstrated through extensive experiments.

paragraphs: Neural architecture search automates network design, but evaluating candidate architectures through training can be expensive. Training-free metrics aim to make search more scalable. This paper addresses a theoretical gap around gradient-based versions of these metrics: how they relate, why they work empirically, and how their strengths might be combined more effectively.

The authors present a unified theoretical analysis that studies relationships among the metrics and provides guarantees concerning their generalization performance. Bringing the measures into one framework makes their behavior more interpretable and supplies a basis for improving search. The analysis is then used to develop hybrid neural architecture search, called HNAS.

HNAS aims to combine the search efficiency associated with training-free methods and the search effectiveness associated with training-based methods. Extensive experiments demonstrate these advantages and show consistent improvements to training-free search in the evaluated settings. The contribution connects theory to algorithm design: the framework uses the shared analysis to guide a hybrid approach, rather than treating existing metrics as unrelated empirical scoring rules.
summary.tldr: A unified theory of gradient-based training-free architecture metrics motivates HNAS, a hybrid search framework combining efficiency with effective architecture selection.

title: Unifying and Boosting Gradient-Based Training-Free Neural Architecture Search

abstract: We find a surprising connection between multitask learning and robustness to neuron failures. Our experiments show that bilingual language models retain higher performance under various neuron perturbations, such as random deletions, magnitude pruning and weight noise. Our study is motivated by research in cognitive science showing that symptoms of dementia and cognitive decline appear later in bilingual speakers compared to monolingual patients with similar brain damage, a phenomenon called bilingual cognitive reserve. Our language model experiments replicate this phenomenon on bilingual GPT-2 and other models.We provide a theoretical justification of this robustness by mathematically analyzing linear representation learning and showing that multitasking creates more robust representations. We open-source our code and models in the following URL: https://github.com/giannisdaras/multilingual\_robustness.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether learning multiple tasks can make neural representations more resistant to structural damage. Its motivation comes from bilingual cognitive reserve: cognitive-science research describing later appearance of dementia and cognitive-decline symptoms in bilingual speakers than in monolingual patients with similar brain damage. The authors study a corresponding phenomenon in language models.

Their experiments find that bilingual models retain higher performance under several kinds of perturbation. These include random neuron deletions, magnitude pruning, and noise added to weights. The study reports this behavior in bilingual GPT-2 and other models, providing an artificial-model counterpart to the motivating observation about bilingual cognitive reserve.

The paper also supplies a theoretical justification by analyzing linear representation learning. In that setting, multitasking produces more robust representations. Together, the experiments and linear analysis connect learning multiple tasks with resilience to failures inside a model. The neural experiments reproduce an analogous robustness pattern, while the formal result explains the connection within the analyzed linear setting. This gives a computational perspective on the motivating cognitive phenomenon.
summary.tldr: Bilingual language models retain more performance under structural perturbations, and a linear analysis links multitask learning to representation robustness.

title: Multitasking Models are Robust to Structural Failure: A Neural Model for Bilingual Cognitive Reserve

abstract: Numerous real-world systems, ranging from healthcare to energy grids, involve users competing for finite and potentially scarce resources. Designing policies for resource allocation in such real-world systems is challenging for many reasons, including the changing nature of user types and their (possibly urgent) need for resources. Researchers have developed numerous machine learning solutions for determining resource allocation policies in these challenging settings. However, a key limitation has been the absence of good methods and test-beds for benchmarking these policies; almost all resource allocation policies are benchmarked in environments which are either completely synthetic or do not allow _any_ deviation from historical data. In this paper we introduce AllSim, which is a benchmarking environment for realistically simulating the impact and utility of policies for resource allocation in systems in which users compete for such scarce resources. Building such a benchmarking environment is challenging because it needs to successfully take into account _the entire collective_ of potential users and the impact a resource allocation policy has on all the other users in the system. AllSim's benchmarking environment is modular (each component being parameterized individually), learnable (informed by historical data), and customizable (adaptable to changing conditions). These, when interacting with an allocation policy, produce a dataset of simulated outcomes for evaluation and comparison of such policies. We believe AllSim is an essential step towards a more systematic evaluation of policies for scarce resource allocation compared to current approaches for benchmarking such methods.

paragraphs: Resource allocation policies affect systems in which many users compete for limited supplies, including healthcare and energy. Evaluating these policies is difficult because users and their needs can change. Existing benchmarks commonly rely on entirely synthetic environments or historical records that cannot represent outcomes departing from what actually happened.

AllSim introduces a simulation environment intended to bridge these evaluation settings. Its components are individually parameterized, can learn from historical data, and can be customized for changing conditions. When connected to an allocation policy, the environment produces simulated outcome data that can be used to evaluate and compare alternative policies.

A central design concern is the whole population of potential users. Allocating a scarce resource to one user also changes what is available to others, so evaluation needs to capture those collective effects. The paper presents AllSim as a step toward more systematic benchmarking of such interactions. Its contribution is an adaptable evaluation environment, rather than a claim that one allocation policy is universally best.
summary.tldr: AllSim combines historical data and customizable simulation to compare resource allocation policies while accounting for their effects across users.

title: AllSim: Simulating and Benchmarking Resource Allocation Policies in Multi-User Systems

abstract: Randomized smoothing is a leading approach for constructing classifiers that are certifiably robust against adversarial examples. Existing work on randomized smoothing has focused on classifiers with continuous inputs, such as images, where $\ell_p$-norm bounded adversaries are commonly studied. However, there has been limited work for classifiers with discrete or variable-size inputs, such as for source code, which require different threat models and smoothing mechanisms. In this work, we adapt randomized smoothing for discrete sequence classifiers to provide certified robustness against edit distance-bounded adversaries. Our proposed smoothing mechanism randomized deletion (RS-Del) applies random deletion edits, which are (perhaps surprisingly) sufficient to confer robustness against adversarial deletion, insertion and substitution edits. Our proof of certification deviates from the established Neyman-Pearson approach, which is intractable in our setting, and is instead organized around longest common subsequences. We present a case study on malware detection—a binary classification problem on byte sequences where classifier evasion is a well-established threat model. When applied to the popular MalConv malware detection model, our smoothing mechanism RS-Del achieves a certified accuracy of 91% at an edit distance radius of 128 bytes.

paragraphs: Sequence classifiers face attacks that can insert, delete, or replace discrete elements, potentially changing the input length. This differs from the continuous perturbations commonly studied for image classifiers. RS-Del adapts randomized smoothing to provide formal robustness certificates against adversaries whose changes are bounded by edit distance.

Its smoothing mechanism randomly deletes elements from the input sequence. Although the randomization uses deletion alone, the authors show that it can certify resistance to adversarial insertions and substitutions as well as deletions. The proof uses longest common subsequences, avoiding a conventional certification approach that is computationally intractable in this setting.

The paper evaluates the method in malware detection, where inputs are byte sequences and evasion is a relevant threat. Applied to MalConv, RS-Del reaches 91% certified accuracy at a radius of 128 byte edits. This ties classification accuracy to a formal guarantee within the specified edit budget, extending certified smoothing to a setting with discrete, variable-length inputs.
summary.tldr: RS-Del uses random deletions to certify sequence classifiers against bounded insertion, deletion, and substitution attacks.

title: RS-Del: Edit Distance Robustness Certificates for Sequence Classifiers via Randomized Deletion

abstract: Randomized experiments have been the gold standard for assessing the effectiveness of a treatment, policy, or intervention, spanning various fields, including social sciences, biomedical studies, and e-commerce. The classical complete randomization approach assigns treatments based on a pre-specified probability and may lead to inefficient use of data. Adaptive experiments improve upon complete randomization by sequentially learning and updating treatment assignment probabilities using accrued evidence during the experiment. Hence, they can help achieve efficient data use and higher estimation efficiency. However, their application can also raise fairness and equity concerns, as assignment probabilities may vary drastically across groups of participants. Furthermore, when treatment is expected to be extremely beneficial to certain groups of participants, it is more appropriate to expose many of these participants to favorable treatment. In response to these challenges, we propose a fair adaptive experiment strategy that simultaneously enhances data use efficiency, achieves an ``envy-free'' treatment assignment guarantee, and improves the overall welfare of participants. An important feature of our proposed strategy is that we do not impose parametric modeling assumptions on the outcome variables, making it more versatile and applicable to a wider array of applications. Through our theoretical investigation, we characterize the convergence rate of the estimated treatment effects and the associated standard deviations at the group level and further prove that our adaptive treatment assignment algorithm, despite not having a closed-form expression, approaches the optimal allocation rule asymptotically. Our proof strategy takes into account the fact that the allocation decisions in our design depend on sequentially accumulated data, which poses a significant challenge in characterizing the properties and conducting statistical inference of our method. We further provide simulation evidence and two synthetic data studies to showcase the performance of our fair adaptive experiment strategy.

This can use data more efficiently than fixed randomization, but it also means participant groups may receive very different chances of treatment. The paper addresses that tension while recognizing that groups expected to benefit greatly from treatment may appropriately receive it more often.

The proposed strategy combines efficient data use, an envy-free treatment-assignment guarantee, and improved overall participant welfare. It does not require parametric models for outcome variables. This matters because the allocation strategy can be studied without first committing to a particular parametric description of how participant outcomes are distributed.

The theoretical analysis characterizes convergence rates for group-level treatment-effect estimates and their associated standard deviations. It also proves that the assignment algorithm approaches the optimal allocation rule asymptotically, despite lacking a closed-form expression. The proof accounts for decisions depending on previously collected data, a dependence that complicates statistical inference. Simulations and two synthetic-data studies illustrate the strategy's performance alongside these guarantees.
summary.tldr: A fair adaptive experiment strategy balances estimation efficiency, an envy-free assignment guarantee, and participant welfare.

title: Fair Adaptive Experiments

abstract: We introduce Alexa Arena, a user-centric simulation platform to facilitate research in building assistive conversational embodied agents. Alexa Arena features multi-room layouts and an abundance of interactable objects. With user-friendly graphics and control mechanisms, the platform supports the development of gamified robotic tasks readily accessible to general human users, allowing high-efficiency data collection and EAI system evaluation. Along with the platform, we introduce a dialog-enabled task completion benchmark with online human evaluations.

paragraphs: Alexa Arena is a simulation platform for studying assistive agents that combine conversation with actions in an environment. Its focus is the interaction between people and embodied agents: users can participate in tasks involving a simulated world, while researchers develop and evaluate systems intended to help them complete those tasks.

The environment provides layouts containing multiple rooms and many objects that can be interacted with. User-friendly graphics and controls support robotic tasks presented in a game-like form. Making those tasks accessible to general users is central to the platform's purpose, because human participation supplies data for research and enables evaluation of how an embodied system performs during interaction.

Alongside the simulator, the authors introduce a task-completion benchmark that includes dialogue and online human evaluation. This pairs a place to build interactive tasks with a way to assess agents completing them with people. The stated contribution is research infrastructure for efficient data collection and evaluation, with conversation and environmental interaction brought together in the same platform.
summary.tldr: Alexa Arena provides an accessible simulator and human-evaluated benchmark for conversational agents that act in interactive environments.

title: Alexa Arena: A User-Centric Interactive Platform for Embodied AI

abstract: Sparse linear models are one of several core tools for interpretable machine learning, a field of emerging importance as predictive models permeate decision-making in many domains. Unfortunately, sparse linear models are far less flexible as functions of their input features than black-box models like deep neural networks. With this capability gap in mind, we study a not-uncommon situation where the input features dichotomize into two groups: explanatory features, which are candidates for inclusion as variables in an interpretable model, and contextual features, which select from the candidate variables and determine their effects. This dichotomy leads us to the contextual lasso, a new statistical estimator that fits a sparse linear model to the explanatory features such that the sparsity pattern and coefficients vary as a function of the contextual features. The fitting process learns this function nonparametrically via a deep neural network. To attain sparse coefficients, we train the network with a novel lasso regularizer in the form of a projection layer that maps the network's output onto the space of $\ell_1$-constrained linear models. An extensive suite of experiments on real and synthetic data suggests that the learned models, which remain highly transparent, can be sparser than the regular lasso without sacrificing the predictive power of a standard deep neural network.

paragraphs: Sparse linear models are interpretable because they base predictions on a limited set of features with explicit coefficients. Their simplicity also restricts flexibility. The contextual lasso addresses a setting in which inputs divide into explanatory features, whose effects should be interpretable, and contextual features, which determine which explanatory variables matter and how strongly they contribute.

The method fits a linear model in the explanatory features, but allows both its selected variables and coefficients to change with context. A deep neural network learns this dependence without prescribing a fixed parametric form. A projection layer maps the network's output into the space of linear models satisfying an l1 constraint, providing the lasso-style regularization needed for sparse coefficients.

Experiments on real and synthetic data suggest that the resulting models can be sparser than ordinary lasso while retaining the predictive power of a standard deep network. The interpretation is local to the chosen context: the active explanatory variables and their effects remain explicit, while the neural network supplies flexibility in how those effects vary.
summary.tldr: The contextual lasso uses a neural network to choose context-dependent sparse linear coefficients, combining flexibility with explicit feature effects.

title: The Contextual Lasso: Sparse Linear Models via Deep Neural Networks

abstract: In many applications of machine learning, a large number of variables are considered. Motivated by machine learning of interacting particle systems, we consider the situation when the number of input variables goes to infinity. First, we continue the recent investigation of the mean field limit of kernels and their reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, completing the existing theory. Next, we provide results relevant for approximation with such kernels in the mean field limit, including a representer theorem. Finally, we use these kernels in the context of statistical learning in the mean field limit, focusing on Support Vector Machines. In particular, we show mean field convergence of empirical and infinite-sample solutions as well as the convergence of the corresponding risks. On the one hand, our results establish rigorous mean field limits in the context of kernel methods, providing new theoretical tools and insights for large-scale problems. On the other hand, our setting corresponds to a new form of limit of learning problems, which seems to have not been investigated yet in the statistical learning theory literature.
