paragraphs: A neighborhood graph reflects both relationships among sampled points and the density from which those points were drawn. This paper asks how to study such a graph as though its points had instead come from another density. The proposed solution changes edge weights to adjust the graph’s cuts and volumes.

The authors introduce the f-adjusted graph and prove that its cuts and volumes approach the desired alternatives as sample size grows without bound. They also give an algebraic interpretation: the adjusted normalized Laplacian belongs to a natural family of diagonal modifications of the original normalized Laplacian. This connects a geometric change of sampling density to a matrix operation.

Algorithms based on cuts and volumes, including spectral clustering, can then operate on the adjusted graph. The method offers a way to investigate an alternative sampling distribution without access to a new sample from it. The authors identify sample-bias correction, data uniformization, and multiscale graph analysis as applications, with the correctness guarantee stated in the large-sample limit.
summary.tldr: Reweighting a neighborhood graph makes its cuts and volumes asymptotically behave as if the data came from a different density.

title: The f-Adjusted Graph Laplacian: a Diagonal Modification with a Geometric Interpretation

abstract: Scalable training of Bayesian nonparametric models is a notoriously difficult challenge. We explore the use of coresets - a data summarization technique originating from computational geometry - for this task. Coresets are weighted subsets of the data such that models trained on these coresets are provably competitive with models trained on the full dataset. Coresets sublinear in the dataset size allow for fast approximate inference with provable guarantees. Existing constructions, however, are limited to parametric problems. Using novel techniques in coreset construction we show the existence of coresets for DP-Means - a prototypical nonparametric clustering problem - and provide a practical construction algorithm. We empirically demonstrate that our algorithm allows us to efficiently trade off computation time and approximation error and thus scale DP-Means to large datasets. For instance, with coresets we can obtain a computational speedup of 45x at an approximation error of only 2.4% compared to solving on the full data set. In contrast, for the same subsample size, the “naive” approach of uniformly subsampling the data incurs an approximation error of 22.5%.

paragraphs: Training nonparametric models on large datasets can be computationally demanding. This paper investigates coresets: weighted subsets intended to preserve enough information that fitting a model to the summary remains provably competitive with fitting it to all observations. A sufficiently small coreset can therefore reduce computation while providing a principled approximation to the full-data problem.

The authors establish the existence of coresets for DP-Means, a nonparametric clustering problem, and provide a practical construction algorithm. This extends coreset construction beyond the parametric problems covered by earlier constructions. The contribution combines a theoretical justification for the summary with a procedure that makes the idea usable for large clustering datasets.

Experiments demonstrate a tradeoff between computation time and approximation error. In one reported example, the coreset produces a 45-fold speedup with 2.4% approximation error relative to solving on the full dataset. Uniform subsampling at the same subset size incurs 22.5% error. This comparison illustrates why deliberately constructing a weighted summary can preserve the clustering problem more effectively than simply selecting observations uniformly.
summary.tldr: Provably justified weighted data summaries make DP-Means clustering faster while offering a controllable tradeoff between computation and approximation error.

title: Coresets for Nonparametric Estimation - the Case of DP-Means

abstract: Alternating Gibbs sampling is a modification of classical Gibbs sampling where several variables are simultaneously sampled from their joint conditional distribution. In this work, we investigate the mixing rate of alternating Gibbs sampling with a particular emphasis on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) and variants.
originalAbstract: Alternating Gibbs sampling is a modification of classical Gibbs sampling where several variables are simultaneously sampled from their joint conditional distribution. In this work, we investigate the mixing rate of alternating Gibbs sampling with a particular emphasis on Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) and variants.

paragraphs: The paper studies alternating Gibbs sampling, a modification of the classical Gibbs sampling procedure. Its defining feature is that several variables are sampled together from their joint conditional distribution. The unit of an update is therefore a collection of variables, with their joint conditional relationship retained during that update.

The central question is the sampler's mixing rate: how quickly the sampling process approaches the distribution it is intended to represent. This places the emphasis on the behavior of repeated sampling updates. Describing which conditional distribution to sample from specifies the update rule; studying mixing asks how that rule behaves as the process continues.

The investigation gives particular attention to restricted Boltzmann machines and related models. Within that focus, the contribution is an analysis of convergence behavior for a sampling procedure that updates multiple variables simultaneously. The abstract identifies the algorithmic mechanism and the quantity being investigated, so the supported takeaway is the study of mixing rates in these models, without a stated direction or magnitude of improvement.
summary.tldr: The paper investigates how quickly alternating Gibbs sampling mixes, focusing on restricted Boltzmann machines and related models.

title: Mixing Rates for the Alternating Gibbs Sampler over Restricted Boltzmann Machines and Friends

abstract: The pre-dominant approach to language modeling to date is based on recurrent neural networks. Their success on this task is often linked to their ability to capture unbounded context. In this paper we develop a finite context approach through stacked convolutions, which can be more efficient since they allow parallelization over sequential tokens. We propose a novel simplified gating mechanism that outperforms Oord et al. (2016) and investigate the impact of key architectural decisions. The proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art on the WikiText-103 benchmark, even though it features long-term dependencies, as well as competitive results on the Google Billion Words benchmark. Our model reduces the latency to score a sentence by an order of magnitude compared to a recurrent baseline. To our knowledge, this is the first time a non-recurrent approach is competitive with strong recurrent models on these large scale language tasks.

We propose a novel simplified gating mechanism that outperforms Oord et al. (2016) and investigate the impact of key architectural decisions. The proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art on the WikiText-103 benchmark, even though it features long-term dependencies, as well as competitive results on the Google Billion Words benchmark. Our model reduces the latency to score a sentence by an order of magnitude compared to a recurrent baseline. To our knowledge, this is the first time a non-recurrent approach is competitive with strong recurrent models on these large scale language tasks.

paragraphs: This paper explores language modeling with stacked convolutions that use a finite amount of context. The motivation is computational: convolutional processing allows parallelization across tokens in a sequence. The work tests whether this approach can deliver strong language-modeling performance despite using bounded context, including on a benchmark containing long-term dependencies.

The authors introduce a simplified gating mechanism and investigate important architectural choices. They report that the gate outperforms an earlier mechanism considered in the paper. Combined with stacked convolutions, it produces a non-recurrent model whose design supports efficient sequence processing while retaining competitive predictive performance on large language tasks.

The model achieves state-of-the-art results on WikiText-103 and competitive results on Google Billion Words. It also reduces the latency of scoring a sentence by an order of magnitude relative to a recurrent baseline. The authors qualify their historical claim: to their knowledge, this is the first non-recurrent approach competitive with strong recurrent models on these large-scale tasks.
summary.tldr: Gated convolutional language models achieve strong large-scale benchmark results while reducing sentence-scoring latency through parallelizable finite-context processing.

title: Language Modeling with Gated Convolutional Networks

abstract: Training deep neural networks is a highly nontrivial task, involving carefully selecting appropriate training algorithms, scheduling step sizes and tuning other hyperparameters. Trying different combinations can be quite labor-intensive and time consuming. Recently, researchers have tried to use deep learning algorithms to exploit the landscape of the loss function of the training problem of interest, and learn how to optimize over it in an automatic way. In this paper, we propose a new learning-to-learn model and some useful and practical tricks. Our optimizer outperforms generic, hand-crafted optimization algorithms and state-of-the-art learning-to-learn optimizers by DeepMind in many tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithms on a number of tasks, including deep MLPs, CNNs, and simple LSTMs.

paragraphs: Training a deep network requires choices about the optimization algorithm, step-size schedule, and other hyperparameters. Exploring combinations can take substantial manual effort and computation. This paper develops a learning-to-learn approach in which a model learns how to optimize, building on the idea of using deep learning to exploit a training problem’s loss landscape.

The authors propose a new learned optimizer together with practical techniques for using it. The object being learned is the optimization behavior itself, making the training procedure part of what can improve through learning. This addresses the burden of relying entirely on manually selected optimization rules and settings for neural-network training.

The reported optimizer outperforms generic handcrafted algorithms and existing DeepMind learning-to-learn optimizers on many tasks. Demonstrations include deep multilayer perceptrons, convolutional networks, and simple LSTMs. The wording matters: the advantage is reported across many evaluated tasks, rather than asserted for every optimization problem. These results support learned optimization across several neural-network families.
summary.tldr: A learned optimizer and practical training techniques outperform handcrafted and earlier learned optimizers on many evaluated tasks.

title: Learning Gradient Descent: Better Generalization and Longer Horizons

abstract: The large model capacity of latent space models (LSMs) enables them to achieve great performance on various applications, but meanwhile renders LSMs to be prone to overfitting. Several recent studies investigate a new type of regularization approach, which encourages components in LSMs to be diverse, for the sake of alleviating overfitting. While they have shown promising empirical effectiveness, in theory why larger “diversity” results in less overfitting is still unclear. To bridge this gap, we propose a new diversity-promoting approach that is both theoretically analyzable and empirically effective. Specifically, we use near-orthogonality to characterize “diversity” and impose angular constraints (ACs) on the components of LSMs to promote diversity. A generalization error analysis shows that larger diversity results in smaller estimation error and larger approximation error. An efficient ADMM algorithm is developed to solve the constrained LSM problems. Experiments demonstrate that ACs improve generalization performance of LSMs and outperform other diversity-promoting approaches.

paragraphs: Latent space models have enough capacity to capture complex patterns, but that flexibility can also lead to overfitting. Encouraging different model components to be diverse had shown empirical promise. This paper asks for a more precise account of diversity and a theoretical explanation of its effect on generalization.

The authors describe diversity through near-orthogonality and impose constraints on the angles between components. Their analysis exposes a trade-off: increasing diversity reduces estimation error while increasing approximation error. In other words, the restriction can improve learning from limited observations while also reducing the model's ability to represent the target. The analysis therefore does not imply that more diversity is always better.

An efficient ADMM algorithm solves the resulting constrained learning problems. Experiments show improved generalization and stronger results than the other diversity-promoting approaches considered. The contribution joins a concrete geometric constraint, an optimization method, and a theoretical account of competing errors, making the benefits and costs of diversity more explicit.
summary.tldr: Angular constraints improve reported generalization while revealing that greater component diversity trades lower estimation error for higher approximation error.

title: Learning Latent Space Models with Angular Constraints

abstract: Recent work on generative text modeling has found that variational autoencoders (VAE) with LSTM decoders perform worse than simpler LSTM language models (Bowman et al., 2015). This negative result is so far poorly understood, but has been attributed to the propensity of LSTM decoders to ignore conditioning information from the encoder. In this paper, we experiment with a new type of decoder for VAE: a dilated CNN. By changing the decoder’s dilation architecture, we control the size of context from previously generated words. In experiments, we find that there is a trade-off between contextual capacity of the decoder and effective use of encoding information. We show that when carefully managed, VAEs can outperform LSTM language models. We demonstrate perplexity gains on two datasets, representing the first positive language modeling result with VAE. Further, we conduct an in-depth investigation of the use of VAE (with our new decoding architecture) for semi-supervised and unsupervised labeling tasks, demonstrating gains over several strong baselines.

paragraphs: Earlier text-generation results found that variational autoencoders with LSTM decoders could perform worse than simpler LSTM language models. One proposed explanation was that the decoder ignored information supplied by the encoder. This paper investigates that issue by changing how much previously generated text the decoder can use.

The authors replace the LSTM decoder with a dilated convolutional network. Adjusting its dilation architecture controls the amount of preceding context available during generation. Their experiments reveal a trade-off: a decoder's capacity to use context interacts with how effectively it uses the encoded information. Decoder design therefore becomes a way to manage the contribution of the latent representation.

When this balance is carefully managed, the authors show that their variational autoencoders outperform LSTM language models, with perplexity improvements on two datasets. They also investigate semi-supervised and unsupervised labeling, reporting gains over several strong baselines. These findings support the usefulness of controlling decoder context for both language modeling and the labeling tasks studied.
summary.tldr: Dilated convolutional decoders help text VAEs balance contextual capacity with use of encoded information, improving reported modeling and labeling results.

title: Improved Variational Autoencoders for Text Modeling using Dilated Convolutions

abstract: In this paper, we showcase the interplay between discrete and continuous optimization in network-structured settings. We propose the first fully decentralized optimization method for a wide class of non-convex objective functions that possess a diminishing returns property. More specifically, given an arbitrary connected network and a global continuous submodular function, formed by a sum of local functions, we develop Decentralized Continuous Greedy (DCG), a message passing algorithm that converges to the tight $(1-1/e)$ approximation factor of the optimum global solution using only local computation and communication. We also provide strong convergence bounds as a function of network size and spectral characteristics of the underlying topology. Interestingly, DCG readily provides a simple recipe for decentralized discrete submodular maximization through the means of continuous relaxations. Formally, we demonstrate that by lifting the local discrete functions to continuous domains and using DCG as an interface we can develop a consensus algorithm that also achieves the tight $(1-1/e)$ approximation guarantee of the global discrete solution once a proper rounding scheme is applied.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization across a connected network where a global objective is the sum of local functions. The relevant objectives have diminishing returns, giving structure to an otherwise nonconvex problem. The aim is to obtain a strong global solution using computation and communication available locally at the network’s nodes.

The proposed Decentralized Continuous Greedy algorithm uses message passing to achieve the tight approximation factor 1−1/e for the studied continuous submodular setting. This is an approximation guarantee relative to the global optimum. The analysis also bounds convergence in terms of network size and spectral properties of the topology, connecting optimization progress to the structure of communication.

The authors then use continuous optimization to handle discrete submodular problems. Local discrete functions are extended to continuous domains, the decentralized method coordinates optimization, and a suitable rounding procedure returns a discrete solution. With proper rounding, the resulting consensus algorithm retains the same tight approximation factor. This provides a shared route to decentralized solutions in both settings.
summary.tldr: A decentralized message-passing algorithm achieves a tight submodular approximation guarantee and extends from continuous to discrete optimization through relaxation and rounding.

title: Decentralized Submodular Maximization: Bridging Discrete and Continuous Settings

abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) have demonstrated dominating performance in many fields; since AlexNet, networks used in practice are going wider and deeper. On the theoretical side, a long line of works have been focusing on why we can train neural networks when there is only one hidden layer. The theory of multi-layer networks remains unsettled. In this work, we prove simple algorithms such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD) can find Global Minima on the training objective of DNNs in Polynomial Time. We only make two assumptions: the inputs do not degenerate and the network is over-parameterized. The latter means the number of hidden neurons is sufficiently large: polynomial in L, the number of DNN layers and in n, the number of training samples. As concrete examples, starting from randomly initialized weights, we show that SGD attains 100% training accuracy in classification tasks, or minimizes regression loss in linear convergence speed eps e^{-T}, with running time polynomial in n and L. Our theory applies to the widely-used but non-smooth ReLU activation, and to any smooth and possibly non-convex loss functions. In terms of network architectures, our theory at least applies to fully-connected neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNN), and residual neural networks (ResNet).

paragraphs: This paper addresses a basic theoretical question: why can simple training algorithms successfully optimize networks with many layers? Earlier theory had concentrated heavily on networks with one hidden layer. The authors establish conditions under which stochastic gradient descent can reach a global minimum of a deep network’s training objective in polynomial time.

The result rests on two stated assumptions: the inputs must not degenerate, and the network must have sufficiently many hidden neurons. The required width is polynomial in the number of layers and training examples. Under these conditions, the analysis starts from random weights and establishes perfect training classification accuracy or a linear convergence rate for regression loss.

The theory covers ReLU activations despite their lack of smoothness, and allows smooth losses that may themselves be nonconvex. Its architectural coverage includes fully connected, convolutional, and residual networks. The contribution is a conditional explanation of successful training across several important network families. Its guarantees concern the training objective; perfect training accuracy does not by itself establish accuracy on unseen examples.
summary.tldr: Under nondegenerate inputs and sufficient overparameterization, stochastic gradient descent can globally optimize deep networks’ training objectives in polynomial time.

title: A Convergence Theory for Deep Learning via Over-Parameterization

abstract: Researchers have proposed a range of model compression techniques to reduce the computational and memory footprint of deep neural networks (DNNs). In this work, we introduce Learned Intermediate representation Training (LIT), a novel model compression technique that outperforms a range of recent model compression techniques by leveraging the highly repetitive structure of modern DNNs (e.g., ResNet). LIT uses a teacher DNN to train a student DNN of reduced depth by leveraging two key ideas: 1) LIT directly compares intermediate representations of the teacher and student model and 2) LIT uses the intermediate representation from the teacher model’s previous block as input to the current student block during training, improving stability of intermediate representations in the student network. We show that LIT can substantially reduce network size without loss in accuracy on a range of DNN architectures and datasets. For example, LIT can compress ResNet on CIFAR10 by 3.4$\times$ outperforming network slimming and FitNets. Furthermore, LIT can compress, by depth, ResNeXt 5.5$\times$ on CIFAR10 (image classification), VDCNN by 1.7$\times$ on Amazon Reviews (sentiment analysis), and StarGAN by 1.8$\times$ on CelebA (style transfer, i.e., GANs).

paragraphs: Learned Intermediate representation Training, or LIT, compresses deep networks by teaching a shallower student from a deeper teacher. The method exploits the repeated block structure found in architectures such as ResNet. Its focus is on reducing depth while preserving useful intermediate computations learned by the larger network.

LIT directly compares the teacher's and student's intermediate representations. During training, it also feeds the teacher's previous-block representation into the current student block. The authors identify this second choice as improving the stability of the student's intermediate representations. Together, these ideas provide guidance inside the network rather than relying only on its final output.

The authors report substantial size reductions without accuracy loss across several architectures and datasets. Examples include 3.4-fold ResNet compression on CIFAR10, outperforming network slimming and FitNets, and 5.5-fold depth compression for ResNeXt. They also report compression of VDCNN for sentiment analysis and StarGAN for style transfer. These results demonstrate the technique across the evaluated image, text, and generative-model tasks, extending its evidence beyond a single architecture.
summary.tldr: LIT trains shallower networks using teacher intermediate representations, achieving substantial reported compression without accuracy loss across several tasks.

title: LIT: Learned Intermediate Representation Training for Model Compression

abstract: We introduce Deep Reasoning Networks (DRNets), an end-to-end framework that combines deep learning with constraint reasoning for solving pattern de-mixing problems, typically in an unsupervised or very-weakly-supervised setting. DRNets exploit problem structure and prior knowledge by tightly combining constraint reasoning with stochastic-gradient-based neural network optimization. Our motivating task is from materials discovery and concerns inferring crystal structures of materials from X-ray diffraction data (Crystal-Structure-Phase-Mapping). Given the complexity of its underlying scientific domain, we start by introducing DRNets on an analogous but much simpler task: de-mixing overlapping hand-written Sudokus (Multi-MNIST-Sudoku). On Multi-MNIST-Sudoku, DRNets almost perfectly recovered the mixed Sudokus’ digits, with 100% digit accuracy, outperforming the supervised state-of-the-art MNIST de-mixing models. On Crystal-Structure-Phase-Mapping, DRNets significantly outperform the state of the art and experts’ capabilities, recovering more precise and physically meaningful crystal structures.

paragraphs: Deep Reasoning Networks address pattern de-mixing: recovering individual components from observations in which several patterns overlap. The framework combines neural learning with constraint reasoning, typically with no supervision or very weak supervision. Its main idea is to use known problem structure during learning, so the network’s interpretation of a mixture is guided by relationships that its components should satisfy.

The authors tightly integrate these constraints with stochastic-gradient optimization in an end-to-end system. They first introduce the approach through overlapping handwritten Sudoku puzzles, a simpler analogue of their scientific application. On this task, the reported digit accuracy is 100%, with nearly perfect recovery of the mixed puzzles, exceeding the supervised MNIST de-mixing models used for comparison.

The motivating application is inferring crystal structures from X-ray diffraction data. Here, the authors report substantial improvements over existing methods and expert capabilities, recovering structures that are more precise and physically meaningful. Together, the two applications illustrate how constraint reasoning can help separate ambiguous observations by bringing domain knowledge directly into neural optimization.
summary.tldr: Deep Reasoning Networks combine neural optimization with domain constraints to recover overlapping patterns in Sudoku puzzles and crystal-structure data.

title: Deep Reasoning Networks for Unsupervised Pattern De-mixing with Constraint Reasoning

abstract: In this paper, we introduce a novel form of value function, $Q(s, s’)$, that expresses the utility of transitioning from a state $s$ to a neighboring state $s’$ and then acting optimally thereafter. In order to derive an optimal policy, we develop a forward dynamics model that learns to make next-state predictions that maximize this value. This formulation decouples actions from values while still learning off-policy. We highlight the benefits of this approach in terms of value function transfer, learning within redundant action spaces, and learning off-policy from state observations generated by sub-optimal or completely random policies. Code and videos are available at http://sites.google.com/view/qss-paper.

In order to derive an optimal policy, we develop a forward dynamics model that learns to make next-state predictions that maximize this value. This formulation decouples actions from values while still learning off-policy. We highlight the benefits of this approach in terms of value function transfer, learning within redundant action spaces, and learning off-policy from state observations generated by sub-optimal or completely random policies. paragraphs: This paper introduces a value function that scores a transition between two states. Q(s, s′) measures the utility of moving from the current state to a neighboring state and then behaving optimally afterward. The representation places the value on the state transition, separating the question of which outcome is desirable from the actions used to reach it.

To derive an optimal policy, the authors develop a forward dynamics model that learns next-state predictions chosen to maximize this value. The overall formulation still supports off-policy learning, so learning can use observations generated by behavior other than the policy being developed. This connects transition evaluation with a model that seeks valuable subsequent states.

The paper highlights benefits for transferring value functions, handling redundant action spaces, and learning from state observations produced by suboptimal or completely random policies. These applications share a motivation: useful information about transitions need not be tied directly to a particular action representation or to expert-quality behavior. The stated contribution is a way to exploit that separation within off-policy learning.
summary.tldr: A state-to-state value function separates values from actions and supports off-policy learning through a model that predicts valuable next states.

title: Estimating Q(s,s’) with Deep Deterministic Dynamics Gradients

abstract: Humans intuitively recognize objects’ physical properties and predict their motion, even when the objects are engaged in complicated interactions. The abilities to perform physical reasoning and to adapt to new environments, while intrinsic to humans, remain challenging to state-of-the-art computational models. In this work, we present a neural model that simultaneously reasons about physics and makes future predictions based on visual and dynamics priors. The visual prior predicts a particle-based representation of the system from visual observations. An inference module operates on those particles, predicting and refining estimates of particle locations, object states, and physical parameters, subject to the constraints imposed by the dynamics prior, which we refer to as visual grounding. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in environments involving rigid objects, deformable materials, and fluids. Experiments show that our model can infer the physical properties within a few observations, which allows the model to quickly adapt to unseen scenarios and make accurate predictions into the future.

paragraphs: Predicting motion from visual observations requires reasoning about both what is present and how it behaves physically. This paper introduces a neural model that combines visual and dynamics priors to infer physical properties and predict future states. Its goal is to support physical reasoning and adaptation when the environment changes.

The visual prior converts observations into a particle-based representation of the system. An inference module then predicts and refines particle locations, object states, and physical parameters while respecting constraints supplied by the dynamics prior. The authors call this process visual grounding: visual estimates are refined through the requirements of the physical model.

The method is demonstrated in environments containing rigid objects, deformable materials, and fluids. Experiments show that it can infer physical properties from a few observations, allowing rapid adaptation to unseen scenarios and accurate future predictions. These results support combining visual evidence with dynamical constraints so that perception and physical inference contribute jointly to forecasting.
summary.tldr: A particle-based model combines visual evidence and dynamics constraints to infer physical properties and adapt its predictions to unseen scenarios.

title: Visual Grounding of Learned Physical Models

abstract: Despite recent advancements in the field of Deep Reinforcement Learning, Deep Q-network (DQN) models still show lackluster performance on problems with high-dimensional action spaces. The problem is even more pronounced for cases with high-dimensional continuous action spaces due to a combinatorial increase in the number of the outputs. Recent works approach the problem by dividing the network into multiple parallel or sequential (action) modules responsible for different discretized actions. However, there are drawbacks to both the parallel and the sequential approaches. Parallel module architectures lack coordination between action modules, leading to extra complexity in the task, while a sequential structure can result in the vanishing gradients problem and exploding parameter space. In this work, we show that the compositional structure of the action modules has a significant impact on model performance. We propose a novel approach to infer the network structure for DQN models operating with high-dimensional continuous actions. Our method is based on the uncertainty estimation techniques introduced in the paper. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on MuJoCo environments with high-dimensional continuous action spaces. Furthermore, we demonstrate the improvement of the introduced approach on a realistic AAA sailing simulator game.

paragraphs: Deep Q-networks struggle with high-dimensional continuous actions because representing combinations of discretized actions can require a combinatorial number of outputs. One response is to divide the network into action modules. This paper examines how the arrangement of those modules affects the model’s ability to control a system.

The authors describe weaknesses in two established arrangements. Parallel modules lack coordination, which adds complexity to the task. Sequential modules can encounter vanishing gradients and a rapidly expanding parameter space. Their proposed method infers the network’s compositional structure using uncertainty-estimation techniques introduced in the paper, making module organization part of the solution rather than treating it as a fixed design choice.

The authors show that compositional structure substantially affects performance. Their method achieves state-of-the-art results on the tested MuJoCo environments with high-dimensional continuous actions, and they also demonstrate improvement in a realistic AAA sailing simulator game. These findings support adapting the relationships among action modules as a useful way to improve DQN control in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Inferring how DQN action modules connect using uncertainty estimates improves reported performance on high-dimensional continuous-control tasks.

title: Inferring DQN structure for high-dimensional continuous control

abstract: In many real-world applications, data are collected in the form of a stream, whose feature space can evolve over time. For instance, in the environmental monitoring task, features can be dynamically vanished or augmented due to the existence of expired old sensors and deployed new sensors. Furthermore, besides the evolvable feature space, the data distribution is usually changing in the streaming scenario. When both feature space and data distribution are evolvable, it is quite challenging to design algorithms with guarantees, particularly theoretical understandings of generalization ability. To address this difficulty, we propose a novel discrepancy measure for data with evolving feature space and data distribution, named the \emph{evolving discrepancy}. Based on that, we present the generalization error analysis, and the theory motivates the design of a learning algorithm which is further implemented by deep neural networks. Empirical studies on synthetic data verify the rationale of our proposed discrepancy measure, and extensive experiments on real-world tasks validate the effectiveness of our algorithm.

Empirical studies on synthetic data verify the rationale of our proposed discrepancy measure, and extensive experiments on real-world tasks validate the effectiveness of our algorithm.

paragraphs: Learning from a stream becomes especially difficult when both the available measurements and their distribution change. In environmental monitoring, for example, old sensors can disappear and new ones can add features. This paper addresses that combined problem, where a model must cope with changes in what is observed as well as changes in the incoming data.

The authors introduce evolving discrepancy, a measure designed for comparisons involving both an evolving feature space and an evolving distribution. They use it to analyze generalization error. This gives the algorithm’s design a theoretical basis for handling the two forms of change together.

The resulting learning algorithm is implemented with deep neural networks. Synthetic experiments support the rationale behind the discrepancy measure, while extensive experiments on real tasks demonstrate the algorithm’s effectiveness. These two evaluations serve complementary purposes: one examines the proposed way of describing change, and the other tests the learning method motivated by that description.
summary.tldr: Evolving discrepancy supports generalization analysis and a neural learning algorithm for streams whose features and distributions both change.

title: Learning with Feature and Distribution Evolvable Streams

abstract: In this work, we study dynamic clustering problems from the perspective of online learning. We consider an online learning problem, called \textit{Dynamic $k$-Clustering}, in which $k$ centers are maintained in a metric space over time (centers may change positions) such as a dynamically changing set of $r$ clients is served in the best possible way. The connection cost at round $t$ is given by the \textit{$p$-norm} of the vector formed by the distance of each client to its closest center at round $t$, for some $p\geq 1$. We design a \textit{$\Theta\left( \min(k,r) \right)$-regret} polynomial-time online learning algorithm, while we show that, under some well-established computational complexity conjectures, \textit{constant-regret} cannot be achieved in polynomial-time. In addition to the efficient solution of Dynamic $k$-Clustering, our work contributes to the long line of research of combinatorial online learning.

paragraphs: Dynamic k-Clustering studies how to maintain k centers while the clients they serve change over time. Centers may move within a metric space, and each client connects to its nearest center. At each round, the connection cost combines those distances using a p-norm, with p at least one. This makes the problem a sequence of related clustering decisions.

The paper approaches this setting through online learning, where decisions must be made as the sequence unfolds. It gives a polynomial-time algorithm with a stated regret guarantee of order min(k, r), where r is the number of clients. The result explicitly links the guarantee to the smaller of the center count and client count.

The authors also establish a computational obstacle: under established complexity conjectures, a polynomial-time algorithm cannot achieve constant regret. This is a conditional hardness result, alongside the constructive algorithm. Together, the results describe both an efficient approach and a constraint on stronger guarantees, contributing to the study of online learning over combinatorial decisions.
summary.tldr: The paper gives a polynomial-time dynamic clustering algorithm with a min(k, r)-scale regret guarantee and a conditional barrier to constant regret.

title: Efficient Online Learning for Dynamic k-Clustering

abstract: Standard training via empirical risk minimization (ERM) can produce models that achieve low error on average but high error on minority groups, especially in the presence of spurious correlations between the input and label. Prior approaches to this problem, like group distributionally robust optimization (group DRO), generally require group annotations for every training point. On the other hand, approaches that do not use group annotations generally do not improve minority performance. For example, we find that joint DRO, which dynamically upweights examples with high training loss, tends to optimize for examples that are irrelevant to the specific groups we seek to do well on. In this paper, we propose a simple two-stage approach, JTT, that achieves comparable performance to group DRO while only requiring group annotations on a significantly smaller validation set. JTT first attempts to identify informative training examples, which are often minority examples, by training an initial ERM classifier and selecting the examples with high training loss. Then, it trains a final classifier by upsampling the selected examples. Crucially, unlike joint DRO, JTT does not iteratively upsample examples that have high loss under the final classifier. On four image classification and natural language processing tasks with spurious correlations, we show that JTT closes 85% of the gap in accuracy on the worst group between ERM and group DRO.

paragraphs: A model can achieve good average accuracy while performing poorly on minority groups, particularly when training data contain spurious input-label correlations. Methods such as group distributionally robust optimization address this but generally require group labels for every training example. Just Train Twice, or JTT, reduces that annotation requirement to a much smaller validation set.

JTT first trains an ordinary empirical-risk-minimization classifier and selects training examples with high loss. Those examples are often informative minority examples. It then trains a final classifier while upsampling the selected set. The selection remains fixed during this second stage, distinguishing JTT from methods that continually change which examples receive greater weight based on the final classifier’s current losses.

On four image-classification and language-processing tasks with spurious correlations, JTT closes 85% of the worst-group accuracy gap between ordinary training and group DRO. This supports using an initial model’s errors to identify useful training emphasis. The method avoids training-set group annotations while still requiring group information for validation.
summary.tldr: JTT improves worst-group performance by retraining with extra emphasis on an initial model’s high-loss examples, using group labels only for validation.

title: Just Train Twice: Improving Group Robustness without Training Group Information

abstract: Game optimization has been extensively studied when decision variables lie in a finite-dimensional space, of which solutions correspond to pure strategies at the Nash equilibrium (NE), and the gradient descent-ascent (GDA) method works widely in practice. In this paper, we consider infinite-dimensional zero-sum games by a min-max distributional optimization problem over a space of probability measures defined on a continuous variable set, which is inspired by finding a mixed NE for finite-dimensional zero-sum games. We then aim to answer the following question: \textit{Will GDA-type algorithms still be provably efficient when extended to infinite-dimensional zero-sum games?} To answer this question, we propose a particle-based variational transport algorithm based on GDA in the functional spaces. Specifically, the algorithm performs multi-step functional gradient descent-ascent in the Wasserstein space via pushing two sets of particles in the variable space. By characterizing the gradient estimation error from variational form maximization and the convergence behavior of each player with different objective landscapes, we prove rigorously that the generalized GDA algorithm converges to the NE or the value of the game efficiently for a class of games under the Polyak-Ł{ojasiewicz} (PL) condition. To conclude, we provide complete statistical and convergence guarantees for solving an infinite-dimensional zero-sum game via a provably efficient particle-based method. Additionally, our work provides the first thorough statistical analysis for the particle-based algorithm to learn an objective functional with a variational form using universal approximators (\textit{i.e.}, neural networks (NNs)), which is of independent interest.

Such distributional decisions are motivated by mixed strategies, but they create an infinite-dimensional optimization problem. The authors ask whether the familiar gradient descent-ascent approach can remain provably efficient in this broader setting.

summary.tldr: A particle-based descent-ascent method efficiently solves a class of distributional zero-sum games under a Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition.

title: Infinite-Dimensional Optimization for Zero-Sum Games via Variational Transport

abstract: Motivated by modern applications, such as online advertisement and recommender systems, we study the top-$k$ extreme contextual bandits problem, where the total number of arms can be enormous, and the learner is allowed to select $k$ arms and observe all or some of the rewards for the chosen arms. We first propose an algorithm for the non-extreme realizable setting, utilizing the Inverse Gap Weighting strategy for selecting multiple arms. We show that our algorithm has a regret guarantee of $O(k\sqrt{(A-k+1)T \log (|F|T)})$, where $A$ is the total number of arms and $F$ is the class containing the regression function, while only requiring $\tilde{O}(A)$ computation per time step. In the extreme setting, where the total number of arms can be in the millions, we propose a practically-motivated arm hierarchy model that induces a certain structure in mean rewards to ensure statistical and computational efficiency. The hierarchical structure allows for an exponential reduction in the number of relevant arms for each context, thus resulting in a regret guarantee of $O(k\sqrt{(\log A-k+1)T \log (|F|T)})$. Finally, we implement our algorithm using a hierarchical linear function class and show superior performance with respect to well-known benchmarks on simulated bandit feedback experiments using extreme multi-label classification datasets. On a dataset with three million arms, our reduction scheme has an average inference time of only 7.9 milliseconds, which is a 100x improvement.

paragraphs: The paper studies contextual bandits in which a learner chooses several options at once from a potentially enormous collection. It observes all or some rewards for the chosen options and must improve future choices. Advertising and recommendation motivate this setting, where selecting useful candidates must remain computationally feasible.

For the non-extreme realizable setting, the authors extend inverse gap weighting to selecting k options. They provide a regret guarantee and computation roughly linear in the number of options per step. For millions of options, they introduce a hierarchy that imposes structure on mean rewards. On a dataset with three million options, average inference takes 7.9 milliseconds, a reported hundredfold improvement. The efficiency results rely on exploiting the proposed hierarchy rather than treating every option independently.
summary.tldr: A structured arm hierarchy makes selecting multiple contextual-bandit actions efficient even in experiments with millions of options.

title: Top-k eXtreme Contextual Bandits with Arm Hierarchy

abstract: Least squares estimators, when trained on few target domain samples, may predict poorly. Supervised domain adaptation aims to improve the predictive accuracy by exploiting additional labeled training samples from a source distribution that is close to the target distribution. Given available data, we investigate novel strategies to synthesize a family of least squares estimator experts that are robust with regard to moment conditions. When these moment conditions are specified using Kullback-Leibler or Wasserstein-type divergences, we can find the robust estimators efficiently using convex optimization. We use the Bernstein online aggregation algorithm on the proposed family of robust experts to generate predictions for the sequential stream of target test samples. Numerical experiments on real data show that the robust strategies systematically outperform non-robust interpolations of the empirical least squares estimators.

paragraphs: Least-squares prediction can be unreliable when only a few labeled examples are available from the target domain. Supervised domain adaptation tries to improve it using labeled data from a nearby source distribution. This paper develops a family of least-squares experts that account for uncertainty through robustness with respect to moment conditions.

The authors specify these conditions using Kullback-Leibler or Wasserstein-type divergences. With those formulations, the robust estimators can be computed efficiently through convex optimization. The result is a collection of experts built to handle distributional uncertainty, giving the sequential prediction procedure multiple robust estimators to draw upon.

For an incoming stream of target test samples, the method combines the experts using Bernstein online aggregation. Experiments on real data show that the robust strategies systematically outperform non-robust interpolations of empirical least-squares estimators. The finding supports both the construction of robust experts and their use in sequential target prediction. The setting still draws on a source distribution close to the target, with limited labeled target data motivating the transfer.
summary.tldr: Convex optimization constructs distributionally robust least-squares experts that are combined online to improve sequential domain adaptation.

title: Sequential Domain Adaptation by Synthesizing Distributionally Robust Experts

abstract: Devising domain- and model-agnostic evaluation metrics for generative models is an important and as yet unresolved problem. Most existing metrics, which were tailored solely to the image synthesis setup, exhibit a limited capacity for diagnosing the different modes of failure of generative models across broader application domains. In this paper, we introduce a 3-dimensional evaluation metric, ($\alpha$-Precision, $\beta$-Recall, Authenticity), that characterizes the fidelity, diversity and generalization performance of any generative model in a domain-agnostic fashion. Our metric unifies statistical divergence measures with precision-recall analysis, enabling sample- and distribution-level diagnoses of model fidelity and diversity. We introduce generalization as an additional, independent dimension (to the fidelity-diversity trade-off) that quantifies the extent to which a model copies training data{—}a crucial performance indicator when modeling sensitive data with requirements on privacy. The three metric components correspond to (interpretable) probabilistic quantities, and are estimated via sample-level binary classification. The sample-level nature of our metric inspires a novel use case which we call model auditing, wherein we judge the quality of individual samples generated by a (black-box) model, discarding low-quality samples and hence improving the overall model performance in a post-hoc manner.

paragraphs: Evaluating synthetic data requires distinguishing several kinds of success and failure. Samples may resemble real data, cover its variety, or simply reproduce training examples. This paper introduces three evaluation components—alpha-Precision, beta-Recall, and Authenticity—to characterize fidelity, diversity, and generalization separately in a framework intended to work across domains and generative models.

The framework connects statistical divergence measures with precision-recall analysis. Its components have probabilistic interpretations and are estimated through binary classification at the sample level. This supports diagnosis of both individual examples and entire generated distributions. Treating generalization as its own dimension makes copying training data visible independently of the balance between realism and variety, which is particularly relevant when the training data are sensitive.

The sample-level construction also enables model auditing. An auditor can assess individual outputs from a black-box generator and discard low-quality examples after generation, improving overall output quality without changing the model itself. The contribution therefore combines a more differentiated evaluation framework with a practical filtering use case. Measuring copying provides a relevant indicator for privacy-sensitive applications, rather than itself establishing a privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Three sample-level metrics separate synthetic-data fidelity, diversity, and copying, while enabling post-generation auditing and filtering.

title: How Faithful is your Synthetic Data? Sample-level Metrics for Evaluating and Auditing Generative Models

abstract: Coreset (or core-set) is a small weighted subset $Q$ of an input set $P$ with respect to a given monotonic function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ that provably approximates its fitting loss $\sum_{p\in P}f(p\cdot x)$ to any given $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$. Using $Q$ we can obtain an approximation of $x^*$ that minimizes this loss, by running existing optimization algorithms on $Q$. In this work we provide: (i) A lower bound which proves that there are sets with no coresets smaller than $n=|P|$ for general monotonic loss functions. (ii) A proof that, with an additional common regularization term and under a natural assumption that holds e.g. for logistic regression and the sigmoid activation functions, a small coreset exists for any input $P$. (iii) A generic coreset construction algorithm that computes such a small coreset $Q$ in $O(nd+n\log n)$ time, and (iv) Experimental results with open-source code which demonstrate that our coresets are effective and are much smaller in practice than predicted in theory.

paragraphs: A coreset is a small weighted selection of data that approximates the full dataset’s fitting loss for every candidate parameter vector. If such a subset exists, an existing optimizer can run on it to obtain an approximate solution to the original problem. This paper studies when that compression is possible for monotonic loss functions.

The first result establishes a barrier: for general monotonic losses, some datasets have no coreset smaller than the full dataset. The authors then show that adding a common regularization term changes the situation. Under an additional natural assumption, satisfied by examples including logistic regression and sigmoid functions, a small coreset exists for any input dataset.

They provide a generic construction taking O(nd + n log n) time, where n is the number of points and d their dimension. Experiments find the resulting coresets effective and substantially smaller than the theoretical bounds predict. The contribution pairs an impossibility result with sufficient conditions for useful compression, clarifying why monotonicity alone cannot guarantee a smaller learning problem.
summary.tldr: Small coresets are impossible for some general monotonic losses, but regularization and an additional assumption enable efficient generic constructions.

title: Generic Coreset for Scalable Learning of Monotonic Kernels: Logistic Regression, Sigmoid and more

abstract: Self-supervised Contrastive Learning (CL) has been recently shown to be very effective in preventing deep networks from overfitting noisy labels. Despite its empirical success, the theoretical understanding of the effect of contrastive learning on boosting robustness is very limited. In this work, we rigorously prove that the representation matrix learned by contrastive learning boosts robustness, by having: (i) one prominent singular value corresponding to each sub-class in the data, and significantly smaller remaining singular values; and (ii) a large alignment between the prominent singular vectors and the clean labels of each sub-class. The above properties enable a linear layer trained on such representations to effectively learn the clean labels without overfitting the noise. We further show that the low-rank structure of the Jacobian of deep networks pre-trained with contrastive learning allows them to achieve a superior performance initially, when fine-tuned on noisy labels. Finally, we demonstrate that the initial robustness provided by contrastive learning enables robust training methods to achieve state-of-the-art performance under extreme noise levels, e.g., an average of 27.18% and 15.58% increase in accuracy on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 with 80% symmetric noisy labels, and 4.11% increase in accuracy on WebVision.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why self-supervised contrastive learning can help networks resist incorrect training labels. It moves beyond the observation that such pretraining works well and analyzes the structure of the learned representation matrix. The goal is to explain how a representation can preserve useful class information while reducing overfitting to label noise.

The authors identify two relevant properties: a prominent singular value for each data subclass, with much smaller remaining values, and strong alignment between the prominent singular vectors and clean subclass labels. They prove that these properties enable a linear layer to learn clean labels effectively without fitting the noise. The explanation connects robustness to both the representation’s spectral structure and its alignment with the desired predictions.

For full-network fine-tuning, the analysis links the low-rank Jacobian of contrastively pretrained networks to stronger initial performance with noisy labels. Experiments further show that robust training methods can exploit this initial advantage to reach state-of-the-art performance under extreme noise. The distinction matters: the fine-tuning result concerns an initial robustness benefit that subsequent training methods can use.
summary.tldr: The paper explains contrastive learning’s resistance to label noise through representation structure and shows how its initial robustness benefits later training.

title: Investigating Why Contrastive Learning Benefits Robustness against Label Noise

abstract: In many machine learning applications, it is important for the model to provide confidence scores that accurately capture its prediction uncertainty. Although modern learning methods have achieved great success in predictive accuracy, generating calibrated confidence scores remains a major challenge. Mixup, a popular yet simple data augmentation technique based on taking convex combinations of pairs of training examples, has been empirically found to significantly improve confidence calibration across diverse applications. However, when and how Mixup helps calibration is still a mystery. In this paper, we theoretically prove that Mixup improves calibration in high-dimensional settings by investigating natural statistical models. Interestingly, the calibration benefit of Mixup increases as the model capacity increases. We support our theories with experiments on common architectures and datasets. In addition, we study how Mixup improves calibration in semi-supervised learning. While incorporating unlabeled data can sometimes make the model less calibrated, adding Mixup training mitigates this issue and provably improves calibration. Our analysis provides new insights and a framework to understand Mixup and calibration.

paragraphs: A classifier’s confidence should reflect how uncertain its predictions actually are. Strong predictive accuracy does not ensure this calibration. Mixup, which creates training examples through convex combinations of pairs of examples, has empirically improved calibration in many applications. This paper seeks a theoretical explanation of when and how that benefit arises.

The authors analyze natural statistical models and prove calibration improvements from Mixup in high-dimensional settings. Within the analysis, the calibration benefit grows as model capacity increases. Experiments on common architectures and datasets support the theoretical findings. The result ties Mixup’s usefulness to the modeled setting and capacity, rather than asserting an unconditional improvement for every learner.

Adding Mixup mitigates this issue and yields provable calibration improvements in the studied framework. Together, these analyses provide a way to understand how the augmentation affects confidence estimates, including situations where learning from additional unlabeled data creates a calibration problem.
summary.tldr: Statistical analyses explain Mixup’s calibration benefits in high-dimensional and semi-supervised settings, with supporting experiments.

title: When and How Mixup Improves Calibration

abstract: Sample efficiency and exploration remain major challenges in online reinforcement learning (RL). A powerful approach that can be applied to address these issues is the inclusion of offline data, such as prior trajectories from a human expert or a sub-optimal exploration policy. Previous methods have relied on extensive modifications and additional complexity to ensure the effective use of this data. Instead, we ask: can we simply apply existing off-policy methods to leverage offline data when learning online? In this work, we demonstrate that the answer is yes; however, a set of minimal but important changes to existing off-policy RL algorithms are required to achieve reliable performance. We extensively ablate these design choices, demonstrating the key factors that most affect performance, and arrive at a set of recommendations that practitioners can readily apply, whether their data comprise a small number of expert demonstrations or large volumes of sub-optimal trajectories. We see that correct application of these simple recommendations can provide a $\mathbf{2.5\times}$ improvement over existing approaches across a diverse set of competitive benchmarks, with no additional computational overhead.

Previously collected trajectories offer a way to reduce that burden, whether they come from human experts or imperfect exploration policies. This paper asks whether existing off-policy learning methods can use such offline data effectively without the extensive machinery introduced by earlier approaches.

The authors find that they can, provided several small but consequential changes are made. They systematically vary design choices to identify which ones most affect performance, then turn those findings into practical recommendations. The recommendations address settings ranging from a few expert demonstrations to large collections of suboptimal trajectories, making data quality and quantity part of the investigation.

Correctly applying these recommendations produces a reported 2.5-fold improvement over existing approaches across the evaluated competitive benchmarks, with no additional computational overhead. The result supports a comparatively simple route to combining stored experience with continued online learning. It also makes clear that merely adding offline data is not the whole prescription: the identified implementation choices matter for reliable performance.
summary.tldr: Small, carefully tested changes let existing off-policy reinforcement learning methods use offline data effectively during online learning.

title: Efficient Online Reinforcement Learning with Offline Data

abstract: We propose energy natural gradient descent, a natural gradient method with respect to a Hessian-induced Riemannian metric as an optimization algorithm for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) and the deep Ritz method. As a main motivation we show that the update direction in function space resulting from the energy natural gradient corresponds to the Newton direction modulo an orthogonal projection on the model’s tangent space. We demonstrate experimentally that energy natural gradient descent yields highly accurate solutions with errors several orders of magnitude smaller than what is obtained when training PINNs with standard optimizers like gradient descent or Adam, even when those are allowed significantly more computation time.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a training algorithm for physics-informed neural networks and the deep Ritz method. Called energy natural gradient descent, it changes how optimization directions are measured using a geometry induced by the objective’s Hessian. The aim is to obtain highly accurate solutions by making better use of the structure of the optimization problem.

Its mathematical motivation comes from looking at the function represented by the network, rather than only its parameters. The authors show that the resulting function-space update corresponds to a Newton direction after an orthogonal projection onto the model’s tangent space. In plain language, the update follows the part of that direction that the model can express locally.

Experiments report solution errors several orders of magnitude smaller than those obtained with standard gradient descent or Adam. These comparisons allow the standard optimizers substantially more computation time. The stated result suggests that, in the tested problems, the choice of optimization geometry can matter more for final accuracy than simply spending longer training with a conventional optimizer.
summary.tldr: Energy natural gradient descent uses Hessian-based geometry to train physics-informed networks with substantially smaller errors in the reported experiments.

title: Achieving High Accuracy with PINNs via Energy Natural Gradient Descent

abstract: Learning the continuous dynamics of a system from snapshots of its temporal marginals is a problem which appears throughout natural sciences and machine learning, including in quantum systems, single-cell biological data, and generative modeling. In these settings, we assume access to cross-sectional samples that are uncorrelated over time, rather than full trajectories of samples. In order to better understand the systems under observation, we would like to learn a model of the underlying process that allows us to propagate samples in time and thereby simulate entire individual trajectories. In this work, we propose Action Matching, a method for learning a rich family of dynamics using only independent samples from its time evolution. We derive a tractable training objective, which does not rely on explicit assumptions about the underlying dynamics and does not require back-propagation through differential equations or optimal transport solvers. Inspired by connections with optimal transport, we derive extensions of Action Matching to learn stochastic differential equations and dynamics involving creation and destruction of probability mass. Finally, we showcase applications of Action Matching by achieving competitive performance in a diverse set of experiments from biology, physics, and generative modeling.

paragraphs: Many datasets show how a population looks at different times without tracking the same individuals throughout. Learning dynamics from these snapshots therefore differs from learning directly from complete trajectories. The goal here is to construct a process that can move samples through time and simulate individual paths using only those separate observations.

Action Matching learns a rich family of dynamics from independent samples collected across a system's evolution. The authors derive a tractable training objective that does not require explicit assumptions about the underlying dynamics. It also avoids back-propagating through differential equations or optimal transport solvers, removing those particular computational requirements from training.

Connections to optimal transport motivate extensions for stochastic differential equations and processes in which probability mass can appear or disappear. These extensions broaden the kinds of evolution the method can represent beyond simply moving a fixed amount of mass. Experiments in biology, physics, and generative modeling show competitive performance. The findings support learning useful dynamical models from population snapshots across several application areas.
summary.tldr: Action Matching learns continuous dynamics from independent time snapshots without back-propagating through differential equations or optimal transport solvers.

title: Action Matching: Learning Stochastic Dynamics from Samples

abstract: In large scale machine learning, random sampling is a popular way to approximate datasets by a small representative subset of examples. In particular, sensitivity sampling is an intensely studied technique which provides provable guarantees on the quality of approximation, while reducing the number of examples to the product of the VC dimension $d$ and the total sensitivity $\mathfrak{S}$ in remarkably general settings. However, guarantees going beyond this general bound of $\mathfrak{S} d$ are known in perhaps only one setting, for $\ell_2$ subspace embeddings , despite intense study of sensitivity sampling in prior work. In this work, we show the first bounds for sensitivity sampling for $\ell_p$ subspace embeddings for $p\neq 2$ that improve over the general $\mathfrak{S} d$ bound, achieving a bound of roughly $\mathfrak{S}^{2/p}$ for $1\leq p<2$ and $\mathfrak{S}^{2-2/p}$ for $2<p<\infty$. For $1\leq p<2$, we show that this bound is tight, in the sense that there exist matrices for which $\mathfrak{S}^{2/p}$ samples is necessary. Furthermore, our techniques yield further new results in the study of sampling algorithms, showing that the root leverage score sampling algorithm achieves a bound of roughly $d$ for $1\leq p<2$, and that a combination of leverage score and sensitivity sampling achieves an improved bound of roughly $d^{2/p}\mathfrak{S}^{2-4/p}$ for $2<p<\infty$. Our sensitivity sampling results yield the best known sample complexity for a wide class of structured matrices that have small $\ell_p$ sensitivity.

A broad existing bound requires a sample count proportional to total sensitivity S times VC dimension d. This paper obtains sharper guarantees for ℓp subspace embeddings beyond the previously understood special case p = 2.

That lower bound identifies a genuine obstacle for the sampling method in this range, alongside the improved upper guarantee.

Root leverage score sampling needs roughly d samples when 1 ≤ p < 2, while combining leverage score and sensitivity sampling gives roughly d^(2/p)S^(2−4/p) when p > 2. The sensitivity results provide the best known sample complexity for a broad class of structured matrices with small ℓp sensitivity.
summary.tldr: Sharper sensitivity-sampling bounds reduce sample requirements for ℓp subspace embeddings, with a matching lower bound for 1 ≤ p < 2.

title: Sharper Bounds for $\ell_p$ Sensitivity Sampling

abstract: We propose MusicRL, the first music generation system finetuned from human feedback. Appreciation of text-to-music models is particularly subjective since the concept of musicality as well as the specific intention behind a caption are user-dependent (e.g. a caption such as “upbeat workout music” can map to a retro guitar solo or a technopop beat). Not only this makes supervised training of such models challenging, but it also calls for integrating continuous human feedback in their post-deployment finetuning. MusicRL is a pretrained autoregressive MusicLM model of discrete audio tokens finetuned with reinforcement learning to maximize sequence-level rewards. We design reward functions related specifically to text-adherence and audio quality with the help from selected raters, and use those to finetune MusicLM into MusicRL-R. We deploy MusicLM to users and collect a substantial dataset comprising 300,000 pairwise preferences. Using Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), we train MusicRL-U, the first text-to-music model that incorporates human feedback at scale. Human evaluations show that both MusicRL-R and MusicRL-U are preferred to the baseline. Ultimately, MusicRL-RU combines the two approaches and results in the best model according to human raters. Ablation studies shed light on the musical attributes influencing human preferences, indicating that text adherence and quality only account for a part of it. This underscores the prevalence of subjectivity in musical appreciation and calls for further involvement of human listeners in the finetuning of music generation models. Samples can be found at google-research.github.io/seanet/musiclm/rlhf/.

paragraphs: Music generation is difficult to evaluate because listeners can interpret the same text request differently and value different musical qualities. MusicRL addresses this by fine-tuning the pretrained MusicLM generator with reinforcement learning. The model generates discrete audio tokens, and training uses rewards assigned to complete sequences.

The authors develop two approaches. MusicRL-R uses reward functions focused on text adherence and audio quality, designed with help from selected raters. MusicRL-U learns from 300,000 pairwise preferences collected from users of the deployed MusicLM system. This second approach brings large-scale listener feedback directly into the fine-tuning process.

Human evaluations prefer both versions to the baseline, and MusicRL-RU, which combines the approaches, receives the strongest preference among the evaluated models. Ablation studies indicate that matching the text and producing high-quality audio explain only part of what listeners prefer. The findings support continued involvement of human listeners in training, because explicit quality criteria capture only some of the subjective judgments involved in musical appreciation.
summary.tldr: MusicRL improves listener preference through reinforcement learning that combines quality-focused rewards with large-scale human feedback.

title: MusicRL: Aligning Music Generation to Human Preferences

abstract: Whether future AI models are fair, trustworthy, and aligned with the public's interests rests in part on our ability to collect accurate data about what we want the models to do. However, collecting high-quality data is difficult, and few AI/ML researchers are trained in data collection methods. Recent research in data-centric AI has show that higher quality training data leads to better performing models, making this the right moment to introduce AI/ML researchers to the field of survey methodology, the science of data collection. We summarize insights from the survey methodology literature and discuss how they can improve the quality of training and feedback data. We also suggest collaborative research ideas into how biases in data collection can be mitigated, making models more accurate and human-centric.

paragraphs: Training and feedback data help determine what AI systems learn about human expectations. This position paper argues that collecting those data accurately is part of building models that are fair, trustworthy, and aligned with public interests. It identifies a gap between the importance of data collection and the limited training many AI researchers receive in collection methods.

The authors propose drawing on survey methodology, a field devoted to the science of collecting data. They summarize insights from that literature and discuss how those insights could improve training and feedback datasets. The argument connects data-centric AI's emphasis on data quality with an existing body of knowledge about how collection processes shape the information obtained.

The paper also proposes collaborative research on mitigating biases introduced during collection. Its contribution is a research position and a bridge between fields, rather than a new model or a reported performance benchmark. The intended direction is to improve accuracy and human-centered behavior by improving how evidence about people's expectations enters the training process.
summary.tldr: This position paper argues that survey methodology can improve AI training and feedback data by strengthening collection practices.

title: Position: Insights from Survey Methodology can Improve Training Data

abstract: Practitioners commonly download pretrained machine learning models from open repositories and finetune them to fit specific applications. We show that this practice introduces a new risk of privacy backdoors. By tampering with a pretrained model’s weights, an attacker can fully compromise the privacy of the finetuning data. We show how to build privacy backdoors for a variety of models, including transformers, which enable an attacker to reconstruct individual finetuning samples, with a guaranteed success! We further show that backdoored models allow for tight privacy attacks on models trained with differential privacy (DP). The common optimistic practice of training DP models with loose privacy guarantees is thus insecure if the model is not trusted. Overall, our work highlights a crucial and overlooked supply chain attack on machine learning privacy.

We show how to build privacy backdoors for a variety of models, including transformers, which enable an attacker to reconstruct individual finetuning samples, with a guaranteed success! We further show that backdoored models allow for tight privacy attacks on models trained with differential privacy (DP).
