paragraphs: Downloading a pretrained model and fine-tuning it on private data creates a supply-chain dependency on the model's weights. This paper shows how an attacker can exploit that dependency by modifying the pretrained weights before fine-tuning. The resulting privacy backdoor can compromise data that the attacker did not supply as part of the original model.

The authors construct such backdoors for several model types, including transformers. Their constructions enable reconstruction of individual fine-tuning samples with guaranteed success. The central finding is that corrupted initial weights can create a route to extracting private training examples, making the trustworthiness of the starting model relevant to privacy.

The paper also demonstrates tight privacy attacks on backdoored models trained with differential privacy. Its conclusion specifically challenges the practice of relying on loose differential-privacy guarantees when the pretrained model is untrusted. This does not establish that differential privacy's formal guarantees disappear; it shows why weak guarantees can be inadequate in the presence of deliberately corrupted pretrained weights.
summary.tldr: Corrupted pretrained weights can enable guaranteed reconstruction of individual fine-tuning samples and expose the insecurity of loose privacy guarantees for untrusted models.

title: Privacy Backdoors: Stealing Data with Corrupted Pretrained Models

abstract: Differentially private ML approaches seek to learn models which may be publicly released while guaranteeing that the input data is kept private. One issue with this construction is that further model releases based on the same training data (e.g. for a new task) incur a further privacy budget cost. Privacy-preserving synthetic data generation is one possible solution to this conundrum. However, models trained on synthetic private data struggle to approach the performance of private, ad-hoc models. In this paper, we present a novel method based on sum-product networks that is able to perform both privacy-preserving classification and privacy-preserving data generation with a single model. To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first approach that provides both discriminative and generative capabilities to differentially private ML. We show that our approach outperforms the state of the art in terms of stability (i.e. number of training runs required for convergence) and utility of the generated data.

paragraphs: Differential privacy supports releasing learned models while protecting the data used to train them. A complication arises when the same training data is reused for further model releases: those releases incur additional privacy budget costs. Generating private synthetic data offers one possible response, but models trained on such data can perform worse than private models designed directly for a task.

This paper proposes a sum-product-network method that combines private classification and private data generation in one model. The same learned model can therefore serve a predictive role and a generative role. The authors describe this combination of discriminative and generative capabilities as, to their knowledge, a first for differentially private machine learning.

The reported comparisons show improvements over the state of the art in generated-data utility and training stability. Here stability specifically concerns the number of training runs needed for convergence. These findings matter because a reusable private model must produce useful outputs and train reliably; the proposed approach addresses both within a shared modeling framework.
summary.tldr: A differentially private sum-product network supports both classification and synthetic data generation, with reported gains in training stability and generated-data utility.

title: Differentially Private Sum-Product Networks

abstract: This paper explores a novel multi-modal alternating learning paradigm pursuing a reconciliation between the exploitation of uni-modal features and the exploration of cross-modal interactions. This is motivated by the fact that current paradigms of multi-modal learning tend to explore multi-modal features simultaneously. The resulting gradient prohibits further exploitation of the features in the weak modality, leading to modality competition, where the dominant modality overpowers the learning process. To address this issue, we study the modality-alternating learning paradigm to achieve reconcilement. Specifically, we propose a new method called ReconBoost to update a fixed modality each time. Herein, the learning objective is dynamically adjusted with a reconcilement regularization against competition with the historical models. By choosing a KL-based reconcilement, we show that the proposed method resembles Friedman’s Gradient-Boosting (GB) algorithm, where the updated learner can correct errors made by others and help enhance the overall performance. The major difference with the classic GB is that we only preserve the newest model for each modality to avoid overfitting caused by ensembling strong learners. Furthermore, we propose a memory consolidation scheme and a global rectification scheme to make this strategy more effective. Experiments over six multi-modal benchmarks speak to the efficacy of the proposed method.

paragraphs: When multiple modalities are trained simultaneously, a dominant modality can overpower learning from a weaker one. ReconBoost studies alternating updates as a way to balance learning useful features within each modality with learning interactions across modalities. It updates one modality at a time rather than adjusting every modality together.

The training objective changes dynamically through a regularization term that manages competition with historical models. The contribution is an update strategy that makes room for individual modalities to improve while coordinating their contribution to the overall prediction, with boosting providing a theoretical connection for the chosen regularization.
summary.tldr: ReconBoost alternates modality updates and uses boosting-related regularization to reduce competition and improve multimodal learning.

title: ReconBoost: Boosting Can Achieve Modality Reconcilement

abstract: While large language models (LLMs) surge with the rise of generative AI, algorithms to explain LLMs highly desire. Existing feature attribution methods adequate for discriminative language models like BERT often fail to deliver faithful explanations for LLMs, primarily due to two issues: (1) For every specific prediction, the LLM outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary–a large number of tokens with unequal semantic distance; (2) As an autoregressive language model, the LLM handles input tokens while generating a sequence of probability distributions of various tokens. To address above two challenges, this work proposes GiLOT that leverages Optimal Transport to measure the distributional change of all possible generated sequences upon the absence of every input token, while taking into account the tokens’ similarity, so as to faithfully estimate feature attribution for LLMs. We have carried out extensive experiments on top of Llama families and their fine-tuned derivatives across various scales to validate the effectiveness of GiLOT for estimating the input attributions. The results show that GiLOT outperforms existing solutions on a number of faithfulness metrics under fair comparison settings. Source code is publicly available at https://github.com/holyseven/GiLOT.

paragraphs: Explaining a generative language model requires accounting for more than a single predicted label. At each step, the model produces a distribution over vocabulary tokens with different semantic relationships, and it repeats this process across a generated sequence. These properties make attribution methods developed for discriminative language models poorly suited to faithful explanations of generation.

GiLOT uses optimal transport to assess how removing each input token changes the distribution of possible generated sequences. Its comparison accounts for token similarity, so changes between semantically related tokens can be treated differently from changes between dissimilar ones. The resulting distributional change provides an estimate of each input token's contribution to generation.

The authors evaluate GiLOT on Llama models and fine-tuned derivatives at multiple scales. Under fair comparison settings, it outperforms existing methods on several faithfulness metrics. The findings support evaluating input importance through changes in the structured distribution of generated outputs, with both semantic relationships and sequential generation included in the explanation method.
summary.tldr: GiLOT attributes language-model outputs to input tokens using optimal transport that accounts for semantic similarity and changes across generated sequences.

title: GiLOT: Interpreting Generative Language Models via Optimal Transport

abstract: Self-supervised learning (SSL) has gained increasing attention in the graph learning community, owing to its capability of enabling powerful models pre-trained on large unlabeled graphs for general purposes, facilitating quick adaptation to specific domains. Though promising, existing graph SSL frameworks often struggle to capture both high-level abstract features and fine-grained features simultaneously, leading to sub-optimal generalization abilities across different downstream tasks. To bridge this gap, we present Multi-granularity Graph Semantic Ensemble via Knowledge Distillation, namely MGSE, a plug-and-play graph knowledge distillation framework that can be applied to any existing graph SSL framework to enhance its performance by incorporating the concept of multi-granularity. Specifically, MGSE captures multi-granular knowledge by employing multiple student models to learn from a single teacher model, conditioned by probability distributions with different granularities. We apply it to six state-of-the-art graph SSL frameworks and evaluate their performances over multiple graph datasets across different domains, the experimental results show that MGSE can consistently boost the performance of these existing graph SSL frameworks with up to 9.2% improvement.

paragraphs: Graph self-supervised learning uses unlabeled graphs to prepare models for later tasks. This paper focuses on a representational gap: existing approaches can struggle to capture broad, abstract information and detailed features at the same time. Since downstream tasks may depend on different levels of detail, that gap can weaken generalization.

The proposed MGSE framework adds knowledge distillation across multiple granularities. Several student models learn from a single teacher, with probability distributions of different granularities conditioning that learning. This creates a mechanism for incorporating knowledge at different resolutions. The authors present it as a plug-and-play framework that can be applied to existing graph self-supervised learning methods.

They evaluate MGSE with six state-of-the-art frameworks across graph datasets from multiple domains. The reported results show consistent improvements for those frameworks, with gains reaching 9.2%. The evidence supports the value of explicitly incorporating multiple levels of semantic detail into graph pretraining. The maximum gain describes the evaluated results, while the broader design aims to make this enhancement reusable across frameworks.
summary.tldr: MGSE distills graph knowledge at multiple granularities and improves six evaluated self-supervised frameworks by up to 9.2%.

title: From Coarse to Fine: Enable Comprehensive Graph Self-supervised Learning with Multi-granular Semantic Ensemble

abstract: Model compression is one of the most popular approaches to improve the accessibility of Large Language Models (LLMs) by reducing their memory footprint. However, the gaining of such efficiency benefits often simultaneously demands extensive engineering efforts and intricate designs to mitigate the performance decline. In this work, we leverage (Soft) Prompt Tuning in its most vanilla form and discover such conventionally learned soft prompts can recover the performance of compressed LLMs. More surprisingly, we observe such recovery effect to be transferable among different tasks and models (albeit natural tokenizer and dimensionality limitations), resulting in further overhead reduction and yet, subverting the common belief that learned soft prompts are task-specific. Our work is fully orthogonal and compatible with model compression frameworks such as pruning and quantization, where we enable up to $8\times$ compressed LLM (with a joint 4-bit quantization and 50% weight pruning compression) to match its uncompressed counterparts on popular benchmarks. We note that we are the first to reveal vanilla Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques have the potential to be utilized under a compression recovery context, opening a new line of opportunities for model accessibility advancement while freeing our fellow researchers from the previously present engineering burdens and constraints. The code is available at https://github.com/zirui-ray-liu/compress-then-prompt.
originalAbstract: Model compression is one of the most popular approaches to improve the accessibility of Large Language Models (LLMs) by reducing their memory footprint. However, the gaining of such efficiency benefits often simultaneously demands extensive engineering efforts and intricate designs to mitigate the performance decline. In this work, we leverage (Soft) Prompt Tuning in its most vanilla form and discover such conventionally learned soft prompts can recover the performance of compressed LLMs. More surprisingly, we observe such recovery effect to be transferable among different tasks and models (albeit natural tokenizer and dimensionality limitations), resulting in further overhead reduction and yet, subverting the common belief that learned soft prompts are task-specific. Our work is fully orthogonal and compatible with model compression frameworks such as pruning and quantization, where we enable up to $8\times$ compressed LLM (with a joint 4-bit quantization and 50% weight pruning compression) to match its uncompressed counterparts on popular benchmarks. We note that we are the first to reveal vanilla Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) techniques have the potential to be utilized under a compression recovery context, opening a new line of opportunities for model accessibility advancement while freeing our fellow researchers from the previously present engineering burdens and constraints. The code is available at https://github.com/zirui-ray-liu/compress-then-prompt.

paragraphs: Compressing a language model reduces its memory footprint but can also damage performance. This paper investigates a simple recovery technique: ordinary soft prompt tuning. The authors find that learned soft prompts can restore performance in compressed models without requiring a specially designed recovery mechanism for each compression framework.

A notable observation is that the recovery effect can transfer across tasks and models. This challenges the assumption that learned soft prompts must be tied to a single task. The transfer remains subject to tokenizer and dimensionality compatibility, so the finding does not imply that any prompt can be applied unchanged to any model.

The approach is compatible with pruning and quantization. On popular benchmarks, the authors demonstrate models compressed by up to eight times matching uncompressed counterparts, using joint four-bit quantization and 50% weight pruning. These results identify standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning as a potential tool for compression recovery. Transferable prompts could further reduce adaptation overhead by reusing recovery effects across compatible settings.
summary.tldr: Standard soft prompt tuning can recover compressed language-model performance, with transfer across compatible tasks and models.

title: Soft Prompt Recovers Compressed LLMs, Transferably

abstract: Service providers of large language model (LLM) applications collect user instructions in the wild and use them in further aligning LLMs with users’ intentions. These instructions, which potentially contain sensitive information, are annotated by human workers in the process. This poses a new privacy risk not addressed by the typical private optimization. To this end, we propose using synthetic instructions to replace real instructions in data annotation and model fine-tuning. Formal differential privacy is guaranteed by generating those synthetic instructions using privately fine-tuned generators. Crucial in achieving the desired utility is our novel filtering algorithm that matches the distribution of the synthetic instructions to that of the real ones. In both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback, our extensive experiments demonstrate the high utility of the final set of synthetic instructions by showing comparable results to real instructions. In supervised fine-tuning, models trained with private synthetic instructions outperform leading open-source models such as Vicuna.

paragraphs: User instructions collected by language-model services can contain sensitive information. When human workers annotate those instructions for further training, the annotation process itself creates a privacy risk. This paper addresses that exposure by replacing real instructions with synthetic ones for both annotation and model fine-tuning.

The synthetic instructions come from generators that have been privately fine-tuned, providing a formal differential privacy guarantee. A filtering algorithm then makes the distribution of retained synthetic instructions resemble that of the original instructions. This matching step is central to usefulness: the replacement data needs to reflect the instruction patterns relevant to alignment.

Experiments evaluate the resulting instructions in supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback. The authors report results comparable to those obtained with real instructions in both settings. In supervised fine-tuning, models trained on the private synthetic data also outperform leading open-source models such as Vicuna. The findings demonstrate that protecting the instruction data used for annotation can coexist with effective alignment in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Differentially private synthetic instructions replace sensitive user data while retaining strong alignment performance in experiments.

title: Privacy-Preserving Instructions for Aligning Large Language Models

abstract: We propose a novel algorithm for online resource allocation with non-stationary customer arrivals and unknown click-through rates. We assume multiple types of customers arriving in a nonstationary stochastic fashion, with unknown arrival rates in each period. Additionally, customers’ click-through rates are assumed to be unknown and only learnable online. By leveraging results from the stochastic contextual bandit with knapsack and online matching with adversarial arrivals, we develop an online scheme to allocate the resources to nonstationary customers. We prove that under mild conditions, our scheme achieves a “best-of-both-world” result: the scheme has a sublinear regret when the customer arrivals are near-stationary, and enjoys an optimal competitive ratio under general (non-stationary) customer arrival distributions. Finally, we conduct extensive numerical experiments to show our approach generates near-optimal revenues for all different customer scenarios.

paragraphs: This paper studies resource allocation when different types of customers arrive over time and their arrival patterns can change. The allocator does not know each period's arrival rates. It also does not know customers' click-through rates, which must be learned while resources are being allocated.

The proposed scheme combines ideas from stochastic contextual bandits with resource constraints and online matching under adversarial arrivals. This combination addresses two demands at once: learning how customers respond and remaining effective when the customer mix changes. The theoretical goal is an algorithm whose performance adapts to how predictable the arrival process turns out to be.

Under mild conditions, the authors establish two complementary guarantees. When arrivals are nearly stationary, regret grows sublinearly. Under general nonstationary arrival distributions, the scheme achieves an optimal competitive ratio. Extensive numerical experiments also report near-optimal revenues across the customer scenarios tested. The findings connect favorable performance in relatively stable environments with a worst-case-style guarantee for broader arrival patterns, with the theoretical conclusions retaining their stated conditions.
summary.tldr: The allocation scheme learns customer responses online and, under mild conditions, combines low regret near stationarity with an optimal competitive ratio under broader arrivals.

title: Online Resource Allocation with Non-Stationary Customers

abstract: This work investigates the effectiveness of schedule-free methods, developed by A. Defazio et al. (NeurIPS 2024), in nonconvex optimization settings, inspired by their remarkable empirical success in training neural networks. Specifically, we show that schedule-free SGD achieves optimal iteration complexity for nonsmooth, non-convex optimization problems. Our proof begins with the development of a general framework for online-to-nonconvex conversion, which converts a given online learning algorithm into an optimization algorithm for nonconvex losses. Our general framework not only recovers existing conversions but also leads to two novel conversion schemes. Notably, one of these new conversions corresponds directly to schedule-free SGD, allowing us to establish its optimality. Additionally, our analysis provides valuable insights into the parameter choices for schedule-free SGD, addressing a theoretical gap that the convex theory cannot explain.

paragraphs: Schedule-free optimization methods have shown strong empirical results in neural-network training, motivating a theoretical question: how effective are they when the objective is nonconvex? This paper proves that schedule-free SGD achieves optimal iteration complexity for nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization problems. The claim concerns the number of iterations required in the analyzed optimization setting.

The proof comes from a broader framework that turns online learning algorithms into algorithms for optimizing nonconvex losses. One of those new conversions corresponds directly to schedule-free SGD, connecting the practical method to the theory needed to establish its optimality.

Its contribution is therefore both a result about a particular optimizer and a general construction for developing nonconvex optimization algorithms. The stated optimality is an iteration-complexity guarantee; the paper's motivation comes from empirical training success, while its main finding provides a theoretical foundation for that method in a broader class of objectives.
summary.tldr: A general online-to-nonconvex conversion framework establishes optimal iteration complexity for schedule-free SGD in nonsmooth, nonconvex optimization.

title: General framework for online-to-nonconvex conversion: Schedule-free SGD is also effective for nonconvex optimization

abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) is a widely adopted visual imitation learning method in robot manipulation. Current BC approaches often enhance generalization by leveraging large datasets and incorporating additional visual and textual modalities to capture more diverse information. However, these methods overlook whether the learned representations contain redundant information and lack a solid theoretical foundation to guide the learning process. To address these limitations, we adopt an information-theoretic perspective and introduce mutual information to quantify and mitigate redundancy in latent representations. Building on this, we incorporate the Information Bottleneck (IB) principle into BC, which extends the idea of reducing redundancy by providing a structured framework for compressing irrelevant information while preserving task-relevant features. This work presents the first comprehensive study on redundancy in latent representations across various methods, backbones, and experimental settings, while extending the generalizability of the IB to BC. Extensive experiments and analyses on the CortexBench and LIBERO benchmarks show consistent performance improvements with IB across various settings, underscoring the importance of reducing input data redundancy and highlighting its practical value for real-world applications.

paragraphs: Visual behavior cloning teaches robot manipulation from demonstrations. Common approaches seek better generalization through larger datasets or additional visual and textual information. This paper asks whether the representations learned from those inputs retain redundant information, and whether actively reducing that redundancy can improve the resulting policy.

The authors use mutual information to quantify and mitigate redundancy in latent representations. They then incorporate the Information Bottleneck principle into behavior cloning, giving learning a structured objective: compress information that is irrelevant while preserving features needed for the task. This makes the content retained in the representation a central design concern.

The study examines redundancy across methods, model backbones, and experimental settings. Evaluations on CortexBench and LIBERO report consistent performance improvements from incorporating the Information Bottleneck across the tested settings. The results support representation compression as a useful complement to richer inputs and larger datasets, showing practical value in controlling which information a behavior-cloning model carries forward into its learned representation.
summary.tldr: Applying the Information Bottleneck to behavior cloning reduces irrelevant representation content and consistently improves performance in the reported benchmark settings.

title: Rethinking Latent Redundancy in Behavior Cloning: An Information Bottleneck Approach for Robot Manipulation

abstract: We introduce a novel one-parameter variational objective that lower bounds the data evidence and enables the estimation of approximate fractional posteriors. We extend this framework to hierarchical construction and Bayes posteriors, offering a versatile tool for probabilistic modelling. We demonstrate two cases where gradients can be obtained analytically and a simulation study on mixture models showing that our fractional posteriors can be used to achieve better calibration compared to posteriors from the conventional variational bound. When applied to variational autoencoders (VAEs), our approach attains higher evidence bounds and enables learning of high-performing approximate Bayes posteriors jointly with fractional posteriors. We show that VAEs trained with fractional posteriors produce decoders that are better aligned for generation from the prior.

paragraphs: The paper introduces a variational learning objective with one adjustable parameter for estimating approximate fractional posteriors. The objective remains a lower bound on the data evidence, connecting posterior approximation to a quantity used to assess probabilistic models. The authors extend the construction to hierarchical settings and ordinary Bayes posteriors.

They identify two cases where gradients can be calculated analytically. In simulations with mixture models, the fractional posteriors can achieve better calibration than posteriors obtained with the conventional variational bound. This finding concerns the quality of uncertainty estimates, adding a reason to consider the alternative objective beyond its mathematical formulation.

Applied to variational autoencoders, the method obtains higher evidence bounds and jointly learns high-performing approximate Bayes and fractional posteriors. The authors also find that training with fractional posteriors produces decoders better aligned with generation from the prior. Together, these results connect the choice of posterior-learning objective with uncertainty calibration, evidence bounds, and the behavior of a generative model when it produces samples from its prior.
summary.tldr: A new variational objective learns fractional posteriors, with reported benefits for calibration, evidence bounds, and prior-based generation in VAEs.

title: Variational Learning of Fractional Posteriors

abstract: Despite their tremendous success and versatility, Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) such as Large Language Models (LLMs) suffer from inference inefficiency and rely on advanced computational infrastructure. To address these challenges and make these models more accessible and cost-effective, in this paper, we propose algorithms to improve the inference time and memory efficiency of DNNs with binary and ternary weight matrices. Particularly focusing on matrix multiplication as the bottleneck operation of inference, we observe that, once trained, the weight matrices of a model no longer change. This allows us to preprocess these matrices and create indices that help reduce the storage requirements by a logarithmic factor while enabling our efficient inference algorithms. Specifically, for a $n\times n$ weight matrix, our efficient algorithm guarantees a time complexity of $O(\frac{n^2}{\log n})$, a logarithmic factor improvement over the standard vector-matrix multiplication. Besides theoretical analysis, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the practical efficiency of our algorithms. Our results confirm the superiority of our approach both with respect to time and memory, as we observed a reduction in the multiplication time up to 29x and memory usage up to 6x. When applied to LLMs, our experiments show up to a 5.24x speedup in the inference time.

paragraphs: Running a neural network repeatedly involves multiplying inputs by its weight matrices. This paper focuses on networks whose weights take binary or ternary values. Its starting observation is that trained weights remain fixed during inference, making it possible to prepare a more efficient representation before processing inputs.

The proposed algorithms preprocess these matrices and construct indices that support faster multiplication while reducing storage requirements by a logarithmic factor. For an n-by-n weight matrix, the stated multiplication time is O(n²/log n), a logarithmic improvement over standard vector-matrix multiplication. The method therefore exploits both the restricted weight values and the opportunity to reuse preprocessing.

Experiments assess whether these theoretical savings translate into practical benefits. The authors report multiplication speedups of up to 29 times and memory reductions of up to six times. Applied to language models, the algorithms achieve inference speedups of up to 5.24 times. These are reported maxima across the experiments, and the full-model result measures a different scope from the multiplication result.
summary.tldr: Preprocessing fixed binary and ternary weights enables faster, smaller matrix operations and reported language-model inference speedups of up to 5.24 times.

title: An Efficient Matrix Multiplication Algorithm for Accelerating Inference in Binary and Ternary Neural Networks

abstract: Current causal discovery approaches require restrictive model assumptions in the absence of interventional data to ensure structure identifiability. These assumptions often do not hold in real-world applications leading to a loss of guarantees and poor performance in practice. Recent work has shown that, in the bivariate case, Bayesian model selection can greatly improve performance by exchanging restrictive modelling for more flexible assumptions, at the cost of a small probability of making an error. Our work shows that this approach is useful in the important multivariate case as well. We propose a scalable algorithm leveraging a continuous relaxation of the discrete model selection problem. Specifically, we employ the Causal Gaussian Process Conditional Density Estimator (CGP-CDE) as a Bayesian non-parametric model, using its hyperparameters to construct an adjacency matrix. This matrix is then optimised using the marginal likelihood and an acyclicity regulariser, giving the maximum a posteriori causal graph. We demonstrate the competitiveness of our approach, showing it is advantageous to perform multivariate causal discovery without infeasible assumptions using Bayesian model selection.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships without interventions often requires restrictive assumptions to identify a unique causal structure. When those assumptions fail, the associated guarantees can disappear. Earlier work on two variables suggested that Bayesian model selection could replace restrictive modeling assumptions with more flexible ones, accepting a small probability of error.

This paper extends that approach to multiple variables. It uses a Bayesian nonparametric model called the Causal Gaussian Process Conditional Density Estimator. The model’s hyperparameters define an adjacency matrix, which represents proposed relationships between variables. A continuous relaxation makes it possible to optimize this representation instead of handling model selection solely as a discrete search.

The optimization combines marginal likelihood with an acyclicity regularizer and returns a maximum a posteriori causal graph. The regularizer encourages a graph without directed cycles, while the Bayesian criterion guides selection among models. The authors report competitive performance, supporting Bayesian selection as a useful multivariate approach. The result favors more flexible assumptions and probabilistic model selection rather than establishing assumption-free, error-free causal identification.
summary.tldr: A continuous Bayesian model-selection method extends flexible causal discovery to multiple variables and reports competitive performance.

title: Continuous Bayesian Model Selection for Multivariate Causal Discovery

abstract: Despite the success of Transformers, handling longer contexts remains challenging due to the limited length generalization and quadratic complexity of self-attention, which often requires post-training with a larger attention window, significantly increasing computational and memory costs. In this paper, we propose a novel attention mechanism based on dynamic context, Grouped Cross Attention (GCA), which can generalize to 1000 $\times$ the pre-training context length while maintaining the ability to access distant information with a constant attention window size. For a given input sequence, we split it into chunks and use each chunk to retrieve top-$k$ relevant past chunks for subsequent text generation. Specifically, unlike most previous works that use an off-the-shelf retriever, our key innovation allows the retriever to learn how to retrieve past chunks that better minimize the auto-regressive loss of subsequent tokens in an end-to-end manner, which adapts better to causal language models. Such a mechanism accommodates retrieved chunks with a fixed-size attention window to achieve long-range information access, significantly reducing computational and memory costs during training and inference. Experiments show that GCA-based models achieve near-perfect accuracy in passkey retrieval for 16M context lengths, which is $1000 \times$ the training length.

paragraphs: Long inputs create two problems for Transformers: standard self-attention becomes expensive, and models may not generalize well beyond the lengths seen during training. Enlarging the attention window through additional training increases memory and computation. Grouped Cross Attention addresses these issues by changing which context is available within a fixed-size attention window.

The method divides an input into chunks and retrieves the most relevant earlier chunks for subsequent text generation. Its retriever is trained jointly with the language model to reduce the prediction loss on later tokens. This makes retrieval sensitive to what helps causal language modeling, rather than relying on a separately supplied retrieval system.

Retrieved chunks give the model access to distant information without expanding its attention window. The paper reports reduced computational and memory costs during training and inference. In passkey retrieval experiments, GCA-based models achieve near-perfect accuracy with 16-million-token contexts, 1,000 times their training length. This result demonstrates substantial length generalization on the stated retrieval task and supports learning retrieval directly around the model’s prediction objective.
summary.tldr: Grouped Cross Attention learns to retrieve useful past chunks, enabling distant-context access with a fixed attention window and strong passkey retrieval results.

title: Efficient Length-Generalizable Attention via Causal Retrieval for Long-Context Language Modeling

abstract: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning (GCRL) learns a goal-conditioned value function to train policies for diverse goals with pre-collected datasets. Hindsight experience replay addresses the issue of sparse rewards by treating intermediate states as goals but fails to complete goal-stitching tasks where achieving goals requires stitching different trajectories. While cross-trajectory sampling is a potential solution that associates states and goals belonging to different trajectories, we demonstrate that this direct method degrades performance in goal-conditioned tasks due to the overestimation of values on unconnected pairs. To this end, we propose Conservative Goal-Conditioned Implicit Value Learning (CGCIVL), a novel algorithm that introduces a penalty term to penalize value estimation for unconnected state-goal pairs and leverages the quasimetric framework to accurately estimate values for connected pairs. Evaluations on OGBench, a benchmark for offline GCRL, demonstrate that CGCIVL consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods across diverse tasks.

paragraphs: Offline goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains an agent to reach different goals using previously collected trajectories. Sparse rewards make this difficult. Reinterpreting intermediate states as goals supplies more learning examples, but this approach fails on goal-stitching tasks, where reaching a goal requires combining portions of different recorded trajectories.

Pairing states and goals across trajectories is a possible remedy, but the authors find that doing so directly can degrade performance. The problem is overestimating the value of state-goal pairs that are unconnected. Their method, Conservative Goal-Conditioned Implicit Value Learning, adds a penalty for these pairs and uses a quasimetric framework to estimate values for connected pairs.

This combination addresses both sides of the learning problem: discouraging unsupported high values while modeling connections that can support useful behavior. On OGBench, the authors report that the method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across diverse tasks. The results support making cross-trajectory learning sensitive to connectivity, rather than assuming that arbitrary pairings provide equally reliable training targets.
summary.tldr: CGCIVL improves offline goal learning by penalizing unconnected state-goal pairs while modeling the values of connected pairs.

title: Conservative Offline Goal-Conditioned Implicit V-Learning

abstract: Diversity in training data, architecture, and providers is assumed to mitigate homogeneity in LLMs. However, we lack empirical evidence on whether different LLMs differ meaningfully. We conduct a large-scale empirical evaluation on over 350 LLMs overall, using two popular leaderboards and a resume-screening task. We find substantial correlation in model errors—on one leaderboard dataset, models agree 60% of the time when both models err. We identify factors driving model correlation, including shared architectures and providers. Crucially, however, larger and more accurate models have highly correlated errors, even with distinct architectures and providers. Finally, we show the effects of correlation in two downstream tasks: LLM-as-judge evaluation and hiring—the latter reflecting theoretical predictions regarding algorithmic monoculture.

paragraphs: Different language models may appear to offer independent perspectives because they have different architectures, training histories, or providers. This paper asks whether those differences translate into meaningfully different errors. The authors evaluate more than 350 models overall using two popular leaderboards and a resume-screening task.

They find substantial correlation between mistakes. On one leaderboard dataset, pairs of models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong. That figure is conditional on both models making an error; it does not describe their overall error rate. Shared architectures and providers help explain correlation, but larger and more accurate models also show highly correlated errors across those boundaries.

The study then examines consequences for evaluation with language-model judges and for hiring decisions. The hiring findings reflect theoretical predictions about algorithmic monoculture, where similar automated decisions create shared patterns of outcomes. The central implication is that model variety and individual accuracy do not by themselves establish diversity of behavior: understanding shared mistakes requires measuring those mistakes directly.
summary.tldr: An evaluation of over 350 LLMs finds substantial shared errors, including among accurate models from different providers and architectures.

title: Correlated Errors in Large Language Models

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown great potential as general-purpose AI assistants across various domains. To fully leverage this potential in specific applications, many companies provide fine-tuning API services, enabling users to upload their own data for LLM customization. However, fine-tuning services introduce a new safety threat: user-uploaded data, whether harmful or benign, can break the model’s alignment, leading to unsafe outputs. Moreover, existing defense methods struggle to address the diversity of fine-tuning datasets (e.g., varying sizes, tasks), often sacrificing utility for safety or vice versa. To address this issue, we propose Safe Delta, a safety-aware post-training defense method that adjusts the delta parameters (i.e., the parameter change before and after fine-tuning). Specifically, Safe Delta estimates the safety degradation, selects delta parameters to maximize utility while limiting overall safety loss, and applies a safety compensation vector to mitigate residual safety loss. Through extensive experiments on four diverse datasets with varying settings, our approach consistently preserves safety while ensuring that the utility gain from benign datasets remains unaffected.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning lets users adapt a language model to their applications, but it can also weaken previously learned safety behavior. The paper emphasizes that this can happen with benign as well as harmful training data. Existing defenses can struggle across different dataset sizes and tasks, trading away useful customization to retain safety or doing the reverse.

Safe Delta operates after fine-tuning by adjusting the parameter changes introduced during customization. It first estimates safety degradation, then selects changes intended to maximize utility while constraining overall safety loss. A safety compensation vector addresses the remaining loss. Working with the difference between the original and fine-tuned parameters makes the customization update itself the object of the defense.

Experiments on four diverse datasets under varying settings show consistent safety preservation while retaining utility gains from benign data. The reported findings support this selective adjustment strategy across the tested diversity of fine-tuning conditions. The method’s practical significance lies in preserving the benefits of customization while managing the safety changes that customization can introduce.
summary.tldr: Safe Delta adjusts fine-tuning parameter changes to preserve safety while retaining the utility gains from benign customization data in reported experiments.

title: Safe Delta: Consistently Preserving Safety when Fine-Tuning LLMs on Diverse Datasets

abstract: Bipartite ranking is a fundamental supervised learning problem, with the goal of learning a ranking over instances with maximal area under the ROC curve (AUC) against a single binary target label. However, one may often observe multiple binary target labels, e.g., from distinct human annotators. How can one synthesize such labels into a single coherent ranking? In this work, we formally analyze two approaches to this problem—loss aggregation and label aggregation—by characterizing their Bayes-optimal solutions. We show that while both approaches can yield Pareto-optimal solutions, loss aggregation can exhibit label dictatorship: one can inadvertently (and undesirably) favor one label over others. This suggests that label aggregation can be preferable to loss aggregation, which we empirically verify.

paragraphs: Bipartite ranking learns to order examples so that positive cases rank above negative ones, with performance measured by area under the ROC curve. The usual formulation assumes one binary target. This paper studies what happens when several binary labels are available for each example, such as judgments from different human annotators, but the system must still produce one ranking.

The authors compare two ways to combine that supervision. Loss aggregation combines the objectives associated with the different labels, while label aggregation combines the labels themselves. They characterize the Bayes-optimal solutions for both approaches, examining the rankings each method favors at the population level.

Both approaches can produce Pareto-optimal solutions, meaning that improving performance for one label would require sacrificing performance for another. Yet loss aggregation can still let one label dominate the resulting ranking, a phenomenon the paper calls label dictatorship. This shows why Pareto optimality alone does not rule out undesirable favoritism. The analysis suggests that label aggregation can be preferable, and the experiments support that conclusion.
summary.tldr: Combining ranking losses can unintentionally favor one label, making label aggregation a preferable option in the studied setting.

title: Bipartite Ranking From Multiple Labels: On Loss Versus Label Aggregation

abstract: Perception in the real world requires robustness to diverse viewing conditions. Existing approaches often rely on specialized architectures or training with predefined data augmentations, limiting adaptability. Taking inspiration from mental rotation in human vision, we propose FoCal, a test-time robustness framework that transforms the input into the most typical view. At inference time, FoCal explores a set of transformed images and chooses the one with the highest likelihood under foundation model priors. This test-time optimization boosts robustness while requiring no retraining or architectural changes. Applied to models like CLIP and SAM, it significantly boosts robustness across a wide range of transformations, including 2D and 3D rotations, contrast and lighting shifts, and day-night changes. We also explore potential applications in active vision. By reframing invariance as a test-time optimization problem, FoCal offers a general and scalable approach to robustness. Our code is available at: https://github.com/sutkarsh/focal .

paragraphs: FoCal improves visual robustness by transforming an input into a more typical view at inference time. Inspired by mental rotation in human vision, it treats the viewing condition as something that can be adjusted before perception. This addresses a different point in the workflow from approaches that rely on specialized architectures or predefined training augmentations.

The framework explores a set of transformed images and uses foundation-model priors to choose the candidate with the highest likelihood. That selection is a test-time optimization over possible views of the input. It requires no retraining or architectural changes, making the transformation procedure the central mechanism for improving robustness in an existing perception model.

Applied to models including CLIP and SAM, FoCal significantly improves robustness across tested changes such as two- and three-dimensional rotations, contrast, lighting, and day-night shifts. The authors also explore possible active-vision applications. The reported results support using foundation-model knowledge to select favorable input views, showing that robustness can be improved through inference-time input adaptation.
summary.tldr: FoCal uses foundation-model priors to select a more typical input view at inference time, improving robustness without retraining.

title: Test-Time Canonicalization by Foundation Models for Robust Perception

abstract: We study the stochastic linear bandits with heavy-tailed noise. Two principled strategies for handling heavy-tailed noise, truncation and median-of-means, have been introduced to heavy-tailed bandits. Nonetheless, these methods rely on specific noise assumptions or bandit structures, limiting their applicability to general settings. The recent work [Huang et al.2024] develop a soft truncation method via the adaptive Huber regression to address these limitations. However, their method suffers undesired computational cost: it requires storing all historical data and performing a full pass over these data at each round. In this paper, we propose a one-pass algorithm based on the online mirror descent framework. Our method updates using only current data at each round, reducing the per-round computational cost from $\mathcal{O}(t \log T)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$ with respect to current round $t$ and the time horizon $T$, and achieves a near-optimal and variance-aware regret of order $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(d T^{\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2(1+\varepsilon)}} \sqrt{\sum_{t=1}^T \nu_t^2} + d T^{\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2(1+\varepsilon)}}\big)$ where $d$ is the dimension and $\nu_t^{1+\varepsilon}$ is the $(1+\varepsilon)$-th central moment of reward at round $t$.

paragraphs: This paper studies linear bandits whose reward noise is heavy-tailed, making unusually large deviations an important part of the learning problem. Existing truncation and median-of-means methods depend on particular assumptions or structures. Adaptive Huber regression offers a more broadly applicable way to soften extreme observations, but the prior approach discussed here repeatedly processes the entire observation history.

The authors develop a one-pass algorithm using online mirror descent. Each round's update uses only the current data, removing the need for a fresh pass through historical observations. Relative to the current round and the overall time horizon, the stated per-round computation falls from O(t log T) to O(1). This claim concerns those time variables rather than every possible computational dimension.

The algorithm also achieves a near-optimal, variance-aware regret guarantee. Its bound depends on the feature dimension, the horizon, and quantities describing the reward noise's central moments. The contribution is therefore both computational and statistical: an efficient incremental update retains a strong learning guarantee whose scale reflects the noise encountered over time.
summary.tldr: A one-pass Huber-based linear bandit algorithm reduces computation over time while retaining near-optimal, noise-sensitive regret guarantees.

title: Heavy-Tailed Linear Bandits: Huber Regression with One-Pass Update

abstract: In recent years, One-shot Federated Learning (OSFL) methods based on Diffusion Models (DMs) have garnered increasing attention due to their remarkable performance. However, most of these methods require the deployment of foundation models on client devices, which significantly raises the computational requirements and reduces their adaptability to heterogeneous client models. In this paper, we propose FedLMG, a heterogeneous one-shot Federated learning method with Local Model-Guided diffusion models. In our method, clients do not need access to any foundation models but only train and upload their local models, which is consistent with traditional FL methods. On the clients, we employ classification loss and batch normalization loss to capture the broad category features and detailed contextual features of the client distributions. On the server, based on the uploaded client models, we utilize backpropagation to guide the server’s DM in generating synthetic datasets that comply with the client distributions, which are then used to train the aggregated model. By using the local models as a medium to transfer client knowledge, our method significantly reduces the computational requirements on client devices and effectively adapts to scenarios with heterogeneous clients. Extensive quantitation and visualization experiments on three large-scale real-world datasets, along with theoretical analysis, demonstrate that the synthetic datasets generated by FedLMG exhibit comparable quality and diversity to the client datasets, which leads to an aggregated model that outperforms all compared methods and even the performance ceiling, further elucidating the significant potential of utilizing DMs in FL.

These findings support local models as an effective knowledge-transfer medium while reducing client computation and accommodating heterogeneous clients.
summary.tldr: FedLMG uses uploaded local models to guide server-side diffusion, enabling heterogeneous one-shot federated learning without foundation models on clients.

title: One-Shot Heterogeneous Federated Learning with Local Model-Guided Diffusion Models

abstract: We study the challenging problem of unsupervised multi-object segmentation on single images. Existing methods, which rely on image reconstruction objectives to learn objectness or leverage pretrained image features to group similar pixels, often succeed only in segmenting simple synthetic objects or discovering a limited number of real-world objects. In this paper, we introduce unMORE, a novel two-stage pipeline designed to identify many complex objects in real-world images. The key to our approach involves explicitly learning three levels of carefully defined object-centric representations in the first stage. Subsequently, our multi-object reasoning module utilizes these learned object priors to discover multiple objects in the second stage. Notably, this reasoning module is entirely network-free and does not require human labels. Extensive experiments demonstrate that unMORE significantly outperforms all existing unsupervised methods across 6 real-world benchmark datasets, including the challenging COCO dataset, achieving state-of-the-art object segmentation results. Remarkably, our method excels in crowded images where all baselines collapse. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/vLAR-group/unMORE.

paragraphs: Unsupervised multi-object segmentation aims to identify separate objects in a single image without human labels. Existing approaches often learn through image reconstruction or group pixels using pretrained features, but can struggle with complex real-world objects and crowded scenes. unMORE introduces a two-stage pipeline designed to discover many such objects.

The first stage explicitly learns three levels of object-centric representations. These learned representations provide object priors for a second-stage multi-object reasoning module. That reasoning module is network-free and requires no human labels. The design therefore separates learning useful object information from the subsequent reasoning that identifies multiple objects in an image.

Experiments across six real-world benchmark datasets, including COCO, show substantial improvements over the existing unsupervised methods evaluated. The paper particularly highlights crowded images, where unMORE succeeds while the compared baselines collapse. These findings support the value of explicitly learned object-centric representations combined with a separate reasoning stage. The network-free claim applies to the reasoning module, while representation learning remains part of the overall pipeline.
summary.tldr: unMORE combines learned object-centric representations with network-free reasoning to improve unsupervised segmentation of complex and crowded real-world images.

title: unMORE: Unsupervised Multi-Object Segmentation via Center-Boundary Reasoning

abstract: Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) technologies provide biologists with rich insights into single-cell biology by preserving spatial context of cells. Building foundational models for ST can significantly enhance the analysis of vast and complex data sources, unlocking new perspectives on the intricacies of biological tissues. However, modeling ST data is inherently challenging due to the need to extract multi-scale information from tissue slices containing vast numbers of cells. This process requires integrating macro-scale tissue morphology, micro-scale cellular microenvironment, and gene-scale gene expression profile. To address this challenge, we propose SToFM, a multi-scale Spatial Transcriptomics Foundation Model. SToFM first performs multi-scale information extraction on each ST slice, to construct a set of ST sub-slices that aggregate macro-, micro- and gene-scale information. Then an SE(2) Transformer is used to obtain high-quality cell representations from the sub-slices. Additionally, we construct SToCorpus-88M, the largest high-resolution spatial transcriptomics corpus for pretraining. SToFM achieves outstanding performance on a variety of downstream tasks, such as tissue region semantic segmentation and cell type annotation, demonstrating its comprehensive understanding of ST data through capturing and integrating multi-scale information.

paragraphs: Spatial transcriptomics measures gene expression while retaining information about where cells are located. Understanding these data requires linking several scales: the overall tissue structure, a cell’s local surroundings, and its gene expression profile. SToFM is a foundation model designed to combine those scales when learning representations of cells within tissue slices.

The framework first extracts information at multiple scales and constructs smaller spatial transcriptomics sub-slices that bring the three kinds of evidence together. An SE(2) Transformer then processes these sub-slices to produce cell representations. The authors also build SToCorpus-88M, described as the largest high-resolution spatial transcriptomics pretraining corpus, to support learning from this type of data.

The model achieves strong reported performance across downstream tasks, including tissue region segmentation and cell type annotation. These tasks use the learned representations at different biological levels, connecting cell identity with tissue organization. The results support integrating spatial context and gene expression in a shared model, showing that the combined information can be useful across multiple forms of spatial transcriptomics analysis.
summary.tldr: SToFM integrates tissue structure, cellular surroundings, and gene expression to learn cell representations that perform strongly across spatial transcriptomics tasks.

title: SToFM: a Multi-scale Foundation Model for Spatial Transcriptomics

abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) provides rigorous finite-sample coverage guarantees, yet its statistical efficiency hinges critically on the size of the calibration set. In data-scarce regimes, CP often suffers from volatile quantile estimation, leading to overly conservative and wide prediction intervals. To address this, we propose Random Score Alignment-Conformal Prediction (RSA-CP), a simple framework designed to improve sample efficiency in small-sample CP. Instead of requiring the computationally intensive generation of full synthetic datasets, RSA-CP enhances calibration by directly aligning real scores with a high-resolution reference score distribution. By employing an optimal transport mapping, our framework refines "step-like" quantile increments through a globally optimal use of reference information. We provide theoretical guarantees establishing that RSA-CP maintains robust coverage without any distributional assumptions on the reference scores. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that RSA-CP consistently produces shorter and more precise prediction intervals while maintaining finite-sample coverage guarantees. Overall, RSA-CP offers a computationally efficient and theoretically grounded solution for robust uncertainty quantification under limited data.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction supplies finite-sample coverage guarantees, but a small calibration set can make its estimated quantiles unstable. This often produces prediction intervals that are wider and more conservative than desired. RSA-CP aims to improve calibration efficiency when only limited real data is available.

The framework directly aligns real calibration scores with a high-resolution reference score distribution. It uses an optimal transport mapping to make globally optimal use of that reference information and refine the coarse increments in the calibration quantiles. Working at the score level avoids the computational cost of generating complete synthetic datasets.

The authors prove coverage guarantees that do not require distributional assumptions about the reference scores. Empirical evaluations show consistently shorter, more precise prediction intervals while maintaining finite-sample coverage guarantees. The contribution links reference-based refinement to theoretical coverage control: additional score information can improve interval efficiency without imposing a prescribed distribution on the reference scores. This makes the method particularly relevant to the small-sample calibration problem motivating the paper.
summary.tldr: RSA-CP aligns calibration scores with a reference distribution to shorten small-sample prediction intervals while preserving coverage guarantees.

title: RSA-CP: Efficient Conformal Prediction in Small-Sample Regimes via Random Score Alignment

abstract: We develop a geometric theory of projection heads in self-supervised learning by modeling the head as a trainable Riemannian metric on the backbone representation manifold. We show that linear heads perform implicit subspace whitening, while nonlinear heads adapt local metrics to satisfy the specific topological constraints of the loss, with head depth empirically dictating this capacity. Analyzing dimensional collapse, we prove that smooth nonlinear heads natively induce negative eigenvalues in the Hessian at collapsed equilibria, making them unstable. We empirically validate this by continuously tracking the optimization geometry during training, which reveals that smooth activations like Swish can generate explicit negative curvature to escape collapse, whereas linear and ReLU heads under continuous-time gradient flow cannot, relying instead on discrete-time optimization dynamics and BatchNorm. Finally, we geometrically characterize how metric degeneracy governs the information-invariance trade-off, explaining why the head must be discarded. Evaluated across contrastive and decorrelation-based objectives on foundation models, our results demonstrate that the projection head acts as a universal geometric buffer, decoupling the semantic backbone from the rigid, destructive constraints of the pretraining objective.

paragraphs: Projection heads transform backbone representations before a self-supervised training loss is applied. This paper explains their role geometrically by treating the head as a trainable metric that changes how representation-space distances are measured. Linear heads implicitly whiten a subspace, while nonlinear heads adapt local geometry to the loss’s topological constraints; experiments connect head depth to this capacity.

The analysis also addresses dimensional collapse, where representations lose informative directions. The authors prove that smooth nonlinear heads introduce negative Hessian eigenvalues at collapsed equilibria, making those equilibria unstable. Tracking training geometry supports this mechanism for smooth activations such as Swish. Under continuous-time gradient flow, linear and ReLU heads cannot escape through that mechanism, instead relying on discrete optimization dynamics and BatchNorm.

The theory connects metric degeneracy to the trade-off between retaining information and enforcing invariance, explaining why the head is discarded. Evaluations across contrastive and decorrelation-based objectives support its role as a geometric buffer: it absorbs constraints imposed by the training objective while allowing the backbone to retain semantic information.
summary.tldr: A geometric theory explains how projection heads reshape learning, help escape collapse, and separate useful backbone representations from pretraining constraints.

title: The Geometry of Projection Heads: Conditioning, Invariance, and Collapse

abstract: Tokenization is used almost universally by modern language models, enabling efficient text representation using multi-byte or multi-character tokens. However, prior work has shown that tokenization can introduce distortion into the model’s generations, an issue known as the Prompt Boundary Problem (PBP). For example, users are often advised not to end their prompts with a space because it prevents the model from including the space as part of the next token. While this heuristic is effective in English, the underlying PBP continues to affect code generation and languages such as Chinese, where tokens often do not line up with word and syntactic boundaries. In this work, we present an inference-time method to convert any autoregressive LM with a BPE tokenizer into a character-level or byte-level LM. Our method efficiently solves the PBP and is also able to unify the vocabularies of language models with different tokenizers, allowing one to ensemble LMs with different tokenizers at inference time or transfer the post-training from one model to another using proxy-tuning.

paragraphs: Language models usually generate tokens containing multiple characters or bytes. This can distort generation when a prompt ends inside a unit that the tokenizer would otherwise group together. The paper studies this Prompt Boundary Problem, which appears in familiar advice about trailing spaces and also affects code and languages such as Chinese, where token and syntactic boundaries may differ.

The authors introduce an inference-time method that converts any autoregressive language model using a BPE tokenizer into a character-level or byte-level model. The method efficiently resolves the boundary problem at generation time. Its scope is explicitly models with BPE tokenizers, allowing finer-grained generation while working with those models' existing token-based representations.

A shared character or byte vocabulary also creates a common interface between models whose original tokenizers differ. The paper identifies two uses: combining such models in an inference-time ensemble and transferring post-training behavior through proxy-tuning. The contribution therefore connects a generation-boundary fix with interoperability, enabling models to coordinate through a representation that does not depend on matching token inventories.
summary.tldr: An inference-time conversion enables byte- or character-level sampling from BPE language models, resolving prompt-boundary distortion and supporting cross-tokenizer combinations.

title: Sampling from Your Language Model One Byte at a Time

abstract: Agentic reasoning enables large reasoning models (LRMs) to dynamically acquire external knowledge, yet optimizing the retrieval process remains challenging due to the lack of dense, principled reward signals. In this paper, we introduce InfoReasoner, a unified framework that incentivizes effective information seeking via a synthetic semantic information gain reward. Theoretically, we redefine information gain as uncertainty reduction over the model’s belief states, establishing key properties including non-negativity, telescoping additivity, and channel monotonicity. Practically, to enable scalable optimization without manual intermediate retrieval annotations, we instantiate this principle as a semantic information gain reward computed from the model’s output distributions using semantic clustering via bidirectional textual entailment. This training reward provides dense credit for retrieval steps while remaining anchored to final-answer correctness, enabling efficient training via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Experiments on seven question-answering benchmarks, MATH500, and WebDetective show consistent gains over strong retrieval-augmented baselines, supporting our dense semantic information gain as a practical training signal for agentic retrieval.

paragraphs: Reasoning models that retrieve information need feedback about which retrieval steps actually help. Final-answer correctness alone provides limited guidance about intermediate searches. InfoReasoner introduces a denser training signal based on how much retrieved information reduces uncertainty in the model’s beliefs, while keeping that signal connected to answer correctness.

The theoretical formulation establishes non-negativity, additivity across successive steps, and channel monotonicity for this notion of information gain. The practical implementation estimates semantic uncertainty from the model’s output distributions. It groups outputs using bidirectional textual entailment, so mutually supporting meanings inform the reward. This supplies credit for individual retrieval steps without requiring people to annotate those intermediate actions.

The framework trains with Group Relative Policy Optimization and reports consistent improvements over strong retrieval-augmented baselines on seven question-answering benchmarks, MATH500, and WebDetective. These findings support semantic information gain as a useful optimization signal for information seeking. The contribution connects a principled account of uncertainty reduction to a scalable reward that can guide the retrieval process throughout reasoning.
summary.tldr: InfoReasoner rewards retrieval steps for reducing semantic uncertainty while anchoring training to final-answer correctness.

title: Optimizing Agentic Reasoning with Retrieval via Synthetic Semantic Information Gain Reward

abstract: We develop approximation and statistical theory for standard Transformer networks in sequence modeling. Given a sequence-to-sequence target on $[0,1]^{d_x \times n}$ whose entries are $\gamma$-Hölder for $\gamma \in (0,1]$ or belong to a first-order Sobolev class, we establish explicit $L^p$-approximation bounds for all $p \in [1,\infty]$, including the previously elusive endpoint $p=\infty$ under softmax attention. In particular, achieving error $\varepsilon$ in $L^p$-norm requires $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-d_x n/\gamma})$ parameters for $\gamma$-Hölder targets and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-d_x n})$ parameters for Sobolev targets, matching the best known scalings in ambient dimension $d_x n$. We further study nonparametric regression with sequential and dependent observations using Transformer networks. Assuming stationary $\beta$-mixing covariates whose temporal dependence weakens over time, we analyze a sliding-window empirical risk minimization procedure and establish excess-risk guarantees for the Transformer-based estimators. Our analysis clarifies the role of attention and enables extensions beyond softmax.

paragraphs: This paper studies how large a standard Transformer must be to approximate sequence-to-sequence functions, and what statistical guarantees follow when it learns from dependent observations. Its approximation results cover targets with specified regularity: Hölder continuity with exponent between zero and one, or membership in a first-order Sobolev class. These assumptions define the function families covered by the theory.

The authors establish error bounds across all Lp norms, including the maximum-error endpoint under softmax attention. For error ε, their constructions use parameter counts scaling as ε raised to −d_x n/γ for Hölder targets and −d_x n for Sobolev targets. These match the best known scalings in the combined input dimension d_x n.

The regression analysis considers stationary covariates whose temporal dependence weakens under a beta-mixing assumption. For a sliding-window empirical risk minimization procedure, it gives excess-risk guarantees for Transformer estimators. Thus the contribution connects representational capacity with learning from sequential data, while clarifying attention’s role and supporting extensions beyond softmax.
summary.tldr: The paper derives Transformer approximation bounds and regression guarantees for regular target functions and temporally dependent data.

title: Approximation Bounds for Transformer Networks with Application to Regression

abstract: Robust signal enhancement at low SNR is fundamentally challenging because noise becomes strongly entangled with the signal and corrupts local time–frequency (TF) evidence. In this regime, fixed resolution short time Fourier transform (STFT) enhancement with purely data driven convolutional biases can become overconfident in unreliable TF regions, causing unstable suppression or residual artifacts. We propose FracKGMF, which couples Fractional Distance Decay Convolution (FracConv) with Knowledge Guided Multi-view Fusion (KGMF) for expressive TF modeling and reliability aware decisions under heavy corruption. FracConv introduces a lightweight fractional distance decay family that reshapes local interactions into long tailed receptive patterns, enabling aggregation of weak but globally consistent cues when per-bin observations are ambiguous. KGMF uses a wiener inspired reliability prior to calibrate multi-view fusion and reduce excessive suppression in uncertain regions. Experiments on speech and EM benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with particularly large gains under extremely low SNR, including a 33 dB average improvement on EM signals at -20 dB.

paragraphs: When noise dominates a signal, local time–frequency observations become unreliable. Enhancement models can then suppress useful content too aggressively or leave artifacts behind. FracKGMF addresses this problem by combining a broader pattern of information aggregation with a mechanism that accounts for uncertainty when combining multiple views.

Its Fractional Distance Decay Convolution changes how local interactions weaken with distance, producing long-tailed receptive patterns. This allows the model to gather weak but mutually consistent cues beyond an ambiguous individual time–frequency bin. Knowledge Guided Multi-view Fusion then uses a Wiener-inspired reliability prior to calibrate how views are combined, reducing excessive suppression where the evidence is uncertain.

Experiments on speech and electromagnetic signal benchmarks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Gains are particularly large under extreme noise, including a reported average improvement of 33 dB on electromagnetic signals at −20 dB. The findings support pairing expressive signal aggregation with reliability-aware fusion: one component collects dispersed evidence, while the other regulates decisions when that evidence remains uncertain.
summary.tldr: FracKGMF combines long-tailed signal aggregation with reliability-guided fusion to improve enhancement under very strong noise.

title: Robust Signal Enhancement via Fractional Detail Views and Knowledge Guided Multi-view Fusion

abstract: Recent advances in generative video models have blurred the boundary between real and synthetic content, raising urgent concerns about digital authenticity. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are appealing for AI-generated video (AIGV) detection due to their broad perceptual and reasoning capabilities; however, existing MLLM-based detectors still suffer from hallucination and unstable reasoning, leading to high false-alarm rates and generic, non-verifiable explanations. To address these issues, we propose Hermes, an evidence-driven agentic framework for trustworthy and explainable AIGV detection. Hermes realizes three key capabilities: (1) Adaptive Instance-Conditioned Detection Strategy Planning, (2) Evidence-Centric Reasoning and Verification, and (3) Graph-Grounded Evidence Deliberation. Specifically, Hermes uses instance-conditioned retrieval-augmented generation to analyze each video and retrieve authenticity-verification knowledge for composing a tailored detection strategy. It then constructs a verifiable Evidence Reasoning Graph (ERG) to keep reasoning grounded in concrete video evidence and reduce attention drift. Finally, multi-agent deliberation audits and refines the ERG to reconcile conflicting evidence and improve reliability. With these capabilities and a library of forensic tools, Hermes enables structured, verifiable, and interpretable decision-making. Extensive experiments show that Hermes achieves state-of-the-art performance while producing auditable explanations for trustworthy video forensics.
