paragraphs: Detecting AI-generated video requires more than a plausible explanation of why footage looks suspicious. Multimodal language-model detectors can hallucinate evidence or reason inconsistently, producing false alarms and explanations that cannot be checked. Hermes organizes detection around concrete video evidence and explicit verification.

For each video, the framework retrieves relevant authenticity-verification knowledge and builds a detection strategy suited to that instance. It then records evidence and reasoning in an Evidence Reasoning Graph. This graph is intended to keep the analysis tied to observable support and reduce attention drift. A library of forensic tools supplies capabilities for the investigation.

Multiple agents subsequently audit and refine the graph, addressing conflicting evidence before a decision is finalized. The resulting explanation is connected to an inspectable reasoning structure. Extensive experiments report state-of-the-art detection performance together with auditable explanations. The contribution combines adaptive investigation with evidence checking, showing how the process behind a detection decision can become part of the system’s output rather than remaining hidden behind a final classification.
summary.tldr: Hermes detects AI-generated videos through tailored forensic investigation, evidence graphs, and multi-agent auditing that produces inspectable explanations.

title: Hermes: An Evidence-Driven Agentic Framework for Trustworthy and Explainable AI-Generated Video Detection

abstract: Foundation models are increasingly being deployed in contexts where understanding the uncertainty of their outputs is critical to ensuring responsible deployment. While Bayesian methods offer a principled approach to uncertainty quantification, their computational overhead renders their use impractical for training or inference at foundation model scale. State-of-the-art models achieve parameter counts in the trillions through carefully engineered sparsity including Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers. In this work, we demonstrate calibrated uncertainty at scale by introducing Variational Mixture-of-Experts Routing (VMoER), a structured Bayesian approach for modelling uncertainty in MoE layers. VMoER confines Bayesian inference to the expert-selection stage which is typically done by a deterministic routing network. We instantiate VMoER using two inference strategies: amortised variational inference over routing logits and inferring a temperature parameter for stochastic expert selection. Across tested foundation models, VMoER improves routing stability under noise by 38%, reduces calibration error by 94%, and increases out-of-distribution AUROC by 12%, while incurring less than 1% additional FLOPs. These results suggest VMoER offers a scalable path toward robust and uncertainty-aware foundation models.

paragraphs: Foundation models increasingly need useful estimates of uncertainty, but applying Bayesian methods throughout very large networks can be computationally expensive. Variational Mixture-of-Experts Routing, or VMoER, concentrates Bayesian inference on the decision about which experts to activate. This targets a limited part of an architecture already designed around sparse computation.

The framework replaces the usual deterministic treatment of expert selection with structured uncertainty modeling. The authors implement two approaches: amortized variational inference over routing logits, and inference of a temperature parameter governing stochastic expert selection. Both place uncertainty in routing rather than requiring Bayesian inference across every model parameter.

Across the tested foundation models, VMoER improves routing stability under noise by 38%, reduces calibration error by 94%, and increases out-of-distribution AUROC by 12%, with less than 1% additional FLOPs. These results combine stronger uncertainty-related behavior with a small computational increment. They suggest that Bayesian expert selection offers a scalable route toward better-calibrated foundation models, with the reported benefits grounded in the models and conditions evaluated.
summary.tldr: VMoER confines Bayesian uncertainty modeling to expert routing, improving calibration and robustness with less than 1% additional FLOPs.

title: Variational Routing: A Scalable Bayesian Framework for Calibrated Mixture-of-Experts Transformers

abstract: Long-form clinical videos are central to visual evidence-based decision-making, with growing importance for applications such as surgical robotics and related settings. However, current multimodal large language models typically process videos with passive sampling or weakly grounded inspection, which limits their ability to iteratively locate, verify, and justify predictions with temporally targeted evidence. To close this gap, we propose MedScope, a tool-using clinical video reasoning model that performs coarse-to-fine evidence seeking over long-form procedures. By interleaving intermediate reasoning with targeted tool calls and verification on retrieved observations, MedScope produces more accurate and trustworthy predictions that are explicitly grounded in temporally localized visual evidence. To address the lack of high-fidelity supervision, we build ClinVideoSuite, an evidence-centric, fine-grained clinical video suite. We then optimize MedScope with Grounding-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (GA-GRPO), which directly reinforces tool use with grounding-aligned rewards and evidence-weighted advantages. On full and fine-grained video understanding benchmarks, MedScope achieves state-of-the-art performance in both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations. Our approach illuminates a path toward medical AI agents that can genuinely “think with videos” through tool-integrated reasoning. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/SII-WenjieLisjtu/MedScope.

paragraphs: Long clinical videos require a model to find the moments that support a prediction. Passive frame sampling or loosely grounded inspection can leave that evidence insufficiently examined. MedScope addresses this by making video understanding an iterative process of locating relevant observations, reasoning about them, and checking the resulting interpretation.

The model uses tools to search from coarse temporal regions toward finer evidence. Intermediate reasoning is interleaved with targeted retrieval and verification of the observations returned. The authors also build ClinVideoSuite to provide detailed, evidence-focused supervision. Their GA-GRPO training method rewards grounded tool use and weights learning advantages according to evidence.

MedScope reports state-of-the-art performance on full-video and fine-grained understanding benchmarks, including both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations. The stated improvement combines stronger predictions with explicit links to localized visual evidence. This matters because the model's inspection process becomes part of how it reaches and supports an answer, rather than leaving evidence selection as a passive preprocessing step.
summary.tldr: MedScope learns to retrieve and verify targeted clinical video evidence, improving grounded video understanding.

title: MedScope: Incentivizing "Think with Videos" for Clinical Reasoning via Coarse-to-Fine Tool Calling

abstract: We study a sampling problem whose target distribution is $\pi \propto \exp(-f-r)$ where the data fidelity term $f$ is Lipschitz smooth while the regularizer term $r=r_1-r_2$ is a non-smooth difference-of-convex (DC) function, i.e., $r_1,r_2$ are convex. By leveraging the DC structure of $r$, we can smooth out $r$ by applying Moreau envelopes to $r_1$ and $r_2$ separately. In line with DC programming, we then redistribute the concave part of the regularizer to the data fidelity and study its corresponding proximal Langevin algorithm (termed DC-LA). We establish convergence of DC-LA to the target distribution $\pi$, up to discretization and smoothing errors, in the $q$-Wasserstein distance for all $q \in \mathbb{N}^*$, under the assumption that $V$ is distant dissipative. Our results improve previous work on non-log-concave sampling in terms of a more general framework and assumptions. Numerical experiments show that DC-LA produces accurate distributions in synthetic settings and provides qualitatively reasonable uncertainty quantification in a real-world Computed Tomography application.

paragraphs: DC-LA addresses sampling from a distribution defined by a smooth data-fitting term and a potentially nonsmooth regularizer. The regularizer must be expressible as one convex function minus another. This structure accommodates a broader sampling problem than one restricted to a convex overall objective, while giving the algorithm specific mathematical components to work with.

The method smooths the two convex components separately using Moreau envelopes. It then moves the concave contribution into the data-fitting term and applies a corresponding proximal Langevin algorithm. The distinction matters: the procedure uses the regularizer's decomposition to construct a tractable sampling method instead of treating its nonsmooth, nonconvex behavior as an undifferentiated obstacle.

Under the stated distant-dissipativity assumption on V, the authors establish convergence toward the target distribution in q-Wasserstein distance for every positive integer q, allowing for discretization and smoothing errors. Synthetic experiments show accurate sampled distributions. A computed tomography application provides qualitatively reasonable uncertainty estimates, supporting the method's practical relevance without claiming exact sampling or quantitatively validated uncertainty in that application.
summary.tldr: DC-LA uses a difference-of-convex decomposition to sample nonsmooth distributions with conditional convergence guarantees and controlled approximation errors.

title: DC-LA: Difference-of-Convex Langevin Algorithm

abstract: Real-world data visualization (DV) requires native environmental grounding, cross-platform evolution, and proactive intent alignment, yet existing benchmarks are often limited to code sandboxes, creation-only tasks, and fully specified intents. We introduce DV-World, a 260-task benchmark for evaluating DV agents across professional visualization lifecycles. DV-World covers three domains: DV-Sheet for native spreadsheet chart/dashboard creation and diagnostic repair; DV-Evolution for adapting reference visual artifacts to new data across programming paradigms; and DV-Interact for proactive intent alignment with a user simulator under ambiguous requirements. Its hybrid evaluation combines Table-value Alignment for numerical precision with rubric-based MLLM-as-a-Judge for semantic-visual assessment. Experiments show that state-of-the-art models achieve below 50% overall performance, exposing major gaps in real-world DV capabilities. DV-World provides a realistic testbed for developing DV agents suited to enterprise workflows. Data and code are available at dv-world-project.github.io.

paragraphs: Creating a useful visualization involves more than writing code for a chart. Professional work also includes repairing existing artifacts, adapting them to different data and tools, and clarifying what a user wants. DV-World evaluates visualization agents across these broader responsibilities through a benchmark containing 260 tasks.

The benchmark has three domains. DV-Sheet covers chart and dashboard creation in native spreadsheets, along with diagnostic repair. DV-Evolution tests adaptation of reference visualizations to new data across programming paradigms. DV-Interact introduces ambiguous requirements and a user simulator, testing whether an agent proactively works toward a clearer understanding of the intended result.

Evaluation combines numerical checks through Table-value Alignment with rubric-based semantic and visual judgments from a multimodal language model. The tested state-of-the-art models achieve below 50% overall performance. These results expose substantial gaps across the benchmark’s professional visualization workflows. By testing numerical accuracy, visual meaning, adaptation, and interaction together, DV-World provides a broader basis for assessing agents intended for enterprise visualization work.
summary.tldr: DV-World tests visualization agents on 260 realistic creation, repair, adaptation, and interaction tasks, where evaluated models score below 50% overall.

title: DV-World: Benchmarking Data Visualization Agents in Real-World Scenarios

abstract: Learning the compositional nature of the physical world requires joint observation of interacting factors. However, because practical data is often decentralized, these factors are fragmented across isolated silos. Existing decentralized generative approaches focus only on modeling the union of siloed data, overlooking novel combinations implied by the collective whole. To bridge this gap, we introduce Decentralized Compositional Flow Matching (DCFM), a framework that enforces structural constraints across the global set of generative factors, without exchanging any raw data. DCFM enables novel combinations to emerge through peer interactions, even when no single data source can independently support the composition. Empirically, DCFM substantially outperforms federated learning and mixture-of-experts baselines across conditional image generation, robotic spatial planning, and medical attribute co-occurrence modeling.

paragraphs: Generative models need evidence about interacting factors to learn how those factors combine. In decentralized settings, relevant observations may be scattered across isolated data sources. A model that merely represents the union of those sources can capture what each contains while overlooking new combinations supported by their collective information.

Decentralized Compositional Flow Matching addresses that gap by enforcing structural constraints across the global set of generative factors. The framework uses interactions among peers without exchanging raw data. Its goal is to make compositions emerge from the distributed evidence even when no individual source contains enough information to support the composition independently.

The authors evaluate the framework on conditional image generation, robotic spatial planning, and medical attribute co-occurrence modeling. Across these settings, it substantially outperforms federated learning and mixture-of-experts baselines. The stated findings support a distinction between aggregating distributed observations and learning how their factors fit together. Here, peer interaction and global structural constraints provide a way to generate combinations that isolated sources cannot supply on their own.
summary.tldr: Decentralized Compositional Flow Matching learns novel factor combinations across data silos without exchanging raw data.

title: Compositional Generative Modeling from Decentralized Data

abstract: Popular offline reinforcement learning (RL) methods rely on explicit conservatism, penalizing out-of-dataset actions or restricting rollout horizons. We question the universality of this principle and revisit a complementary Bayesian perspective for test-time adaptation. By modeling a posterior over world models and training a history-dependent agent to maximize expected return, the Bayesian approach directly addresses epistemic uncertainty without explicit conservatism. We first illustrate in a bandit setting that Bayesianism excels on low-quality datasets where conservatism fails. Scaling to realistic tasks, we find that long-horizon rollouts are essential to control value overestimation once conservatism is removed. We introduce design choices that enable learning from long-horizon rollouts while mitigating compounding model errors, yielding our algorithm, NEUBAY, grounded in the neutral Bayesian principle. On D4RL and NeoRL benchmarks, NEUBAY is competitive with leading conservative algorithms, achieving new state-of-the-art on 7 datasets with rollout horizons of several hundred steps. Finally, we characterize datasets by quality and coverage to identify when NEUBAY is preferable to conservative methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often controls uncertainty by penalizing unfamiliar actions or shortening simulated rollouts. This paper examines a Bayesian alternative: maintain a posterior over possible world models and train a history-dependent agent to maximize expected return. The approach addresses uncertainty about the environment without explicit conservative penalties.

A bandit example shows advantages on low-quality datasets where conservatism fails. In more realistic tasks, the authors find that long rollouts are essential for controlling value overestimation after removing conservatism. Their algorithm, NEUBAY, includes design choices that support learning from these extended rollouts while mitigating the accumulation of world-model errors.

On D4RL and NeoRL, NEUBAY is competitive with leading conservative methods and achieves new state-of-the-art results on seven datasets using rollout horizons of several hundred steps. The authors also examine dataset quality and coverage to identify when their approach is preferable. The findings challenge the universality of explicit conservatism while connecting the choice of approach to the available data.
summary.tldr: NEUBAY combines Bayesian world-model uncertainty with long rollouts to achieve competitive offline RL without explicit conservatism.

title: Long-Horizon Model-Based Offline Reinforcement Learning Without Explicit Conservatism

abstract: Self-supervised pre-training methods in medical imaging typically treat each individual as an isolated instance, learning representations through augmentation-based objectives or masked reconstruction. They often do not adequately capitalize on a key characteristic of physiological features: anatomical structures maintain consistent spatial relationships across individuals (instances), such as the thalamus being medial to the basal ganglia, regardless of variations in brain size, shape, or pathology. We propose leveraging this cross-instance topological consistency as a supervisory signal. The challenge arises from the inherent variability in medical imaging, which can differ significantly across instances and modalities. To tackle this, we focus on two alignment regimes. (i) Intra-instance: with pixel-level correspondences available, a cross-modal triplet objective explicitly preserves local neighborhood topology. (ii) Inter-instance: without such supervision, we derive pseudo-correspondences to control partial neighborhood alignment and prevent topology collapse across modalities. We validate our approach across 7 downstream multi-modal tasks, achieving average improvements of 1.1% and 5.94% in segmentation and classification tasks, respectively, and demonstrating significantly better robustness when modalities are missing at test time.

(i) Intra-instance: with pixel-level correspondences available, a cross-modal triplet objective explicitly preserves local neighborhood topology. (ii) Inter-instance: without such supervision, we derive pseudo-correspondences to control partial neighborhood alignment and prevent topology collapse across modalities. paragraphs: Medical images vary across people and imaging modalities, yet anatomical structures retain consistent spatial relationships. This paper uses that shared organization as a learning signal for self-supervised pretraining. The motivation is that treating each person as an isolated example leaves useful information about relationships across individuals underused.

The method separates alignment into two situations. Within one individual, available pixel correspondences support a cross-modal triplet objective that preserves local neighborhood relationships. Across individuals, where those correspondences are unavailable, the method derives approximate matches. These pseudo-correspondences guide partial neighborhood alignment and help prevent representations from collapsing in ways that lose anatomical organization across modalities.

Evaluation covers seven downstream tasks involving multiple imaging modalities. The authors report average improvements of 1.1% for segmentation and 5.94% for classification, together with significantly better robustness when some modalities are absent at test time. The findings suggest that learning shared anatomical relationships can improve both downstream prediction and resilience to incomplete inputs. The two alignment regimes make those relationships usable even when the available correspondence information differs.
summary.tldr: Learning anatomical relationships across people and imaging modalities improves medical-image prediction and robustness to missing modalities.

title: Beyond Instance-Level Self-Supervision in 3D Multi-Modal Medical Imaging

abstract: Graph neural networks face two fundamental challenges rooted in the linear structure of Euclidean vector spaces: (1) Current architectures represent geometry through vectors (directions, gradients), yet many tasks require matrix-valued representations that capture relationships between directions—such as how atomic orientations covary in a molecule. These second-order representations are naturally captured by points on the symmetric positive definite matrices (SPD) manifold; (2) Standard message passing applies shared transformations across edges. Sheaf neural networks address this via edge-specific transformations, but existing formulations remain confined to vector spaces and therefore cannot propagate matrix-valued features. We address both challenges by developing the first sheaf neural network operates natively on the SPD manifold. Our key insight is that the SPD manifold admits a Lie group structure, enabling well-posed analogs of sheaf operators without projecting to Euclidean space. Theoretically, we prove that SPD-valued sheaves are strictly more expressive than Euclidean sheaves: they admit consistent configurations (global sections) that vector-valued sheaves cannot represent, directly translating to richer learned representations. Empirically, our sheaf convolution transforms effectively rank-1 directional inputs into full-rank matrices encoding local geometric structure. Our dual-stream architecture achieves SOTA on 6/7 MoleculeNet benchmarks, with the sheaf framework providing consistent depth robustness.

title: Sheaf Neural Networks on SPD Manifolds: Second-Order Geometric Representation Learning

abstract: Protein sequences are abundant in repeating segments, both as exact copies and as approximate segments with mutations. These repeats are important for protein structure and function, motivating decades of algorithmic work on repeat identification. Recent work has shown that protein language models (PLMs) identify repeats, by examining their behavior in masked-token prediction. To elucidate their internal mechanisms, we investigate how PLMs detect both exact and approximate repeats. We find that the mechanism for approximate repeats functionally subsumes that of exact repeats. We then characterize this mechanism, revealing two main stages: PLMs first build feature representations using both general positional attention heads and biologically specialized components, such as neurons that encode amino-acid similarity. Then, induction heads attend to aligned tokens across repeated segments, promoting the correct answer. Our results reveal how PLMs solve this biological task by combining language-based pattern matching with specialized biological knowledge, thereby establishing a basis for studying more complex evolutionary processes in PLMs.

The authors identify a two-stage mechanism. First, models construct useful features using positional attention together with biologically specialized components, including neurons that represent similarity between amino acids. The mechanism therefore combines positional pattern matching with representations that account for biological similarity.

The study finds that the mechanism for approximate repeats functionally includes the mechanism for exact repeats. That connects the two behaviors within a broader repeat-detection process. The findings explain how general language-model machinery and specialized biological features cooperate on this task, and provide a foundation for investigating more complex evolutionary patterns inside protein language models.
summary.tldr: Protein language models detect repeats by combining biological similarity features with attention that aligns corresponding sequence positions.

title: Induction Meets Biology: Mechanisms of Repeat Detection in Protein Language Models

abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based scientific agents have accelerated scientific discovery, yet they often suffer from significant inefficiencies due to adherence to fixed initial priors. Existing approaches predominantly operate within a static hypothesis space, which restricts the discovery of novel phenomena, resulting in computational waste when baseline theories fail. To address this, we propose shifting the focus from searching hypotheses to evolving the underlying scientific principles. We present $\textbf{PiEvo}$, a principle-evolvable framework that treats scientific discovery as Bayesian optimization over an expanding principle space. By integrating Information-Directed Hypothesis Selection via Gaussian Process and an anomaly-driven augmentation mechanism, PiEvo enables agents to autonomously refine their theoretical worldview. Evaluation across four benchmarks demonstrates that PiEvo (1) achieves an average solution quality of up to 90.81%$\sim$93.15%, representing a 29.7%$\sim$31.1% improvement over the state-of-the-art, (2) attains an 83.3% speedup in convergence step via significantly reduced sample complexity by optimizing the compact principle space, and (3) maintains robust performance across diverse scientific domains and LLM backbones. Code is publicly available at github.com/amair-lab/PiEvo.

This paper proposes allowing the underlying scientific principles to evolve during discovery. PiEvo treats discovery as Bayesian optimization over a principle space that can expand, so the agent’s initial theoretical framework does not remain fixed.

The framework combines Gaussian-process-based, information-directed hypothesis selection with a mechanism that augments the principle space in response to anomalies. The first component guides which hypotheses to investigate; the second allows unexpected observations to trigger changes in the agent’s theoretical worldview. Searching a compact principle space is intended to reduce the number of samples needed.

Across four benchmarks, the authors report average solution quality reaching 90.81%–93.15%, with reported improvements of 29.7%–31.1% over the state of the art. They also report an 83.3% speedup in convergence steps and robust performance across evaluated scientific domains and language-model backbones. These findings support revising the principles that organize a search as a way to improve both discovery quality and efficiency.
summary.tldr: PiEvo lets scientific agents revise their underlying principles in response to anomalies, improving discovery quality and convergence in four benchmarks.

title: Principle-Evolvable Scientific Discovery via Uncertainty Minimization

abstract: We introduce Categorical Flow Maps, a flow-matching method for accelerated few-step generation of categorical data via self-distillation. Building on recent variational formulations of flow matching and the broader trend towards accelerated inference in diffusion and flow-based models, we define a flow map towards the simplex that transports probability mass toward a predicted endpoint, yielding a parametrisation that naturally constrains model predictions. Since our trajectories are continuous rather than discrete, Categorical Flow Maps can be trained with existing distillation techniques, as well as a new objective based on endpoint consistency. This continuous formulation also automatically unlocks test-time inference: we can directly reuse existing guidance and reweighting techniques in the categorical setting to steer sampling toward downstream objectives. Empirically, we achieve state-of-the-art few-step results on images, molecular graphs, and text, with strong performance even in single-step generation.

paragraphs: Categorical Flow Maps aims to generate categorical data in very few computational steps. The paper develops a flow-matching method with self-distillation, allowing the model to learn accelerated generation. Its central construction moves probability mass toward a predicted endpoint on the probability simplex, the space of valid probability distributions over categories.

Although the outputs are categorical, the paths used by the method are continuous. This choice makes existing distillation techniques usable and supports a new training objective based on endpoint consistency. The parameterization also naturally constrains predictions. These properties connect the categorical generation problem to tools already available for accelerating continuous diffusion and flow models.

The continuous formulation additionally allows guidance and reweighting techniques to steer generation toward downstream objectives at test time. Empirically, the authors report state-of-the-art few-step results for images, molecular graphs, and text, with strong performance even from a single generation step. The contribution brings accelerated sampling and test-time steering into the same framework for these different forms of categorical data.
summary.tldr: Categorical Flow Maps uses continuous probability trajectories and self-distillation for fast, steerable categorical generation.

title: Categorical Flow Maps

abstract: Epistemic uncertainty is often viewed as a reducible uncertainty that vanishes with increasing data. This perspective implicitly assumes parameter identifiability and equates epistemic uncertainty with predictive variability. In overparametrized neural networks, however, model parameters are typically non-identifiable due to symmetries and redundant representations. As a consequence, substantial parameter uncertainty can persist even when the underlying function is fully identified. In this work, we analyze epistemic uncertainty through the lens of non-identifiability and characterize both discrete and continuous sources of residual uncertainty. Focusing on one-hidden-layer ReLU networks, we thoroughly analyze the resulting posterior structure and validate our theoretical insights through empirical studies.

As a consequence, substantial parameter uncertainty can persist even when the underlying function is fully identified. In this work, we analyze epistemic uncertainty through the lens of non-identifiability and characterize both discrete and continuous sources of residual uncertainty. Focusing on one-hidden-layer ReLU networks, we thoroughly analyze the resulting posterior structure and validate our theoretical insights through empirical studies.

paragraphs: Epistemic uncertainty is commonly described as uncertainty that more data can eliminate. This paper examines a hidden assumption behind that view: that identifying what a model predicts also identifies its parameters. In overparametrized neural networks, several parameter configurations can represent the same function, so those two kinds of knowledge can come apart.

The authors analyze this issue through non-identifiability, where different parameter settings cannot be distinguished by the function they produce. Symmetries and redundant representations create both discrete and continuous sources of residual uncertainty. As a result, substantial uncertainty over parameters can remain even when the underlying predictive function is fully determined.

The detailed analysis focuses on ReLU networks with one hidden layer and characterizes the resulting posterior structure. Empirical studies support the theoretical insights. The contribution is a sharper interpretation of what uncertainty in a neural network means: persistent uncertainty about parameters need not imply persistent disagreement about predictions. This distinction matters when interpreting posterior distributions and claims that additional data must remove all epistemic uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Neural-network parameters can remain uncertain even when their predictive function is fully identified because multiple parameter settings represent that function.

title: On the Epistemic Uncertainty of Overparametrized Neural Networks

abstract: Shapley values are a principled attribution measure widely used in interpretable machine learning, but their exact computation scales exponentially with the number of players, motivating a wide range of approximation methods based on value function evaluations of sampled coalitions. This raises the question of whether approximation accuracy can be improved by adaptively selecting coalitions for evaluation based on previous evaluations. This is particularly relevant in settings where the value function is costly and the number of evaluations is severely limited, such as retraining-based feature importance, data valuation, and hyperparameter importance. For this purpose, we propose $\texttt{ShaplEIG}$, a Bayesian experimental design approach that approximates the expensive value function using a Gaussian process surrogate and adaptively selects coalitions based on their expected information gain about the Shapley values. By the linearity of the Shapley values in the value function, we show that the expected information gain is available in closed form. Furthermore, we propose an efficient computation scheme that reduces the complexity from exponential to polynomial in the number of players via elementary symmetric polynomials. In extensive experiments across diverse costly applications, our method consistently improves sample efficiency in the low-budget regime over state-of-the-art baselines.

paragraphs: Shapley values assign credit to contributors by considering their roles across different groups, or coalitions. Computing them exactly becomes exponentially expensive as the number of contributors grows. ShaplEIG addresses situations where evaluating even one coalition is costly, making it important to choose a small evaluation budget carefully.

The method builds a Gaussian process surrogate for the expensive value function. It then adaptively selects the next coalition according to its expected information gain about the Shapley values, using earlier evaluations to guide later choices. Because Shapley values depend linearly on the value function, the authors derive this information gain in closed form.

They also use elementary symmetric polynomials to reduce the proposed computation from exponential to polynomial complexity in the number of contributors. Experiments cover costly applications including retraining-based feature importance, data valuation, and hyperparameter importance. ShaplEIG consistently improves sample efficiency over leading baselines when budgets are small. The contribution combines informed selection of evaluations with a tractable way to calculate which evaluation should be most informative.
summary.tldr: ShaplEIG adaptively chooses informative coalition evaluations to estimate Shapley values more efficiently under small evaluation budgets.

title: $\textttShaplEIG$: Bayesian Experimental Design for Shapley Value Estimation

abstract: Bayesian neural networks promise calibrated uncertainty but require $O(mn)$ parameters for standard mean-field Gaussian posteriors. We argue this cost is often unnecessary, particularly when weight matrices exhibit fast singular value decay. By parameterizing weights as $W = AB^{\top}$ with $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times r}$, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times r}$, we induce a posterior that is singular with respect to the Lebesgue measure, concentrating on the rank-$r$ manifold. This singularity captures structured weight correlations through shared latent factors, geometrically distinct from mean-field’s independence assumption. We derive PAC-Bayes generalization bounds whose complexity term scales as $\sqrt{r(m+n)}$ instead of $\sqrt{m n}$, and prove loss bounds that decompose the error into optimization and rank-induced bias using the Eckart-Young-Mirsky theorem. We further adapt recent Gaussian complexity bounds for low-rank deterministic networks to Bayesian predictive means. Empirically, across MLPs, LSTMs, and Transformers on standard benchmarks, our method achieves competitive predictive performance while using up to $33\times$ fewer parameters than 5-member Deep Ensembles. It substantially improves OOD detection and often improves calibration relative to mean-field and perturbation baselines, while Deep Ensembles can still be stronger on in-distribution likelihood-based metrics.

paragraphs: Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty over weights, but a standard independent Gaussian posterior requires parameters proportional to the full weight matrix. This paper instead expresses each matrix as a product of two smaller factors. Shared factors introduce structured correlations, and the resulting posterior concentrates on rank-r matrices rather than occupying the full weight space.

The authors motivate this restriction especially when singular values decay quickly, so low-rank structure can capture much of a matrix. Their PAC-Bayes bounds have a complexity term scaling as √(r(m+n)) rather than √(mn). Deep ensembles can still perform better on in-distribution likelihood metrics, making the findings a qualified tradeoff between compact uncertainty modeling and different measures of predictive quality.
summary.tldr: Low-rank Bayesian weight posteriors reduce parameter costs while capturing correlations and improving several uncertainty measures in reported experiments.

title: Singular Bayesian Neural Networks

abstract: While Large Language Models (LLMs) excel in language-based agentic tasks, their applicability to unseen, nonlinguistic environments (e.g., symbolic or spatial tasks) remains limited. Previous work attributes this performance gap to the mismatch between the pretraining distribution and the testing distribution. In this work, we demonstrate the primary bottleneck is the prohibitive cost of exploration: mastering these tasks requires extensive trial-and-error, which is computationally unsustainable for parameter-heavy LLMs operating in a high dimensional semantic space. To address this, we propose SCOUT (Sub-Scale Collaboration On Unseen Tasks), a novel framework that decouples exploration from exploitation. We employ lightweight "scouts" (e.g., small MLPs) to probe environmental dynamics at a speed and scale far exceeding LLMs. The collected trajectories are utilized to bootstrap the LLM via Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), followed by multi-turn Reinforcement Learning (RL) to activate its latent world knowledge. Empirically, SCOUT enables a Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct model to achieve an average score of 0.86, significantly outperforming proprietary models, including Gemini-2.5-Pro (0.60), while saving about 60% GPU hours consumption.

summary.tldr: SCOUT uses lightweight models to gather exploratory experience, then trains a language model on it to improve unfamiliar-task performance at lower computational cost.

title: Language-based Trial and Error Falls Behind in the Era of Experience

abstract: Model merging is a promising technique to enhance the capabilities of neural networks (NNs) by integrating multiple downstream fine-tuned models without requiring access to clients’ raw data or substantial computation resources. However, conventional model merging typically requires collecting the full set of fine-tuned model parameters from multiple clients, which may expose them to model-privacy risks. An emerging approach, known as partial model merging (PMM), mitigates this risk by splitting each model into private and shared parts, where only the shared part is merged while the private part remains local to each client. Despite its stricter parameter fusion, PMM can still achieve competitive performance compared to full-parameter sharing. However, the privacy properties of PMM remain underexplored. In this paper, we propose a novel model clone attack and assess the risk of reconstructing the unshared private part of a partially merged model under eight attack scenarios with varying prior knowledge (i.e., partial training data, model parameters and/or model structure). Our comprehensive experiments reveal that merging NNs without adequate protection is highly vulnerable. Even when only a small fraction of training data, model parameters, or model structure is exposed, adversaries can still recover significant portions of the private model’s performance.

paragraphs: Model merging combines capabilities from separately fine-tuned neural networks without collecting the clients’ original training data. Conventional merging nevertheless requires sharing complete model parameters, creating a different kind of privacy exposure. Partial model merging tries to reduce that exposure by keeping one part of each model local and merging only the shared part.

This paper investigates whether the withheld portion remains protected against cloning. The authors introduce an attack that attempts to reconstruct the private component and evaluate it under eight scenarios. These scenarios vary the attacker’s prior access to training examples, model parameters, and model structure. The study therefore examines protection under different kinds of partial knowledge.

The experiments find substantial vulnerability when merging lacks adequate protection. Even limited exposure of training data, parameters, or architecture can allow an attacker to recover significant portions of the private model’s performance. Recovering useful performance does not imply exact recovery of every hidden parameter. The practical finding is that withholding parameters alone can leave valuable model capabilities reproducible by an adversary.
summary.tldr: Experiments show that partial model sharing can still expose private model capabilities to cloning attacks with limited prior knowledge.

title: An Empirical Study on the Resilience of Partial Merging to Model Clone Attacks

abstract: Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) have recently demonstrated their proficiency in holistic visual comprehension. However, most of them struggle to tackle region-level perception guided by visual prompts, especially for cases where multiple regions are referred simultaneously, or scenarios where global contexts are necessary for precise visual referring. We introduce Contextual Latent Steering (CSteer), a training-free approach for guiding general LMMs to refer multiple regions contextually, without expensive fine-tuning or architectural modifications. CSteer starts with pre-computing contextual vectors that implicitly represent visual referring behaviors, such as differentiation among regions and attention to global contexts, followed by representation editing during inference time. Experimental results on multiple datasets indicate that general LMMs with CSteer outperform referring LMMs in most cases, suggesting a promising solution in training-free, and setting new state-of-the-art for this field. Code is available at https://github.com/xing0047/csteer.git.

paragraphs: CSteer addresses a gap between understanding an image as a whole and interpreting specific visually indicated regions. The problem becomes harder when several regions are referenced together or when understanding a region requires broader image context. General multimodal models can struggle with those demands despite strong holistic visual comprehension.

The method precomputes contextual vectors that implicitly encode useful referring behaviors. These include distinguishing between regions and attending to global context. During inference, it edits the model’s internal representations using those vectors. This steers an existing general model toward contextual region-level behavior without fine-tuning or changes to its architecture.

Across multiple datasets, the authors report that general multimodal models equipped with CSteer outperform specialized referring models in most cases and achieve new state-of-the-art results. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is not universal across every evaluated case. The findings suggest that representation editing can make existing visual abilities more useful for simultaneous, context-sensitive region references without requiring a separately trained referring model.
summary.tldr: CSteer edits internal representations at inference to improve contextual understanding of multiple image regions without additional training.

title: Referring Multiple Regions with Large Multimodal Models via Contextual Latent Steering

abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are playing an increasingly important role across multiple domains. In many applications, such as robotics, it is crucial to quantify the uncertainty in the output of these models. We develop Fused Uncertainty with Semantic Evidence (FUSE), a probabilistic framework for capturing two complementary sources of uncertainty in multimodal language modeling: (i) aleatoric embedding-level uncertainty derived from input data vision-language ambiguity, and (ii) epistemic model-level uncertainty estimated from the semantic response diversity of MLLMs. Our approach formulates a Bayesian fusion mechanism that analytically combines these uncertainty sources to produce a scalar measure of uncertainty. This measure serves as a novel uncertainty representation for downstream applications of MLLMs and provides a principled foundation for uncertainty calibration in multimodal systems, improving reliability and downstream performance in MLLM-based reasoning and vision-language tasks. We demonstrate that our method outperforms baselines in providing uncertainty estimates and achieves state-of-the-art uncertainty calibration.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can be uncertain for different reasons. An image and its accompanying language may be ambiguous, or the model itself may produce semantically different interpretations. FUSE treats these as complementary sources of uncertainty, aiming to provide a useful confidence signal for applications where the reliability of a model’s answer matters.

The framework estimates input-related, or aleatoric, uncertainty at the embedding level from vision-language ambiguity. It estimates model-related, or epistemic, uncertainty through the semantic diversity of generated responses. A Bayesian fusion mechanism analytically combines the two into a single scalar uncertainty measure. This connects information about the input with information about how consistently the model interprets it.

The authors report that FUSE outperforms baselines in uncertainty estimation and achieves state-of-the-art calibration. They also report improvements in reliability and downstream performance on reasoning and vision-language tasks. The contribution is therefore both a representation of uncertainty and a mechanism for combining its sources, supporting downstream systems that need more than the model’s final answer alone.
summary.tldr: FUSE combines input ambiguity and semantic response diversity through Bayesian fusion to improve vision-language uncertainty estimation.

title: FUSE: Quantifying Uncertainty in Vision-Language Models by Bayesian Fusing Epistemic and Aleatoric Uncertainty

abstract: Accurate nuclear instance segmentation is a pivotal task in computational pathology, supporting data-driven clinical insights and facilitating downstream translational applications. While large vision foundation models have shown promise for zero-shot biomedical segmentation, most existing approaches still depend on dense supervision and computationally expensive fine-tuning. Consequently, training-free methods present a compelling research direction, yet remain largely unexplored. In this work, we introduce SPROUT, a fully training- and annotation-free prompting framework for nuclear instance segmentation. SPROUT leverages histology-informed priors to construct slide-specific reference prototypes that mitigate domain gaps. These prototypes progressively guide feature alignment through a partial optimal transport scheme. The resulting foreground and background features are transformed into positive and negative point prompts, enabling the Segment Anything Model (SAM) to produce precise nuclear delineations without any parameter updates. Extensive experiments across multiple histopathology benchmarks demonstrate that SPROUT achieves competitive performance without supervision or retraining, establishing a novel paradigm for scalable, training-free nuclear instance segmentation in pathology. Code is available at https://github.com/Y-Research-SBU/SPROUT.

paragraphs: Nuclear instance segmentation identifies individual cell nuclei in pathology images. Although large vision models can help, adapting them often requires dense annotations and expensive fine-tuning. SPROUT proposes a framework that produces prompts for nuclear segmentation without training, annotations, or updates to model parameters.

These prototypes address differences between the slide’s appearance and the model’s representations, progressively guiding feature alignment through partial optimal transport. It shows how domain information can shape the inputs to an existing foundation model, allowing that model to perform the target segmentation task while its learned parameters remain fixed.
summary.tldr: SPROUT uses slide-specific prototypes to automatically prompt SAM for nuclear segmentation without annotations, training, or parameter updates.

title: Supervise Less, See More: Training-free Nuclear Instance Segmentation with Prototype-Guided Prompting

abstract: Parametric CAD is widely used in mechanical and product engineering, but current generative models still have difficulty producing assemblies that are both editable at the parameter level and consistent with inter-part constraints. Methods that generate meshes or history-free B-rep can represent multi-part shape, but they often lack the program structure and constraint logic needed for reliable downstream edits; in contrast, code-based CAD generation offers direct parametric control, yet most published settings and evaluations focus on single-part solids rather than constrained assemblies. We introduce SPADA (Self-testing Parametric Assembly Design Agent), a test-driven agent that synthesizes assembly code together with deterministic verification tests, and uses these tests as an executable contract for controllable generation. SPADA runs an iterative compile-test-repair loop with multimodal feedback, checking both specification logic and physical feasibility through programmatic constraints. To support evaluation, we release SPADA-Bench-Verified, a human-validated benchmark of real-world code-centric assemblies paired with deterministic tests and engineering-style constraints. Experiments show that SPADA could produces complex assemblies while maintaining geometric fidelity, supporting test-driven agents as a concrete path toward reliable, controllable CAD generation.

The paper highlights a gap between shape representations that lack program and constraint structure and code-based CAD research that has largely focused on individual solids.

SPADA generates assembly code together with deterministic tests that serve as an executable specification. It repeatedly compiles, tests, and repairs the result using multimodal feedback. Programmatic constraints check both the intended specification and physical feasibility, giving the agent concrete signals for revising an assembly while preserving controllable parameters.

The reported evidence concerns this demonstrated assembly-generation capability.
summary.tldr: SPADA generates editable CAD assembly code and deterministic tests, then uses a compile-test-repair loop to improve the result.

title: SPADA: A Verifiable Test-Driven Agent for Controllable Parametric CAD Assembly Generation

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed for knowledge synthesis, yet their capacity for compositional generalization in scientific knowledge remains under-characterized. Existing benchmarks primarily focus on single-turn restricted scenarios, failing to capture the capability boundaries exposed by real-world interactive scientific workflows. To address this, we introduce XDomainBench, a diagnostic benchmark for interactive interdisciplinary scientific reasoning. We formalize the composition order and mixture structure to enable systematic stress-testing from single-discipline to inter-disciplinary, comprising 8,598 interactive sessions across 20 domains and 4 task categories, with 8 realistic trajectory patterns covering difficulty and domain-mixture dynamics, simulating real AI4S scenarios. Large-scale evaluation of LLMs reveals a systematic reasoning collapse as composition order increases, stemming from two root causes: (i) direct difficulty increases induced by domain composition, and (ii) indirect interaction-amplified failures where trajectory patterns trigger error accumulation, reasoning breaks, and domain confusion, ultimately leading to session collapse.

paragraphs: Scientific knowledge synthesis can require combining ideas across disciplines over a sequence of interactions. The paper argues that restricted, single-turn benchmarks miss important capability boundaries in these workflows. XDomainBench is designed to test how language models handle increasing knowledge composition and changing domain mixtures throughout an interactive session.

The benchmark contains 8,598 sessions spanning 20 domains and four task categories. It formalizes composition order and mixture structure, allowing systematic tests from single-discipline work to interdisciplinary reasoning. Eight trajectory patterns vary difficulty and domain-mixture dynamics, making the progression of the interaction part of what is evaluated.

Large-scale evaluation reveals systematic reasoning collapse as composition order increases. The authors identify both direct difficulty from combining domains and failures amplified by interaction. Different trajectories can accumulate errors, interrupt reasoning, and produce domain confusion until a session collapses. The findings show why isolated answers provide an incomplete view of scientific synthesis: performance also depends on how knowledge requirements evolve and how earlier errors affect later reasoning.
summary.tldr: XDomainBench tests interactive scientific reasoning across disciplines and reveals reported collapse driven by composition difficulty and interaction-amplified errors.

title: XDomainBench: Diagnosing Reasoning Collapse in High-Dimensional Scientific Knowledge Composition

abstract: Game world modeling (GWM) and reinforcement learning (RL) are often confounded because research papers rarely quantify how difficult the underlying transition prediction problem is at the declared interface (pixels/tokens/latents with finite history). We propose the Transition Complexity Profile (TCP): a small, reproducible set of metrics that characterizes an environment’s (or gameplay dataset’s) induced transition kernel by (i) intrinsic one-step branching, (ii) interaction-induced uncertainty and opponent influence when observable, and (iii) temporal/spatial dependency span via standardized probe curves. TCP is reported with an explicit reference distribution, protocol stochasticity, and a versioned measurement budget (sampling/resampling and fixed probe compute), enabling comparable numbers across benchmarks. We outline how common game families and modern "neural game engine" domains populate this landscape and call for TCP to become standard benchmark metadata and a required statistic in GWM and RL papers.

paragraphs: This paper argues that research on game world models and reinforcement learning often leaves the difficulty of predicting environmental transitions unclear. That difficulty depends on the interface presented to a system, such as pixels, tokens, or latent representations, and on how much history it receives. Without measuring it, comparisons can conflate different underlying prediction problems.

The proposed Transition Complexity Profile summarizes three aspects of the transition process. It measures how many possible next-step outcomes arise intrinsically, uncertainty introduced by interaction and observable opponent influence, and the temporal or spatial reach of dependencies. Standardized probe curves are used to characterize that dependency span. The profile can describe either an environment or a gameplay dataset.

Comparable measurement also requires reporting the reference distribution, randomness in the protocol, and a versioned budget for sampling and probe computation. These details make the profile tied to an explicit measurement procedure. The authors discuss how game families and neural game-engine settings fit this landscape, and call for the profile to become standard benchmark metadata and a required reported statistic.
summary.tldr: The proposed Transition Complexity Profile would make game-transition prediction difficulty explicit and more comparable across benchmarks.

abstract: Relational data appear frequently in many machine learning applications. Relational data consist of the pairwise relations (similarities or dissimilarities) between each pair of implicit objects, and are usually stored in relation matrices and typically no other knowledge is available. Although relational clustering can be formulated as graph partitioning in some applications, this formulation is not adequate for general relational data. In this paper, we propose a general model for relational clustering based on symmetric convex coding. The model is applicable to all types of relational data and unifies the existing graph partitioning formulation. Under this model, we derive two alternative bound optimization algorithms to solve the symmetric convex coding under two popular distance functions, Euclidean distance and generalized I-divergence. Experimental evaluation and theoretical analysis show the effectiveness and great potential of the proposed model and algorithms.

paragraphs: The paper considers clustering when the available data describe only pairwise similarities or dissimilarities between objects. Such relations are stored in a matrix, and separate descriptions of the objects may be unavailable. Although graph partitioning can express some relational clustering problems, the authors argue that it is inadequate as a general formulation.

They propose symmetric convex coding as a general model for relational clustering. The model is presented as applicable to all types of relational data and as unifying the existing graph partitioning formulation. This places graph-based clustering within a broader framework for working directly with relation matrices.

The authors derive two alternative bound-optimization algorithms, using Euclidean distance and generalized I-divergence respectively. These provide concrete procedures for solving the coding problem under two different distance functions. Experimental evaluation and theoretical analysis support the effectiveness and potential of the model and algorithms. The contribution therefore joins a general formulation with optimization methods for learning clusters from pairwise information.
summary.tldr: Symmetric convex coding provides a general relational clustering framework that includes graph partitioning and supports two bound-optimization algorithms.

title: Relational clustering by symmetric convex coding

abstract: We study the problem of discovering a manifold that best preserves information relevant to a nonlinear regression. Solving this problem involves extending and uniting two threads of research. On the one hand, the literature on sufficient dimension reduction has focused on methods for finding the best linear subspace for nonlinear regression; we extend this to manifolds. On the other hand, the literature on manifold learning has focused on unsupervised dimensionality reduction; we extend this to the supervised setting. Our approach to solving the problem involves combining the machinery of kernel dimension reduction with Laplacian eigenmaps. Specifically, we optimize cross-covariance operators in kernel feature spaces that are induced by the normalized graph Laplacian. The result is a highly flexible method in which no strong assumptions are made on the regression function or on the distribution of the covariates. We illustrate our methodology on the analysis of global temperature data and image manifolds.

paragraphs: The paper asks how to discover a manifold that preserves information useful for nonlinear regression. This brings prediction into dimensionality reduction: the desired representation should retain what matters for the regression problem. The authors connect sufficient dimension reduction, traditionally focused on linear subspaces, with manifold learning, traditionally focused on unsupervised representations.

Their method combines kernel dimension reduction with Laplacian eigenmaps. More specifically, it optimizes cross-covariance operators in kernel feature spaces constructed from the normalized graph Laplacian. This mathematical combination makes the learned manifold sensitive to the supervised regression objective, extending the representation beyond the linear-subspace setting.

The approach is described as flexible because it makes no strong assumptions about either the regression function or the distribution of the input variables. The authors illustrate it using global temperature data and image manifolds. These applications demonstrate the methodology's use in finding representations organized around predictive information, bringing the geometry of the data and the needs of regression into one procedure.
summary.tldr: Combining kernel dimension reduction with Laplacian eigenmaps yields supervised manifolds designed to preserve information relevant to nonlinear regression.

title: Regression on manifolds using kernel dimension reduction

abstract: We address the problem of learning classifiers for a large number of tasks. We derive a solution that produces resampling weights which match the pool of all examples to the target distribution of any given task. Our work is motivated by the problem of predicting the outcome of a therapy attempt for a patient who carries an HIV virus with a set of observed genetic properties. Such predictions need to be made for hundreds of possible combinations of drugs, some of which use similar biochemical mechanisms. Multi-task learning enables us to make predictions even for drug combinations with few or no training examples and substantially improves the overall prediction accuracy.
originalAbstract: We address the problem of learning classifiers for a large number of tasks. We derive a solution that produces resampling weights which match the pool of all examples to the target distribution of any given task. Our work is motivated by the problem of predicting the outcome of a therapy attempt for a patient who carries an HIV virus with a set of observed genetic properties. Such predictions need to be made for hundreds of possible combinations of drugs, some of which use similar biochemical mechanisms. Multi-task learning enables us to make predictions even for drug combinations with few or no training examples and substantially improves the overall prediction accuracy.

paragraphs: The paper addresses classification across a large number of related tasks, motivated by predicting HIV therapy outcomes. A prediction depends on observed genetic properties of a patient's virus and the drug combination being considered. Hundreds of combinations create many prediction tasks, and some combinations have few or no training examples of their own.

The proposed solution produces resampling weights that make the pooled examples match the target distribution of a given task. This allows data collected across tasks to contribute according to their relevance to the particular prediction problem. The application also contains relationships between therapies, since some drug combinations act through similar biochemical mechanisms.

The authors report that multi-task learning enables predictions for combinations with little or no direct training data and substantially improves overall prediction accuracy. The important connection is between sharing examples and adapting that shared pool to each target task. The reported outcome concerns predictive performance in therapy screening, showing how related tasks can provide useful information when individual combinations are sparsely represented.
summary.tldr: Task-specific resampling of pooled data improves HIV therapy outcome prediction and supports drug combinations with few or no training examples.

title: Multi-task learning for HIV therapy screening

abstract: We propose a family of supervised dimensionality reduction (SDR) algorithms that combine feature extraction (dimensionality reduction) with learning a predictive model in a unified optimization framework, using data- and class-appropriate generalized linear models (GLMs), and handling both classification and regression problems. Our approach uses simple closed-form update rules and is provably convergent. Promising empirical results are demonstrated on a variety of high-dimensional datasets.
originalAbstract: We propose a family of supervised dimensionality reduction (SDR) algorithms that combine feature extraction (dimensionality reduction) with learning a predictive model in a unified optimization framework, using data- and class-appropriate generalized linear models (GLMs), and handling both classification and regression problems. Our approach uses simple closed-form update rules and is provably convergent. Promising empirical results are demonstrated on a variety of high-dimensional datasets.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning from high-dimensional data by combining the search for a compact representation with the training of a predictor. Its supervised dimensionality reduction framework places feature extraction and prediction inside one optimization problem. This makes the representation part of the predictive learning task, so the two components are learned together.

The framework uses generalized linear models chosen to suit the data and prediction target. It covers both classification and regression, giving a family of algorithms rather than a method tied to just one kind of output. The unifying idea is to coordinate dimensionality reduction with the statistical model used for prediction.

The algorithms have simple closed-form update rules and a proof of convergence. Closed-form updates describe how individual optimization steps are computed; the convergence result addresses the behavior of the overall procedure. Experiments on several high-dimensional datasets provide promising empirical results. Together, the stated contributions combine a unified learning formulation, manageable updates, and theoretical support for the optimization process.
summary.tldr: The paper jointly learns compact representations and GLM predictors using closed-form updates with a convergence guarantee.

title: Closed-form supervised dimensionality reduction with generalized linear models

abstract: Multi-view learning has become a hot topic during the past few years. In this paper, we first characterize the sample complexity of multi-view active learning . Under the α-expansion assumption, we get an exponential improvement in the sample complexity from usual Õ(1/ε) to Õ(log 1/ε), requiring neither strong assumption on data distribution such as the data is distributed uniformly over the unit sphere in ℜ d nor strong assumption on hypothesis class such as linear separators through the origin. We also give an upper bound of the error rate when the α-expansion assumption does not hold. Then, we analyze the combination of multi-view active learning and semi-supervised learning and get a further improvement in the sample complexity. Finally, we study the empirical behavior of the two paradigms, which verifies that the combination of multi-view active learning and semi-supervised learning is efficient.
originalAbstract: Multi-view learning has become a hot topic during the past few years. In this paper, we first characterize the sample complexity of multi-view active learning . Under the α-expansion assumption, we get an exponential improvement in the sample complexity from usual Õ(1/ε) to Õ(log 1/ε), requiring neither strong assumption on data distribution such as the data is distributed uniformly over the unit sphere in ℜ d nor strong assumption on hypothesis class such as linear separators through the origin. We also give an upper bound of the error rate when the α-expansion assumption does not hold. Then, we analyze the combination of multi-view active learning and semi-supervised learning and get a further improvement in the sample complexity. Finally, we study the empirical behavior of the two paradigms, which verifies that the combination of multi-view active learning and semi-supervised learning is efficient.

paragraphs: The paper studies how many labeled examples multi-view active learning needs to reach a target error rate. Its main theoretical result holds under an alpha-expansion assumption. With that assumption, the sample complexity improves from roughly inverse dependence on the target error to logarithmic dependence, with additional logarithmic factors suppressed in the stated notation.

The authors describe this as an exponential improvement. Their result does not require the particular strong restrictions mentioned in the abstract, such as uniformly distributed data on a unit sphere or classifiers restricted to linear separators through the origin. It still depends on alpha-expansion. When that assumption fails, the paper separately supplies an upper bound on the error rate.

The authors then analyze combining multi-view active learning with semi-supervised learning and obtain a further sample-complexity improvement. They also study the combination empirically and report evidence of its efficiency. The contribution thus connects a conditional theoretical reduction in label requirements with experimental support for using the two learning paradigms together.
summary.tldr: Under alpha-expansion, multi-view active learning sharply reduces label requirements, with further gains from combining it with semi-supervised learning.

title: On multi-view active learning and the combination with semi-supervised learning

abstract: Most prior work on active learning of classifiers has focused on sequentially selecting one unlabeled example at a time to be labeled in order to reduce the overall labeling effort. In many scenarios, however, it is desirable to label an entire batch of examples at once, for example, when labels can be acquired in parallel. This motivates us to study batch active learning, which iteratively selects batches of k>1 examples to be labeled. We propose a novel batch active learning method that leverages the availability of high-quality and efficient sequential active-learning policies by attempting to approximate their behavior when applied for k steps. Specifically, our algorithm first uses Monte-Carlo simulation to estimate the distribution of unlabeled examples selected by a sequential policy over k step executions. The algorithm then attempts to select a set of k examples that best matches this distribution, leading to a combinatorial optimization problem that we term “bounded coordinated matching'. While we show this problem is NP-hard in general, we give an efficient greedy solution, which inherits approximation bounds from supermodular minimization theory. Our experimental results on eight benchmark datasets show that the proposed approach is highly effective

paragraphs: Active learning chooses which examples should be labeled to reduce labeling effort. Sequential methods choose one example at a time, using each new answer to guide the next choice. When labels can be obtained in parallel, selecting an entire batch is more convenient, but it removes the opportunity to respond to answers within that batch.

This paper builds a batch method around existing sequential policies. It uses Monte Carlo simulation to estimate which examples a sequential policy would select across several steps. It then seeks a batch whose collection of examples matches that estimated selection distribution. The objective is to approximate the behavior of an effective sequential policy when several labeling requests must be issued together.

The resulting selection problem, called bounded coordinated matching, is NP-hard in general. The authors provide an efficient greedy solution with approximation bounds inherited from supermodular minimization theory. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets show that the approach is highly effective, supporting simulation and coordinated selection as a practical route from sequential policies to batch learning.
summary.tldr: A batch active-learning method simulates sequential selection and uses coordinated matching to choose effective groups of labeling requests.

title: Batch Active Learning via Coordinated Matching

abstract: We develop dependent hierarchical normalized random measures and apply them to dynamic topic modeling. The dependency arises via superposition, subsampling and point transition on the underlying Poisson processes of these measures. The measures used include normalised generalised Gamma processes that demonstrate power law properties, unlike Dirichlet processes used previously in dynamic topic modeling. Inference for the model includes adapting a recently developed slice sampler to directly manipulate the underlying Poisson process. Experiments performed on news, blogs, academic and Twitter collections demonstrate the technique gives superior perplexity over a number of previous models.
originalAbstract: We develop dependent hierarchical normalized random measures and apply them to dynamic topic modeling. The dependency arises via superposition, subsampling and point transition on the underlying Poisson processes of these measures. The measures used include normalised generalised Gamma processes that demonstrate power law properties, unlike Dirichlet processes used previously in dynamic topic modeling. Inference for the model includes adapting a recently developed slice sampler to directly manipulate the underlying Poisson process. Experiments performed on news, blogs, academic and Twitter collections demonstrate the technique gives superior perplexity over a number of previous models.

paragraphs: Dynamic topic modeling represents topical content together with its changing structure. This paper develops dependent hierarchical normalized random measures for that purpose. The main modeling idea is to connect the underlying random measures, giving the topic model a probabilistic mechanism for dependency rather than treating its components as unrelated.

The dependencies are constructed through superposition, subsampling, and transitions of points in underlying Poisson processes. These operations combine processes, select parts of them, and move their points. The family includes normalized generalized Gamma processes with power-law properties, which the authors distinguish from the Dirichlet processes previously used for dynamic topic modeling. This expands the kinds of statistical behavior available to the model.

For inference, the authors adapt a slice sampler to work directly with the underlying Poisson process. Experiments span news, blogs, academic material, and Twitter collections. The method achieves better perplexity than several previous models on those collections. The reported evidence therefore supports improved probabilistic modeling of text across multiple sources, alongside the new construction of dependent measures.
summary.tldr: Dependent random measures with power-law properties support dynamic topic models that improve perplexity over several previous models.

title: Dependent Hierarchical Normalized Random Measures for Dynamic Topic Modeling
